passages.title: Anna Atkins's cyanotypes of algae
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In October 1843 the English botanist Anna Atkins issued the first part of Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions, which she printed privately. None of its plates was made with a camera. Atkins laid dried seaweeds directly on paper coated with iron salts and left the sheets in sunlight; the exposed coating turned a deep Prussian blue, the areas shielded by the specimens remained pale, and a rinse in plain water fixed the image. The process had been announced only the year before by the astronomer John Herschel, a friend of Atkins's family. Over the following decade she added several hundred plates, and the work is often described as the first book to be illustrated with photographic images.

Atkins's purpose was emphatically scientific. Her volumes were meant to accompany a recent, unillustrated manual of British seaweeds, and she explained that she had turned to Herschel's process because accurate drawings of such small and intricate organisms were extremely difficult to make. A drawing, however skilled, passes through the judgment of the hand that makes it; a cyanotype records the outline of the specimen itself.

In recent decades, however, the plates have moved from natural history libraries to art museums, and with the move has come a new interpretation. Some critics now present Atkins as a precursor of modernism, pointing to the resemblance between her pale forms suspended in fields of saturated blue and the camera-less photograms that artists such as Man Ray and László Moholy-Nagy produced in the 1920s. On this view, her achievement lies chiefly in anticipating an abstract visual language that art would not fully claim for another eighty years.

This reading has the merit of attending to qualities that histories of photography, long preoccupied with the camera, largely ignored. Yet it locates the source of those qualities in the wrong place. The features that make the plates look modern are, for the most part, consequences of Atkins's scientific commitments rather than departures from them. The flatness that critics admire as a refusal of illusionistic depth is just what a taxonomist wants from a record of a specimen's form, and the empty ground on which each specimen seems to float, read by some as an abstraction from any setting, is the convention of the botanical plate. Nor was the intense blue an expressive decision; once Atkins had adopted Herschel's process, the color was dictated by chemistry. To be sure, the placement of each specimen, and the spreading of its fronds so that their branching would register clearly, reflect deliberate and often elegant decisions. But those decisions served legibility first. The plates are best understood not as early abstractions that happen to depict seaweed but as scientific documents whose beauty followed, in large part, from the demands of accuracy.

passages.title: Genericness and the primary significance test
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Trademark law protects words that identify the source of a product, but it denies protection to words that name the product itself. A term that begins as a brand may therefore lose its protection if the public comes to use it as the ordinary name for the kind of thing it once distinguished, the fate of "aspirin," "escalator," and "thermos," among others. Under United States law, the question in such cases is the term's "primary significance" to the relevant public: if most consumers understand it to denote a category of goods rather than a particular producer, the mark is generic and anyone may use it. Courts often answer it with surveys that ask respondents to sort a list of terms into brand names and common names.

The legal scholar Teresa Halvorsen argues that this inquiry asks consumers a question their language cannot answer. People, she observes, routinely use a single word in both ways. A shopper may ask for "a band-aid" without caring who made it and yet, shown two boxes, recognize Band-Aid as one company's product; a person who says she will "google" a restaurant may well know that Google is a particular firm. Such speakers do not hold one meaning primarily and the other secondarily; they hold both, moving between them as context requires. A survey that forces a single classification therefore manufactures a primary significance where none exists, and its outcome may depend as much on the framing of the question as on what consumers believe.

Halvorsen proposes that courts set aside the question of meaning and ask instead whether competitors need the term to tell consumers what they are selling. The rule's point, on her account, is not to track usage for its own sake but to prevent a single firm from monopolizing the only practical name for a product. Where rivals can describe their goods intelligibly without the disputed word, the mark should survive, however casually the public uses it; where they cannot, it should fall, even if many consumers still associate the word with its owner.

Much of Halvorsen's critique of the survey method is persuasive: surveys do extract from consumers a ranking of meanings their usage does not contain, and the genericness rule does exist to protect competition rather than to referee shoppers' vocabulary. Her alternative, however, is less independent of public meaning than she supposes. Whether a rival can describe its product intelligibly without the disputed word depends on which alternative words the public understands, so the test reintroduces the inquiry into usage it was meant to replace, in a less disciplined form, since nothing comparable to a survey anchors it.

passages.title: Automatic enrollment in retirement savings plans
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

For decades, policy aimed at increasing retirement saving in the United States relied on information and incentives: employers explained the advantages of their savings plans, and the tax code rewarded participation. Yet participation in voluntary plans, which required employees to sign up, remained stubbornly low, especially among younger and lower-paid workers. An influential 2001 study by the economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea suggested that the obstacle was less a matter of preference than of inertia. At a large firm that changed its plan so that new employees were enrolled automatically unless they chose to opt out, participation among new hires rose from well under half to a large majority, even though the financial terms of the plan were unchanged.

The lesson many economists have drawn is that the design of the default matters a great deal precisely because so many people never get around to making an active decision. If so, making enrollment the default overrides no one's preferences. Those who would have enrolled anyway lose nothing; those who would want to save but postpone the paperwork indefinitely find that their inaction now works in their favor rather than against them; and those who prefer not to participate remain free to leave the plan at the cost of a form. Policymakers on both sides of the Atlantic took note. The Pension Protection Act of 2006 encouraged employers to adopt automatic enrollment, and in 2012 the United Kingdom began requiring employers to enroll eligible workers automatically in workplace pensions. Measured by the share of eligible workers who participate, the results have been striking, and they have been achieved at very little public cost.

Passage B

Automatic enrollment is often presented as a costless correction: those who would have joined anyway are unaffected, and those who would have drifted are rescued from their own procrastination. But a default does more than break ties in favor of action. Employees commonly read it as advice, inferring that the contribution rate and investment fund their employer has selected are the ones it judges appropriate. Studies of automatically enrolled workers have found that many remain at the default contribution rate for years, and that some who would have enrolled at a higher rate under a voluntary plan instead settle at the default's lower one. A default chosen to keep participation high, as a low rate does, can thus reduce the saving of the very workers most inclined to save.

None of this argues for a return to voluntary enrollment, whose failures are real. It argues for treating the choice of a default as a substantive judgment about what employees ought to save, made and revised on that basis, rather than as a neutral device for overcoming inertia. Some plans now raise the default rate automatically each year unless the employee objects, an arrangement that keeps the power of inertia while directing it toward an adequate level of saving.

passages.title: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
For roughly three million years, Earth's climate has alternated between glacial periods and warmer interglacials. Recorded in the chemistry of tiny shells in deep-sea sediments, these alternations at first followed orbital theory closely: glaciations came and went about every 41,000 years, the period over which the tilt of Earth's axis varies, altering the summer sunlight reaching high northern latitudes. Between about 1.2 million and 700,000 years ago, however, the cycles lengthened to roughly 100,000 years, and the ice sheets grew markedly larger. Because Earth's orbit underwent no corresponding change, this shift, the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, is generally thought to have originated within the climate system.

One proposal locates the cause beneath the ice. Before the transition, on this hypothesis, the northern continents were mantled by a thick layer of regolith, soil and weathered rock built up over long ice-free ages. Ice on such soft, wet material slides readily, so ice sheets stayed thin and vulnerable to each rise in summer sunlight. Repeated glaciations, however, scraped the layer away, exposing hard bedrock. Ice gripping bedrock flows more slowly and can grow far thicker, and a thick ice sheet can outlast a warm orbital phase.

A second hypothesis looks to the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide concentrations, on this account, declined gradually over the Pleistocene, allowing ice sheets to survive summer warmth that would earlier have melted them. A separate proposal, which takes no position on what caused the change, holds that a 100,000-year rhythm need not reflect any 100,000-year cause: if large ice sheets collapse only when a peak in summer sunlight arrives while they are near the limit of their stability, deglaciations would follow every second or third tilt cycle, yielding an average interval near 100,000 years. Many proponents of the carbon dioxide account have adopted this idea. Their hypothesis has nonetheless been hard to test, because direct records of ancient air from Antarctic ice have only recently begun to reach back to the transition.

Neither hypothesis has won general acceptance. Skeptics of the regolith account note that it explains why ice sheets grew thicker and more durable but not why they retreated about every 100,000 years. Skeptics of the carbon dioxide account reply that a gradual decline could produce a fairly rapid reorganization only by crossing some threshold, which no one has yet specified. Some researchers have suggested that the two mechanisms operated together, one making thicker ice possible and the other setting the pace of its retreat. The regolith account does make one distinctive prediction: the change in ice behavior should be preceded or accompanied by a shift in glacial debris from weathered-soil material to fresh-bedrock material. Because thicker ice might itself have scoured more deeply, however, a shift in the debris would not by itself show which change came first.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The qualities that have led some critics to treat Atkins's plates as anticipations of modernist abstraction derive largely from the scientific aims the plates served.
Critics who regard Atkins as a precursor of modernism have correctly identified an abstract visual language that her plates share with the photograms of the 1920s.
Atkins's Photographs of British Algae, though produced for a scientific purpose, deserves recognition chiefly as the first book illustrated with photographic images.
The resemblance between Atkins's plates and later modernist photograms is a coincidence that reveals nothing of interest about the plates themselves.
Critics who see Atkins as a precursor of modernism have mistaken products of scientific necessity for artistic choices, since her plates reflect no aesthetic decisions of her own.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the features that make the plates look modern are 'for the most part' consequences of Atkins's scientific commitments, and the last sentence says their beauty followed 'in large part' from accuracy. A states that claim with its qualifier. E is the near-miss: it captures the scientific-origin point but leaves no room for the author's qualifier and contradicts the concession that her arrangements 'reflect deliberate and often elegant decisions'; D overstates the author's rejection, since the author credits the reading with attending to real qualities.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about Atkins's plates and the modernist reading of them.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (the critics' reading) and paragraph 4, especially its first three sentences and its last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Paragraphs 1 and 2 are background: what Atkins made and why. Paragraph 3 gives the critics' view (Atkins as proto-modernist). Paragraph 4 is where the author speaks: the critics see something real but 'locate the source of those qualities in the wrong place.' The look of the plates comes mostly from their scientific job, though her arrangements were deliberate. We need an answer that says: the plates' modern-looking qualities come largely from their scientific purpose. Two traps to expect: one that drops 'largely' and one that turns 'wrong source' into 'nothing to see here.'

choices.note: CORRECT. It names the critics' reading, says the qualities they admire come from scientific aims, and keeps the author's 'largely' ('for the most part,' 'in large part').
This is the critics' view from paragraph 3. The author says the reading 'locates the source of those qualities in the wrong place.' Wrong party.
The 'first book' claim is a background fact from paragraph 1, and the passage never says that is what she deserves recognition for 'chiefly.'

Too strong in the other direction. The author credits the reading with 'the merit of attending to qualities' that others ignored and calls the plates beautiful. The author disputes where those qualities come from, not whether they matter.

Tempting: its first half is very close to the author's thesis. But the second half denies that Atkins made any aesthetic decisions, while the author says 'for the most part' and grants that the placement of specimens reflects 'deliberate and often elegant decisions.' The missing qualifier sinks it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the cyanotype process that Atkins used
choices: had been devised by Atkins herself after she found that drawings of algae were unreliable
had been made public only a short time before Atkins began issuing her work
produced images whose color varied with the length of time the sheets were left in sunlight
was first used by Herschel to record astronomical observations before Atkins adapted it to botany
was developed by Herschel specifically so that botanists could record the outlines of specimens accurately
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the process 'had been announced only the year before' by Herschel, and Atkins issued the first part in 1843, so B paraphrases the text. E is the most tempting: the passage links the process to accurate outlines, but as Atkins's reason for choosing it (second paragraph), not as Herschel's reason for inventing it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage actually says about the cyanotype process.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, the sentences about the iron-salt paper and Herschel's announcement; paragraph 2 for why Atkins used it.

breakdown.analysis: Plain detail question. Paragraph 1: the paper was coated with iron salts, exposed to sunlight, turned blue where exposed, and was fixed by rinsing. Herschel 'announced' the process 'only the year before' Atkins's 1843 first part. Paragraph 2: Atkins chose it because accurate drawings were hard to make. Look for a paraphrase, and keep track of whose purpose is whose.

choices.note: Wrong person. Herschel announced the process; Atkins 'turned to Herschel's process.' The passage never says she invented anything.
CORRECT. 'Announced only the year before' becomes 'made public only a short time before.'
Never stated. The passage says exposed areas turned blue and shielded areas stayed pale; nothing about color changing with exposure time.
Plausible, since Herschel was an astronomer. But the passage says only that he announced the process; nothing about how, or whether, he used it himself.

Tempting, because accurate outlines are exactly why the process suited a botanist. But that's Atkins's reason for turning to it (paragraph 2). The passage says nothing about why Herschel developed it. Right idea, wrong party.

questions.stem: In saying that the color of Atkins's plates 'was dictated by chemistry' (fourth paragraph), the author most probably means that the color
choices: was a necessary result of the process Atkins used rather than an expression of her preference
was prescribed in advance by the conventions that governed botanical plates in Atkins's time
was set out in written instructions that Herschel supplied to Atkins when he first shared his new process with her
was heightened by Atkins through a chemical treatment that she applied to each sheet after it had been exposed
was regarded by Atkins herself as a minor and somewhat regrettable feature of the finished plates
questions.explanation: In the fourth paragraph the author traces features critics read as artistic choices to scientific constraints; the blue came from the iron-salt chemistry described in the first paragraph, not from Atkins's taste. A captures that. B is the near-miss: the preceding sentence invokes 'the convention of the botanical plate,' but to explain the empty ground, not the blue; C takes 'dictated' in its literal sense of instructions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out what 'dictated by chemistry, not chosen' means as used here.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the sentences on flatness and the empty ground and the sentence on the blue; paragraph 1 for how the blue arises.

breakdown.analysis: Why would the author say the color was 'dictated'? The sentence opens 'Nor was the intense blue an expressive decision.' Because critics treat the saturated blue fields as an artistic move. The author's point: the cyanotype process turns exposed paper blue, period. So 'dictated' means 'determined' or 'made unavoidable.' Meaning-in-context questions love to offer the dictionary meaning of the word as a trap.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Dictated by chemistry' = forced by the process; 'not an expressive decision' = not her preference.
Tempting because the sentence just before mentions 'the convention of the botanical plate.' But that convention explains the empty ground around each specimen. The blue is pinned on chemistry.
This is the dictionary sense of 'dictated' (spoken or written out for someone to follow). The author means 'determined,' not literally instructed.
Specific but unsupported. The only treatment the passage mentions is a rinse in plain water to fix the image, and the author's point is that the color wasn't hers to adjust.
The passage never says how Atkins felt about the blue. 'Dictated' is about cause, not about her opinion of it.

questions.stem: The author mentions Man Ray and László Moholy-Nagy (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: identify later artists whose camera-less photographs were directly influenced by Atkins's cyanotypes
suggest that the photogram was not recognized as an artistic medium until the twentieth century
contrast scientific and artistic uses of camera-less photography
indicate the basis of a comparison on which a recent interpretation relies
provide evidence that Atkins intended her plates to be appreciated as works of art
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that some critics present Atkins as a precursor of modernism by 'pointing to the resemblance' between her plates and the 1920s photograms of these two artists, so D is right. A is the most tempting: the passage speaks of resemblance and anticipation, never of influence. E fails because the author argues the plates were scientific in purpose.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the two artists are named: what job the reference does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Who brings up Man Ray and Moholy-Nagy? The critics, not the author. They point to the resemblance between Atkins's blue plates and those artists' 1920s photograms to argue that she anticipated modernism. So the names show what the critics' comparison is based on. Ask 'why is this here?' rather than 'what does it say?'

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a natural reason to name later artists. But the passage says 'resemblance' and 'anticipating,' never influence. Nothing says these artists saw Atkins's work.
The critics say art would not 'fully claim' abstraction for eighty years, but the names aren't there to date when photograms were recognized as art. That isn't the job of the reference.
The author does draw a scientific-versus-artistic line, but in paragraph 4, and not by means of these artists. The names appear only as the critics' point of comparison.
CORRECT. The names supply the other half of the critics' comparison: Atkins's plates look like these artists' photograms.
The opposite of the author's view. Paragraph 2 says Atkins's purpose was 'emphatically scientific,' and the artists are mentioned in the critics' argument, not as evidence of her intentions.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude toward the interpretation of Atkins's work presented in the third paragraph?
choices: appreciation for the attention it draws to the plates' visual qualities, together with doubt about its explanation of those qualities
unqualified rejection of its claim that the plates have real aesthetic value
cautious acceptance of its central claim, tempered by concern that it neglects Atkins's own contributions to the scientific classification of algae
indifference to its conclusions, on the grounds that questions about artistic influence lie outside the history of photography
admiration for its insight into Atkins's intentions, mixed with regret that it has drawn the plates away from libraries
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph opens by crediting the reading with 'the merit of attending to qualities' earlier histories ignored, then says it 'locates the source of those qualities in the wrong place.' A captures both halves. C is the near-miss: it has the right mixed shape, but the author does not accept the reading's central claim (that her achievement lies chiefly in anticipating abstraction), and the passage never mentions her contributions to classification.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down how the author feels about the critics' modernist reading.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First two sentences of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Is the author for or against the critics? Both, in different ways. 'This reading has the merit of attending to qualities that histories of photography... largely ignored' is praise. 'Yet it locates the source of those qualities in the wrong place' is the criticism. So we need a two-part attitude: credit for noticing the look of the plates, skepticism about why they look that way. Attitude answers on the LSAT are usually mixed and moderate; be suspicious of 'unqualified' anything.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Appreciation for the attention it draws' matches 'the merit of attending to qualities'; 'doubt about its explanation' matches 'locates the source... in the wrong place.'
Too strong, and it gets the target wrong. The author never denies the plates have striking visual qualities.

Tempting because it is mixed, like the right answer. But the author doesn't accept the central claim that her achievement lies chiefly in anticipating abstraction, and the passage says nothing about her contributions to classifying algae.
The author clearly engages with the reading and takes a position on it. 'Indifference' is wrong, and the stated grounds appear nowhere.
The author thinks the reading misreads her purpose, so 'insight into Atkins's intentions' is backwards. The move to museums is reported neutrally, without regret.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Earlier histories of photography were right to concentrate on images made with a camera rather than on camera-less processes.
Atkins's plates would have been of greater value to botanists had she drawn her specimens rather than printing them directly.
Some features of Atkins's plates that might be taken for aesthetic choices actually reflect conventions of scientific illustration.
The photograms that artists produced in the 1920s owed their abstract character chiefly to the demands of scientific accuracy.
Atkins arranged her specimens chiefly to produce visually striking compositions, accepting some loss of scientific legibility.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the empty ground around each specimen, 'read by some as an abstraction from any setting,' is 'the convention of the botanical plate'; C generalizes that point modestly with 'some features.' D is tempting because it borrows the author's scientific explanation, but it applies it to the 1920s artists, about whom the author says nothing of the kind. E reverses the priority: the arrangements were 'often elegant' but 'served legibility first.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage supports about Atkins's plates or their interpreters.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially the sentence about flatness and the empty ground, and the sentences about arrangement.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase; the right answer could come from anywhere in paragraph 4. Watch for answers that shift the author's explanation to the wrong group (the 1920s artists) or push a point too far. What does the author actually commit to? That the modern-looking features came mostly from scientific needs: flatness for taxonomy, the empty ground from botanical-plate convention, the blue from chemistry. And that her arrangements were deliberate and 'often elegant' but 'served legibility first.'

choices.note: The opposite. The author credits the modernist reading for attending to qualities that histories 'long preoccupied with the camera' ignored. That's a mild criticism of the earlier focus, not an endorsement.
Reverses paragraph 2. Atkins turned to cyanotypes because accurate drawings were hard to make, and the author says a cyanotype records 'the outline of the specimen itself.'
CORRECT. The empty ground looks like an aesthetic choice to some critics but is 'the convention of the botanical plate.' 'Some features' keeps it safely modest.

Tempting, because it uses the author's own explanation. But the author applies that explanation only to Atkins's plates. Nothing is said about where the 1920s artists' abstraction came from. Wrong subject.
Tempting, because the author does call her arrangements 'deliberate and often elegant.' But it reverses the priority: 'those decisions served legibility first.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Courts should replace the primary significance test for genericness with an inquiry into whether competitors need a disputed term to describe their own products.
Because consumers use many trademarks in two ways, courts cannot reliably decide whether a mark is generic.
Halvorsen's proposal to focus on the needs of competitors would give trademark owners stronger protection than they now receive under the primary significance test.
The surveys that courts use to decide whether a mark is generic are flawed chiefly because their results depend on the way in which their questions are framed.
Halvorsen's objections to the survey-based inquiry are largely sound, but her alternative remains more dependent on public understanding of words than she recognizes.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph calls much of Halvorsen's critique of surveys 'persuasive' but says her alternative 'is less independent of public meaning than she supposes.' E states both halves in new words. A is Halvorsen's proposal, which the author only partly accepts, and D is one supporting point from the second paragraph, overstated with 'chiefly.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's overall position on Halvorsen's critique and proposal.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences; paragraphs 2 and 3 for what Halvorsen says.

breakdown.analysis: Whose views are where? Paragraph 1 is background (the rule and the surveys). Paragraph 2 is Halvorsen's critique. Paragraph 3 is her proposed test. Paragraph 4 is the author: her critique is 'persuasive,' but her alternative 'is less independent of public meaning than she supposes.' We need: she's right about the problem; her fix still depends on what words mean to the public. A main point has to include the author's own verdict, not just a summary of the scholar.

choices.note: Halvorsen's proposal, stated as if the author endorsed it. The author says the test 'reintroduces the inquiry into usage.' Wrong party.
Too strong. Neither Halvorsen nor the author says courts can't decide genericness at all; they argue about how to decide it.
The passage never compares how much protection owners would get under each test. Halvorsen's test could cut either way: some casually used marks survive, some recognized marks fall.

Tempting, since the framing problem is in paragraph 2. But it's one point, 'chiefly' overstates it (the deeper complaint is that surveys force a ranking usage doesn't contain), and it leaves out the author's critique of the proposal.
CORRECT. 'Largely sound' = 'much of Halvorsen's critique... is persuasive'; 'more dependent on public understanding than she recognizes' = 'less independent of public meaning than she supposes.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, under United States law the question of whether a mark has become generic turns on
choices: whether the owner of the mark has tried to discourage generic use of the term
what the word chiefly signifies to most buyers of such goods
whether consumers buy the product because of the reputation of its maker
how long the term has been in use
whether competitors can describe their own goods intelligibly to buyers without having to use the disputed term
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the question is the term's 'primary significance' to the relevant public: whether most consumers understand it to denote a category of goods or a particular producer. B restates this. E is the trap: it is Halvorsen's proposed test, not the current law; C confuses why consumers buy with what they understand the word to mean.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what current U.S. law says decides genericness.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Straight detail. Paragraph 1: 'the question in such cases is the term's "primary significance" to the relevant public: if most consumers understand it to denote a category of goods... the mark is generic.' So the answer will talk about what the word mainly means to consumers. Be careful not to grab Halvorsen's proposal, which is also in the passage but is not the law.

choices.note: Never mentioned. The passage says nothing about owners policing their marks.
CORRECT. 'Primary significance to the relevant public' = what the word chiefly signifies to most buyers and users.
Tempting, because it's about consumers and the maker. But the test is what consumers understand the word to mean, not why they buy. Different question.
Duration of use never comes up.
Tempting: this language is in the passage. But it's Halvorsen's proposed replacement (paragraph 3), not the law described in paragraph 1. Wrong party.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Halvorsen holds that the rule denying trademark protection to generic terms exists in order to
choices: ensure that the legal status of words conforms to the way in which consumers actually speak
preserve the ability of rival sellers to tell buyers what they are offering
allow courts to rely on objective survey evidence rather than on testimony from competitors
protect consumers from being misled about which company actually made the products that they are purchasing
penalize mark owners whose own advertising encourages the public to use their marks as names for products
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that, on Halvorsen's account, the rule's point is 'not to track usage for its own sake but to prevent a single firm from monopolizing the only practical name for a product,' and her test asks whether competitors need the term 'to tell consumers what they are selling.' B paraphrases this. A is the purpose she explicitly denies, and D describes a familiar goal of trademark law, not the one she gives for the genericness rule.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the purpose Halvorsen assigns to the genericness rule.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first and second sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Where does the passage give Halvorsen's view of the rule's purpose? Paragraph 3: 'not to track usage for its own sake but to prevent a single firm from monopolizing the only practical name for a product.' So the answer is about keeping the name available to rivals. Note the 'not... but' structure: one of the wrong answers will be the thing she says the rule is NOT for.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the idea of usage. But this is exactly what Halvorsen says the rule is not for: 'not to track usage for its own sake.' Reversal.
CORRECT. Preventing one firm from monopolizing 'the only practical name' keeps rivals able 'to tell consumers what they are selling.'
Halvorsen distrusts the surveys courts use, and the passage never mentions testimony from competitors. Unsupported.

Tempting, because preventing confusion about source sounds like what trademark law is for. But the passage gives Halvorsen's reason for the genericness rule, and it's about competition, not consumer deception.
Sounds like a policy argument, but nothing in the passage frames the rule as a punishment for owners or mentions advertising.

questions.stem: The author refers to a person who says she will 'google' a restaurant (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that trademarks are used more often as verbs than as nouns
suggest that courts should treat marks used as verbs differently from marks used as nouns
offer an example of a mark that courts applying the primary significance test have already found to be generic
indicate that the surveys used by courts tend to overstate how often consumers use trademarks generically
illustrate how a speaker can use a word generically while knowing that it also names a particular firm
questions.explanation: The example follows Halvorsen's observation that people 'routinely use a single word in both ways': the speaker uses 'google' as an ordinary verb yet knows Google is a particular firm. E states that role. D is tempting because Halvorsen does criticize surveys, but the example illustrates dual usage, not any tendency of surveys to overstate generic use.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the 'google' example is there to show.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences two through four.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before the example: 'People, she observes, routinely use a single word in both ways.' Then come two examples: band-aid and google. Each shows one person using a word as a common name while still knowing it is a brand. So the example illustrates dual use. The survey criticism comes after, as a consequence of that point. Why mention X? Look at the claim right before X.

choices.note: The passage never compares how often marks are used as verbs and as nouns. 'Band-aid' in the same sentence is a noun.
No such distinction is drawn. The verb example and the noun example make the same point.
The passage never says Google has been found generic. The example is about how people talk, not about any court's ruling.

Tempting, since the paragraph ends by attacking surveys. But the attack is that surveys 'manufacture' a single primary meaning, not that they lean toward generic results. The example supports the dual-use premise, not a bias claim.
CORRECT. The person uses 'google' generically but 'may well know that Google is a particular firm': both meanings at once.

questions.stem: Halvorsen would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A mark that most consumers still associate with its original owner should never be held to have become generic.
Courts deciding whether a term is generic should ask consumers to describe a product in their own words rather than sort terms into lists.
A survey showing that most respondents classify a term as a common name would not by itself show that the term should lose protection.
Consumers who casually use a mark as a common name generally do not realize that the term was originally a brand name.
The rule denying protection to generic terms should be abandoned, since the ambiguity of consumers' usage makes it impossible to apply fairly.
questions.explanation: Halvorsen argues that surveys 'manufacture' a primary significance and that a mark should survive, 'however casually the public uses it,' whenever rivals can describe their goods without it (second and third paragraphs). So a survey result alone could not settle the question for her, as C says. A contradicts her statement that a mark should fall 'even if many consumers still associate the word with its owner'; B is the near-miss, but it keeps the inquiry into consumer meaning that she wants courts to set aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim Halvorsen (not the author) would endorse.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 2 and 3.

breakdown.analysis: What does Halvorsen believe? 1. Surveys force a single meaning onto words people use two ways. 2. Courts should drop the meaning question and ask whether competitors need the word. 3. Casual generic use doesn't matter if rivals can do without the word; recognition of the owner doesn't save the mark if they can't. So on her view, consumer classification never decides the case by itself. Look for an answer that downgrades survey results or consumer meaning.

choices.note: Contradicts paragraph 3: the mark 'should fall, even if many consumers still associate the word with its owner.'
Tempting, because it fixes the survey format she criticizes. But Halvorsen wants courts to 'set aside the question of meaning' altogether. A better survey still asks the wrong question.
CORRECT. Under her test, what matters is whether competitors need the term. A survey can't show that, so it can't by itself decide whether the mark loses protection.
Opposite of her examples: the band-aid shopper and the google speaker know the terms are brands.
Too strong. She wants to keep the rule and change the test, and she says plainly what the rule is for.

questions.stem: Which one of the following cases would Halvorsen's proposed test most clearly treat as one in which a mark should lose its protection?
choices: Consumers commonly use a brand name for a household cleaner to refer to all cleaners of that type, but rival makers market their products successfully as 'all-purpose sprays.'
Nearly all consumers recognize a sports drink's brand name, and rivals have begun copying the drink's distinctive packaging.
A survey shows that most consumers classify a brand name for a type of sandal as a common name, even though the brand's owner has advertised heavily to discourage this usage.
The public has no name for a new kind of kitchen appliance except its maker's brand name, which most consumers still recognize as a brand.
Most consumers use a popular brand name for adhesive film generically, and rivals call their product 'clear bonding film,' a longer phrase that buyers understand but seldom use.
questions.explanation: Under Halvorsen's test (third paragraph) a mark falls when rivals cannot describe their goods intelligibly without it, 'even if many consumers still associate the word with its owner.' In D the brand is the only name the public has, so rivals need it. E is the near-miss: the rivals' phrase is longer and seldom used, but buyers understand it, so rivals can describe their goods intelligibly and the mark survives however casually the public uses it; A fails the same way.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Halvorsen's competitive-need test to each case and find the one where the mark most clearly falls.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Her rule as a conditional: rivals can describe their goods intelligibly without the word → the mark survives (however casual public usage is). Rivals cannot → the mark falls (even if consumers still link the word to its owner). So the right answer needs: no workable alternative name for competitors. Consumer recognition doesn't matter, and neither do surveys or casual usage. Don't be swayed by how clumsy a rival's phrase is; the only question is whether buyers can understand it.

choices.note: Tempting: heavy generic use looks like classic genericide. But rivals sell successfully as 'all-purpose sprays,' so they don't need the word. Under her test, the mark survives.
Copying packaging is about imitation, not about needing a word. Nothing suggests rivals lack a name for sports drinks.
This is the survey-based approach Halvorsen rejects. The survey result alone tells her test nothing about competitors' needs.
CORRECT. There is no other name for the product, so competitors can't describe it without the brand. Consumer recognition of the brand doesn't save it; she says exactly that.

Tempting: the generic use is widespread and the rivals' phrase is clumsy. But Halvorsen's condition is intelligibility, not convenience or popularity, and buyers 'understand' the phrase. Rivals can do without the word, so the mark survives.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, the author's criticism of the competitive-need test most strongly suggests that the author holds which one of the following views?
choices: Surveys would provide a more reliable way than a competitive-need test to determine whether rivals need a disputed term.
Courts are generally reluctant to consider evidence concerning the commercial situation of a mark owner's competitors in genericness cases.
Despite their flaws, surveys accurately capture the meanings that consumers attach to trademarks.
The genericness rule exists mainly to ensure that the legal status of a word matches consumers' usage.
A court applying Halvorsen's test would still need some evidence of what consumers take various words to mean.
questions.explanation: The author argues that whether a rival can describe its product intelligibly 'depends on which alternative words the public understands,' so the test 'reintroduces the inquiry into usage' (last paragraph). It follows that a court applying it would still need evidence of consumer understanding, as E says. A is the near-miss: the author says nothing comparable to a survey anchors the new test, but never claims existing surveys could answer the competitive-need question better. C contradicts the author's agreement that surveys extract a ranking 'their usage does not contain.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a view the author's objection to Halvorsen's proposal commits the author to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Why does the author think the competitive-need test doesn't escape the question of meaning? Because whether a rival's description is intelligible depends on what words the public understands. Take one more step: then a judge using the test would have to find out what consumers understand. That's the prephrase. Note that the author agrees with Halvorsen on two things (surveys are flawed, the rule protects competition), so answers that contradict those are out.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author faults the new test for lacking anything 'comparable to a survey.' But that's a point about discipline, not a claim that today's surveys could measure competitors' needs, and the author agrees those surveys are flawed. Goes beyond the text.
Nothing about courts' attitudes toward such evidence.
The author agrees with Halvorsen that surveys extract a ranking 'their usage does not contain.' The opposite of 'accurately capture.'
The author agrees the rule exists 'to protect competition rather than to referee shoppers' vocabulary.' Reversal.

CORRECT. If intelligibility depends on which words the public understands, then deciding the competitive-need question requires evidence about consumer understanding. That's why the author says the test 'reintroduces the inquiry into usage.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's criticism of Halvorsen's proposal in the last paragraph?
choices: The alternative terms available to competitors often change in meaning over time as new kinds of products are introduced to the market.
Most of the marks that have been found generic under the primary significance test would also have been found generic under a competitive-need test.
Mark owners frequently commission their own surveys, which tend to show that consumers regard their marks as brand names rather than common names.
Courts applying the primary significance test have sometimes reached opposite conclusions about whether the same mark had become generic.
Surveys can reliably measure whether consumers understand the alternative terms that a mark owner's competitors would use to describe their goods.
questions.explanation: The author says the competitive-need test reintroduces the inquiry into usage 'in a less disciplined form, since nothing comparable to a survey anchors it.' If surveys can reliably measure whether the public understands rivals' alternative terms, that inquiry would have an anchor after all, so E weakens the criticism. C and D bear on the flaws of the current survey method, which the author already concedes, so they leave the criticism of the proposal untouched.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undercuts the author's objection to the competitive-need test.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The author's objection has two parts: 1. the test still depends on what words the public understands; 2. so it's an inquiry into usage, only 'less disciplined,' since 'nothing comparable to a survey anchors it.' Part 1 is hard to attack. Part 2 is weaker: what if there is a disciplined way to measure whether the public understands rivals' alternative words? Then the test needn't be loose. We want an answer that supplies that anchor. Don't pick answers that just attack the current survey method; the author already agrees with that.

choices.note: If anything this strengthens the author: it makes the competitors' question even more dependent on shifting public usage.
So? If the two tests give the same results, that says nothing about whether the new test escapes the question of meaning or lacks discipline.
Tempting, because it attacks surveys. But the author already concedes that surveys are flawed; this hits the old method, not the author's criticism of the new one.
Same problem as C. Conflicting results under the current test are a reason to doubt the current test, which the author grants. They don't answer the objection to Halvorsen's replacement.
CORRECT. It supplies exactly the anchor the author says is missing. The test would still involve meaning, but no longer in a 'less disciplined form.'

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: comparing the effectiveness of tax incentives and of employer information campaigns in increasing retirement saving
evaluating the effects of enrolling employees in workplace savings plans unless they decline
assessing the evidence that inertia rather than preference accounts for low participation in voluntary savings plans
explaining why younger and lower-paid workers have been less likely than other workers to save for retirement
determining which contribution rate employers should set as the default rate in their retirement savings plans
questions.explanation: Passage A presents automatic enrollment and the evidence for its success; passage B argues that its defaults have effects beyond overcoming inertia. Both, then, evaluate opt-out enrollment, as B says. C is the near-miss: passage A presents the inertia evidence, but passage B accepts it rather than assessing it; E is passage B's concern only.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The opening and closing sentences of each passage.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: voluntary plans had low participation; automatic enrollment raised it; policymakers adopted it. Passage B: automatic enrollment does more than people think; defaults act as advice; choose them carefully. Common ground: what happens when workers are enrolled unless they opt out. For 'both passages' questions, test each answer against both passages; a common trap is something only one passage covers.

choices.note: Passage A mentions information and incentives only as the older approach in its first sentence, and B never mentions them. Not the focus of either.
CORRECT. Enrolling employees 'unless they decline' is automatic enrollment, the subject of both passages.
Tempting: inertia is central to both. But only passage A presents the evidence for it; passage B takes inertia for granted ('the power of inertia') and argues about something else. Only half right.
Passage A notes in passing that these workers had low participation. Neither passage tries to explain why.
Tempting, because passage B ends on default rates. But passage A never discusses contribution rates, and B argues about how the choice should be made, not which rate to set.

questions.stem: Passage A states which one of the following about the firm studied by Madrian and Shea?
choices: It increased the matching contributions it offered to participants at the same time that it adopted automatic enrollment.
It changed what happened to new hires who did nothing, without altering the plan's financial terms.
It enrolled all of its employees automatically, including those who had been hired before the change.
Its change to automatic enrollment increased participation chiefly among older and more highly paid employees.
It required any employee who wished to leave the automatic enrollment plan to obtain the approval of a manager before doing so.
questions.explanation: Passage A says the firm changed its plan so that new employees 'were enrolled automatically unless they chose to opt out' and that participation rose 'even though the financial terms of the plan were unchanged.' B paraphrases both points. C is the near-miss: the passage speaks only of new employees and new hires, so extending the change to existing staff goes beyond it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about the firm in the 2001 study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What did the firm do? New employees were enrolled unless they opted out. What stayed the same? 'The financial terms of the plan.' The answer should paraphrase those two facts: only the default changed, and only for new hires. Watch for scope: 'new employees' is not 'all employees.'

choices.note: Contradicts 'the financial terms of the plan were unchanged.' A bigger employer match would be a change in financial terms.
CORRECT. 'Enrolled automatically unless they chose to opt out' = changed what happens to people who do nothing; 'financial terms... unchanged' = left the terms alone.
Tempting, since the firm did adopt automatic enrollment. But the passage says 'new employees' and 'new hires.' Nothing says existing employees were enrolled. Scope error.
The passage says participation rose among new hires; it doesn't break the increase down by age or pay. If anything, passage A suggests the low participants were younger and lower-paid.
Opposite of passage A, which stresses that employees 'remain free to leave the plan at the cost of a form.' No approval is mentioned.

questions.stem: In passage B, the phrase 'break ties in favor of action' (second sentence) refers to a default's role in
choices: resolving disagreements between employers and their employees over how much of each paycheck should be set aside for retirement
determining the outcome for employees who make no decision, so that they end up participating
encouraging employees to select the investment fund chosen by their employer over the other funds
settling cases in which employees find two different contribution rates equally attractive
persuading employees who have decided against participating to reconsider and join the plan
questions.explanation: Passage B's first sentence describes the standard view: those who would have drifted 'are rescued from their own procrastination.' To 'break ties in favor of action' is to settle the undecided cases by enrolling them, as B says. D takes 'ties' in its everyday sense of two equally attractive options; C describes the additional effect passage B says defaults have, not the tie-breaking role.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'break ties in favor of action' means in passage B.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first and second sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence says a default 'does more than' break ties. So tie-breaking is the role everyone already grants, described in sentence one: people who would have joined anyway are unaffected, and those who would have drifted get enrolled. The 'tie' is the undecided worker, and 'action' is participating. The 'more' that follows (defaults read as advice about rates and funds) is a different effect, so don't confuse the two.

choices.note: No employer-employee disagreement appears anywhere. This misreads 'ties' as disputes.
CORRECT. The undecided worker who would have drifted ends up enrolled: the default settles their case in favor of participating.
Tempting, because B talks about employees following the employer's chosen fund. But that's the 'more than' effect (defaults read as advice), not the tie-breaking the phrase describes.
The dictionary sense of a tie: two options rated equally. B's 'tie' is about indecision between acting and not acting, not about two rates being equally appealing.
The default doesn't reach people who have already decided; it governs what happens to those who don't act. Both passages say decliners can simply opt out.

questions.stem: The authors of the passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: voluntary enrollment plans have generally failed to produce adequate participation
inertia plays an important role in the savings decisions of many employees
employees in automatic enrollment plans should remain free to leave those plans
enrollment by default can leave some workers who would have signed up on their own worse off
a low default contribution rate tends to keep participation higher than a high rate would
questions.explanation: Passage A says that under automatic enrollment 'those who would have enrolled anyway lose nothing'; passage B argues that some of those workers settle at the default's lower rate and save less. So A holds that such workers lose nothing and B holds that some lose something; D states that disagreement. E is the near-miss: passage B asserts it, but passage A never discusses contribution rates, so there is nothing to disagree with; A and B are points on which both authors agree.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim one author accepts and the other rejects.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, third sentence; passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Passage A: those who would have joined anyway 'lose nothing.' Passage B: some who would have enrolled at a higher rate 'settle at the default's lower one,' so the default 'can reduce the saving of the very workers most inclined to save.' That's a clean yes/no on whether would-be enrollees can come out worse off.

choices.note: Both agree. A calls participation in voluntary plans 'stubbornly low'; B says their failures 'are real.'
Both agree. A's whole case rests on inertia, and B's final sentence talks about 'the power of inertia.'
A says employees 'remain free to leave the plan,' and B never disputes it. No disagreement.
CORRECT. A: those who would have enrolled anyway 'lose nothing.' B: some of them now save less than they would have, which is a loss.
Tempting, because B says it outright ('as a low rate does'). But passage A says nothing about contribution rates. To disagree, both authors need a position.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard the results described in the last sentence of passage A as
choices: evidence that automatic enrollment should be replaced by a return to voluntary enrollment plans
a partial gauge, since a count of enrollees reveals nothing about how much each of them is putting aside
misleading, since the gains in participation resulted from changes in plans' financial terms rather than defaults
an accurate indication that automatic enrollment has reached its goals at almost no cost to any employee
evidence that employers have set default contribution rates too high, discouraging some workers from participating
questions.explanation: Passage A judges the results 'striking' when 'measured by the share of eligible workers who participate.' Passage B argues that a default chosen to keep participation high can reduce the saving of workers most inclined to save, so B would see participation alone as a partial gauge. E is the near-miss: passage B does think default rates matter, but its worry is rates set too low, not too high, and it never suggests participation suffered. A is too strong: B says 'none of this argues for a return to voluntary enrollment.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how B's author would react to A's claim that the results have been striking.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last sentence; passage B, end of the first paragraph and start of the second.

breakdown.analysis: Notice A's careful wording: 'Measured by the share of eligible workers who participate, the results have been striking.' B's whole argument is that participation isn't everything: a low default rate keeps participation high while lowering some people's saving. So B wouldn't deny the participation numbers, but would say they leave out how much people save. You have to connect A's last sentence with B's first paragraph. Watch for overreactions and for answers that flip the direction of B's worry.

choices.note: Too strong. B says 'none of this argues for a return to voluntary enrollment, whose failures are real.'
CORRECT. Participation counts people, not amounts. B's point is that a default that keeps participation high can still leave some workers saving less, so the count is only part of the story.
B never questions that defaults caused the gains. And A says the financial terms were unchanged at the studied firm.
That is passage A's view. B denies that automatic enrollment is costless for everyone.

Tempting, because B is concerned with default rates. But it runs the wrong way: B says rates are chosen low to keep participation high, which lowers some workers' saving. It never says rates are too high or that participation suffered.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A advocates a policy on the basis of recent evidence; passage B argues that the policy should be abandoned in favor of the arrangement it replaced.
Passage A describes a general tendency in economic behavior; passage B presents a particular case that illustrates the tendency and extends it to a new domain.
Passage A presents a policy and its supporting evidence; passage B grants that the policy beats its predecessor but disputes a claim about how it works.
Passage A reports the findings of a single influential study; passage B challenges the methods by which that study's findings were originally obtained.
Passage A presents a policy as largely uncontroversial; passage B argues that the policy's critics have exaggerated the costs it imposes on employees.
questions.explanation: Passage A presents automatic enrollment and the Madrian and Shea evidence. Passage B grants that voluntary enrollment's 'failures are real' but rejects the idea, central to A, that a default is 'a neutral device for overcoming inertia,' arguing that it works as advice. C captures both moves. A is too strong, since B explicitly declines to argue for returning to voluntary enrollment; D invents a methodological dispute.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All of passage A; passage B, the first sentence and the whole second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What does B do with A's position? It doesn't reject automatic enrollment: 'None of this argues for a return to voluntary enrollment.' It targets the claim that defaults just break ties ('a costless correction'), which is A's 'overrides no one's preferences' line. So: B grants the policy beats what came before, but disputes how A thinks it works. Relationship answers are long sequences; one wrong half kills the whole answer.

choices.note: The first half fits; the second half is exactly what B says it is not arguing. 'Abandoned' is too strong.
B isn't an instance of a generalization in A, and it doesn't move to a new domain; both passages discuss the same retirement plans.
CORRECT. A: policy plus evidence. B: grants it beats voluntary enrollment ('failures are real') but denies the default is 'a neutral device for overcoming inertia.'
Tempting, since A rests on one study. But B never questions how Madrian and Shea did their work; it cites other studies about default rates.
Backwards. B is the critic, arguing that the policy has costs its supporters overlook, not defending it against critics.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: describe a change in the pattern of glacial cycles and present two explanations along with objections to each
trace the history of the debate over a change in glacial cycles from early orbital explanations to current hypotheses
describe a change in glacial cycles and argue that the evidence needed to decide between two explanations of it cannot be obtained
describe a method by which deep-sea sediments are used to reconstruct the history of ice sheets
explain how the removal of regolith and a decline in carbon dioxide combined to produce a change in glacial cycles
questions.explanation: The first paragraph describes the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, the next two present the regolith and carbon dioxide hypotheses, and the last reports that neither is accepted and gives the skeptics' objection to each. A covers the whole passage. E is the near-miss: the passage reports that 'some researchers have suggested' the two mechanisms operated together, but presents this as one suggestion, not as the explanation the passage sets out to give. C overstates the passage's caution: one hypothesis is 'hard to test' and one piece of evidence would not settle matters 'by itself,' which is not to say the needed evidence cannot be obtained.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the passage as a whole sets out to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Topic sentence of each paragraph, especially the first sentences of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: paragraph 1, the puzzle (cycles went from 41,000 to about 100,000 years with no orbital change). Paragraph 2, hypothesis 1 (regolith). Paragraph 3, hypothesis 2 (carbon dioxide) plus a timing proposal its supporters adopt. Paragraph 4: 'Neither hypothesis has won general acceptance,' the skeptics' objection to each, one suggestion that they combine, and a prediction that is hard to read. The author mostly reports. Watch for answers that turn a reported suggestion into the passage's thesis, or turn 'hard to test' into 'can't be tested.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraph 1 describes the change; paragraphs 2 and 3 present the explanations; paragraph 4 gives the skeptics' objections to each.
Invented frame. The passage mentions orbital theory only to set up the puzzle; it doesn't narrate a debate over time.

Tempting: the passage does stress how hard the evidence is. But 'hard to test' and 'would not by itself show' are not 'cannot be obtained.' Direct records 'have only recently begun to reach back' that far, which suggests better evidence is arriving. Too strong.
The sediment record is mentioned in one clause of paragraph 1. Far too narrow.

Tempting, because the passage mentions exactly this combination. But it's attributed to 'some researchers' in a single sentence, right after 'Neither hypothesis has won general acceptance.' The passage reports the idea; it doesn't set out to explain the transition this way.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that before the Mid-Pleistocene Transition
choices: deglaciations followed every second or third peak in summer sunlight, as they did after the transition
ice sheets rested largely on crystalline bedrock that earlier glaciations had exposed
the tilt of Earth's axis varied over a shorter period than it did after the transition
atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations were lower than they later became
ice sheets usually did not survive the warm phase of each tilt cycle
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says glaciations then 'came and went about every 41,000 years, the period over which the tilt of Earth's axis varies,' changing summer sunlight; so each glaciation ended within a single tilt cycle, which is E. A is the near-miss: it uses the passage's own wording, but the every-second-or-third-peak pattern is the proposed explanation of the later, 100,000-year cycles.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what the earlier glacial cycles must have been like.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, second sentence; paragraph 3, second sentence for contrast.

breakdown.analysis: Before the transition, glaciations came and went every 41,000 years, the same period as the tilt cycle, which governs summer sunlight. If a glaciation ends every tilt cycle, the ice didn't make it through the warm phase of each cycle. After the transition, by contrast, ice sheets survived one or more warm phases. This is a 'combine the timing with the mechanism' inference. Be careful with before/after; the wrong answers swap the two periods.

choices.note: Tempting, because these are the passage's words. But paragraph 3 uses them to explain the roughly 100,000-year interval after the transition. Before it, glaciations ended every tilt cycle.
Reversed. On the regolith hypothesis, before the transition the ice rested on soft regolith; bedrock was exposed later.
Contradicts paragraph 1: 'Earth's orbit underwent no corresponding change.'
Reversed. On the carbon dioxide account, concentrations declined over the Pleistocene, so they were higher earlier, not lower.
CORRECT. Glaciations that come and go with each 41,000-year tilt cycle are ice sheets that don't survive each cycle's warm phase.

questions.stem: The author mentions that many proponents of the carbon dioxide account have adopted the proposal that deglaciations might follow only every second or third tilt cycle (third paragraph) most likely in order to
choices: show that the proposal about every second or third tilt cycle was originally developed as part of the carbon dioxide account
suggest that the carbon dioxide account no longer depends on the existence of any threshold
indicate how that account deals with a feature of the transition that a gradual decline alone would not explain
explain why the carbon dioxide hypothesis has been difficult to test with the evidence available
provide evidence that carbon dioxide concentrations declined gradually over the course of the Pleistocene
questions.explanation: A gradual decline in carbon dioxide explains why ice could survive warmer summers (third paragraph), but nothing in a slow decline produces a roughly 100,000-year rhythm; the skipped-cycle proposal supplies that timing, which is the feature skeptics say the regolith account leaves unexplained (fourth paragraph). C states this role. A reverses the relation: the passage calls it 'a separate proposal' that 'takes no position on what caused the change.' B is the near-miss: adopting the timing idea does not remove the threshold problem, which skeptics still press in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the remark about adoption does for the carbon dioxide account.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second through fourth sentences; paragraph 4, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What does a gradual decline in carbon dioxide explain? Why ice sheets could survive warmer summers and grow bigger. What doesn't it explain by itself? Why they retreated about every 100,000 years: a slow, steady decline has no 100,000-year beat. The skipped-cycle proposal supplies the beat from the regular tilt cycle. So by adopting it, carbon dioxide proponents cover timing, the very thing skeptics say the regolith account lacks. You have to combine paragraph 3 with paragraph 4 to see this.

choices.note: Reverses the relation. The passage calls it 'a separate proposal, which takes no position on what caused the change.' Many in the carbon dioxide camp adopted it; they didn't invent it.

Tempting, since both concern weak spots of the carbon dioxide account. But the threshold objection survives: paragraph 4 says skeptics still ask how a gradual decline could produce a 'fairly rapid reorganization' without a threshold no one has specified. The timing idea doesn't answer that.
CORRECT. A gradual decline explains bigger, longer-lived ice but not a 100,000-year rhythm; the adopted proposal supplies that timing.
That's the job of the next sentence (direct records of ancient air only recently reach that far). The adoption remark comes before it and does something else.
The adoption of a timing mechanism isn't evidence about past carbon dioxide levels. The passage says those levels are hard to establish.

questions.stem: Proponents of the hypothesis described in the second paragraph would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Had the northern continents kept their cover of weathered soil, ice sheets after the transition would probably have remained thinner and less durable.
Once the regolith was removed, ice sheets collapsed only when a peak in summer sunlight arrived while they were near the limit of their stability.
Ice sheets resting on crystalline bedrock generally flowed more rapidly and spread more widely than ice resting on weathered soil.
The weathered soil that once covered the northern continents had been entirely removed before the first glaciations of the past three million years began.
Changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide could not have had any effect on the size of the northern ice sheets during the Pleistocene.
questions.explanation: On the regolith hypothesis, ice on soft, wet regolith 'slides readily' and stays thin and vulnerable, and only the exposure of bedrock let ice sheets grow thick enough to outlast a warm phase. So had the regolith remained, the ice would have stayed thin, as A says. B is the near-miss: it attaches the skipped-cycle timing proposal, which the carbon dioxide camp adopted, to the regolith account, and the passage says that account explains little about timing; E is far stronger than anything the hypothesis needs.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the regolith hypothesis commits its supporters to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2; paragraph 3 for the timing mechanism; paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The regolith hypothesis in a chain: regolith → ice slides → thin, vulnerable ice. Repeated glaciations → regolith scraped off → bedrock exposed → ice grips, grows thick → survives warm phases. So the removal of regolith is what made thick, durable ice possible. Its consequence: no removal → no thick ice. Look for that. Remember a proponent of one hypothesis needn't deny every other factor, and needn't adopt the other side's mechanism either.

choices.note: CORRECT. On the hypothesis, the regolith kept ice thin and vulnerable; without its removal, the later ice sheets wouldn't have become thick and durable.

Tempting: it mentions the regolith and uses the passage's wording. But that collapse mechanism is a separate proposal that many in the carbon dioxide camp adopted (paragraph 3), and skeptics say the regolith account doesn't explain timing at all. Wrong party.
Reversed. Ice on regolith 'slides readily'; ice gripping bedrock 'flows more slowly.'
Contradicts the hypothesis: the layer was removed by 'repeated glaciations,' so it was still present when glaciations began.
Too strong. The regolith account offers its own cause, but nothing in it requires denying that carbon dioxide had any effect at all.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that if the two mechanisms operated together in the way some researchers have suggested, then
choices: the decline in carbon dioxide made thicker ice possible, while the removal of the regolith set the pace at which the ice retreated
glacial debris should show no shift from weathered-soil material to fresh-bedrock material across the transition
ice sheets became thick only once bedrock was widely exposed, but something other than the ground beneath them governed when they retreated
deglaciations would have continued to follow every tilt cycle even after the regolith had been scraped away
atmospheric carbon dioxide must have risen, rather than declined, during the transition
questions.explanation: The suggestion in the last paragraph is that one mechanism made thicker ice possible and the other set the pace of its retreat. The second paragraph ties thicker ice to the exposure of bedrock, and the skeptics note that the regolith account does not explain the timing of retreats; so in the combined view, thick ice awaited the exposure of bedrock while timing came from elsewhere, as C says. A is the near-miss: it uses the passage's own phrasing but assigns the two roles to the wrong mechanisms.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the combined view implies by matching each role to the right mechanism.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, fourth sentence ('one making thicker ice possible and the other setting the pace'); paragraph 2, last two sentences; paragraph 4, second sentence; paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: The suggestion doesn't say which mechanism does which job, so you have to work it out. Paragraph 2: ice gripping bedrock 'can grow far thicker,' so regolith removal makes thicker ice possible. Paragraph 4: the regolith account explains thicker ice 'but not why they retreated about every 100,000 years.' Paragraph 3: many carbon dioxide proponents adopted the skipped-cycle timing idea. So: regolith → thickness; carbon dioxide (with skipped cycles) → pace of retreat. The right answer says thickness waited on bedrock and timing came from something else. Expect a trap that swaps the roles.

choices.note: Tempting, because it repeats the passage's exact phrasing ('made thicker ice possible,' 'set the pace'). But the roles are swapped. The passage ties thicker ice to bedrock exposure and says the regolith account does not explain timing.
The opposite. If regolith removal played its role, the regolith account predicts just such a shift in debris.
CORRECT. Regolith removal (bedrock exposure) made thick ice possible; the timing of retreat came from the other mechanism, not from the ground beneath the ice.
Contradicts the transition itself: afterward, retreats came about every 100,000 years, not every tilt cycle.
Contradicts the carbon dioxide account, which says concentrations declined. The combined view keeps that account's mechanism.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the regolith hypothesis?
choices: Indirect chemical indicators suggest that atmospheric carbon dioxide declined steadily throughout the period of the transition.
Ice also thickened after the transition in regions that never had a thick regolith cover.
The thickest post-transition ice sheets left debris made largely of fresh-bedrock material.
The debris had largely changed from weathered-soil material to fresh-bedrock material before the ice sheets grew thicker.
Glacial debris deposited during the transition contains weathered-soil and fresh-bedrock material in roughly equal proportions.
questions.explanation: The passage says a shift in debris 'would not by itself show which change came first,' since thicker ice might itself have scoured more deeply (last paragraph). D shows that the shift came before the ice thickened, ruling out that reversed sequence and supporting regolith removal as the cause. C is the near-miss: bedrock debris under the thickest ice is just what the reverse-causation story also predicts, so it does little to favor the hypothesis; B weakens it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that gives the regolith hypothesis the most support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 for the hypothesis; paragraph 4, last two sentences, for its prediction and the problem with that prediction.

breakdown.analysis: The regolith hypothesis is causal: regolith removed → thicker ice. Its prediction: debris should shift from soil to bedrock material before or as the ice changed. But the passage flags a problem: maybe it's backward, thicker ice → deeper scouring → bedrock debris. So bedrock debris alone isn't enough. What would beat the reversed-cause story? Timing. If the debris shifted before the ice thickened, the thicker ice can't have caused it. Cause has to come before effect. This is a classic reverse-causation fix.
