choices.note: This supports the rival hypothesis, but the two can operate together, as the passage notes. It does nothing for the regolith account.
Weakens. If ice thickened where there was no regolith to remove, something other than regolith removal made it thicker.

Tempting: it reports the kind of debris the regolith account predicts. But thick ice depositing bedrock debris is exactly what the reversed story (thicker ice → deeper scouring) predicts too, so it doesn't help tell the two apart.
CORRECT. The shift came first, so the thicker ice couldn't have produced it. That removes the reverse-causation worry and supports regolith removal as the cause.
A mixture during the transition fits a shift in progress, but says nothing about whether it came before or after the ice thickened, so the reverse-causation worry remains.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the proposal described in the third paragraph for how a roughly 100,000-year interval between deglaciations could arise?
choices: A fruit tree bears heavily only every second year, since it needs two seasons to store energy, regardless of each year's weather.
A river floods every few years, and hydrologists have traced the floods to an ocean weather pattern that recurs at roughly the same interval as the floods.
A lake's yearly rise and fall has grown larger as the nearby forest has been cleared.
A geyser erupts at irregular intervals, because the rate at which groundwater seeps into its underground chamber varies unpredictably from season to season.
A slope collects snow every winter, but the spring thaw triggers an avalanche only in years when the snowpack has grown deep enough to give way.
questions.explanation: On the proposal in the third paragraph, ice sheets collapse only when a regular peak in summer sunlight arrives while they are already near their stability limit, so collapses follow only some tilt cycles and the average interval is long without any long external cause. In E, a yearly trigger (the thaw) releases an avalanche only in years when the snowpack has built up enough. A matches the multi-year buildup but drops the regular external trigger; B is the explanation the proposal denies, a long cycle traced to an outside cycle of the same length.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation with the same causal structure as the proposal about the 100,000-year rhythm.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Break the proposal into parts: 1. a short, regular external cycle (tilt) supplies a trigger (peaks in summer sunlight); 2. the system builds up over time (ice sheets grow); 3. the event (collapse) happens only when a trigger arrives while the system is near its limit; 4. so only some triggers produce the event, giving a long average interval without any long external cycle. The right answer needs all four. Analogy traps match some elements and drop one.

choices.note: Close, but no external trigger. The tree's cycle is purely internal and happens 'regardless of each year's weather.' In the proposal, the sunlight peak is essential.
This is exactly the explanation the proposal rejects: a long interval traced to an outside cycle of the same length.
A gradual change in the size of a yearly cycle. There is no threshold event and no interval made of several shorter cycles.
Irregular timing from a variable internal rate. There's no regular trigger and no buildup to a limit that a trigger then releases.

CORRECT. A regular trigger (the yearly thaw), buildup across years (the snowpack), and an event only when the trigger meets a pack ready to fail. So avalanches come only every few years with no multi-year outside cause.

passages.title: Renga and the art of linking
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
In late medieval Japan, one of the most prestigious forms of poetry was not the work of a single poet. Renga, or linked verse, was produced by poets meeting in a single session, who took turns adding stanzas of seventeen and fourteen syllables, alternately, until a sequence, conventionally of one hundred stanzas, was complete. A master presided, ruling on whether each proposed stanza met the elaborate conventions governing the whole, and a scribe recorded each stanza as it was accepted. The conventions specified how often a given topic could recur, where in the sequence references to the moon or to blossoms should fall, and, most important, how each new stanza was to relate to those before it.

That last convention is the key to the form and to modern readers' difficulty with it. Each stanza had to be linked to the one immediately preceding it, often by reinterpreting the earlier stanza's scene, but it was forbidden to return to the situation of the stanza before that. A sequence therefore moves constantly: a stanza describing autumn rain on a traveler's sleeve might be followed by one that turns the dampness into a lover's tears, and that in turn by one in which the tears belong to a monk grieving for no one in particular. Read from beginning to end, as one reads a lyric poem, such a sequence seems to have no subject, no development, and no conclusion. Largely on these grounds, Masaoka Shiki, who in the 1890s promoted the opening stanza of linked verse as an independent poem, the haiku, declared that linked verse was not literature at all.

Shiki's judgment has proved durable, but it treats as a defect what the form's rules were built to produce. The rule against returning was meant to prevent precisely the unity Shiki looked for. What renga offers instead is a succession of pairings: the pleasure lies in seeing how a stanza that seemed complete in itself is transformed when another is set beside it, and then the new stanza transformed in its turn. A reader who attends to these successive junctures, rather than to an overall arc, finds in a sequence such as Three Poets at Minase, composed in 1488 by the master Sōgi and two of his disciples, an extraordinary display of inventiveness under constraint.

Some admirers of the form go further, arguing that because renga was a social event, its written record is a mere residue that only participants could properly appreciate. This seems to concede too much to Shiki. The records of sessions led by masters were copied, annotated, and studied by later poets as models of the art of linking, which suggests that those who knew the form best thought the texts themselves worth close reading by people who had not been present.

passages.title: Göbekli Tepe and the origins of farming
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Since excavations began there in the mid-1990s, Göbekli Tepe, a hilltop site in southeastern Turkey, has been cited as evidence that one of archaeology's most familiar sequences must be reversed. The site's oldest monumental structures, circular enclosures ringed by T-shaped limestone pillars, some more than five meters tall and carved in relief with foxes, boars, snakes, and vultures, were erected in the tenth millennium B.C., before crops or herd animals had been domesticated in the region. For Klaus Schmidt, who directed the excavations until his death in 2014, the enclosures were sanctuaries visited periodically by hunter-gatherer groups from a wide area rather than the buildings of a settled community. Because quarrying, carving, and raising the pillars would have required many people working together for long periods, Schmidt further proposed that the need to feed such gatherings may have encouraged the intensive harvesting of wild cereals that eventually led to their cultivation.

The first part of this account has not fared well. Work at the site since 2014 has documented features difficult to reconcile with a purely ceremonial center: cisterns cut into the bedrock to collect rainwater, large quantities of grinding stones and other tools for processing plant foods, and buildings that appear to have been dwellings. Many archaeologists now regard Göbekli Tepe as a settlement in which monumental enclosures stood alongside ordinary houses.

It might seem that this revision also disposes of Schmidt's larger claim, but it does not. His suggestion about farming depended not on the absence of residents but on the scale of the cooperative labor the enclosures demanded. A resident community building monuments still had to be fed, and the abundance of grinding equipment, if anything, indicates that processing wild cereals was a central activity at the site. What the new evidence undercuts is the image of scattered bands converging on a sacred place; it leaves untouched the connection between monument building and the pressure to produce food.

Nor is the proposal undermined, as some have suggested, by the finding that the plant remains recovered at the site are of wild, not domesticated, varieties. That the inhabitants harvested wild cereals intensively for many generations without domesticating them is what one would expect if domestication was a slow and largely unintended consequence of sustained harvesting rather than an innovation adopted once its advantages were seen. On that view, the decisive changes in the plants could have occurred after the period of monument building and away from the hilltop itself. The hypothesis does not require that the builders were the first farmers, only that the demands of building pushed harvesting to an intensity it would not otherwise have reached. Genetic studies have traced one of the earliest domesticated wheats, einkorn, to wild populations in the nearby Karacadağ mountains, within reach of the site though not on it.

passages.title: How masting plants keep time
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Many long-lived plants reproduce in bursts. The individuals of a population produce enormous seed crops in some years and few or none in others, and they do so in synchrony, so that a whole forest of beeches may fruit heavily in one autumn and then scarcely at all for several years. Ecologists usually explain why this behavior, known as masting, persists by pointing to the benefits of concentrated reproduction: seed-eating animals, kept scarce by lean years, can consume only a fraction of a sudden glut, and wind-pollinated plants that flower together pollinate one another more effectively. Such benefits, however, do not explain how individual plants manage to time their reproduction together.

The simplest answer is that they respond to the same weather. In several masting species, heavy flowering follows particular conditions in the preceding year, often a warm summer, and since neighboring plants experience the same summer, a shared cue could keep them in step. A cue of this kind, however, explains timing without explaining magnitude. Seed production in masting species swings from year to year far more widely than temperature or rainfall does, whereas a plant that simply matched its output to each year's conditions would produce crops varying about as much as the conditions themselves.

What ecologists call resource budget models address this gap. In them, a plant adds a roughly constant amount to its stored reserves each year and flowers only when the reserves exceed some threshold. Flowering draws the reserves down, and setting fruit draws them down much further, so that a plant that has fruited heavily must spend several years rebuilding them. The resulting output is irregular and highly variable even when conditions never change. The models also show how pollination itself can synchronize individuals. A wind-pollinated plant that flowers when few neighbors do receives little pollen, sets little fruit, and so keeps enough of its reserves to flower again soon; one that flowers along with many others sets fruit abundantly and is depleted. Over time, plants out of step with the population are drawn into it, a process modelers call pollen coupling.

Field evidence for these mechanisms is accumulating but uneven. In some species, measurements of stored nutrients, particularly nitrogen, have shown the steep decline after mast years that the models require. Experiments that alter reserves directly, by supplying nutrients or removing flowers, would offer a sharper test, but they are difficult to conduct on long-lived trees, and few have been attempted. Yet nothing in the models rules out a role for weather; a population could be coupled by pollen and also cued by temperature, and the relative contribution of each probably differs among species. For most masting plants, the measurements needed to decide the matter have not been made.

passages.title: Whitlock and the excited-utterance exception
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Few exceptions to the rule against hearsay are older or more often invoked than the one for excited utterances. Under the Federal Rules of Evidence, a statement relating to a startling event, made while the speaker was under the stress of excitement that the event caused, may be admitted to prove the truth of what it asserts, whether or not the speaker testifies. The traditional justification, classically stated by John Henry Wigmore, is that such stress suspends reflection, and with it the capacity for calculated lying.

For nearly a century, critics have found this rationale psychologically naive. Research on memory gives little reason to think that a few moments of agitation prevent deliberate falsehood, and considerable reason to think that intense stress can distort perception itself, so that a frightened witness may be sincere and still mistaken. Courts have admitted statements made many minutes or even hours after an event when the speaker still seemed upset. Many commentators would abolish the exception.

The legal scholar Dana Whitlock has offered a different response. The critics are right, she argues, that the exception cannot rest on the reliability of excited statements considered in themselves; but the question a rule of evidence must answer is comparative. The alternative to an excited utterance is usually the same person's testimony months later, by which time that account has been shaped by repeated retelling, conversations with other witnesses, questioning by investigators, and the reconstruction that memory performs over time. An early statement, however imperfect, precedes these influences. Excitement, on her view, matters only as rough evidence that a statement is early in this sense, and courts should ask directly whether the speaker had yet discussed the event with others.

Whitlock's shift from absolute to comparative reliability gives the exception better footing than the traditional rationale, but her argument reaches further than her proposal. If an account's value lies in preceding contamination, a calm statement made immediately after an event has as strong a claim as an excited one, and a stronger claim than an excited statement made hours later; the argument favors early accounts generally, a far larger change than she defends.

In criminal trials, constitutional law already draws a line resembling hers. Under Crawford v. Washington (2004) and Davis v. Washington (2006), the prosecution may not use testimonial statements of a witness who does not testify, whatever hearsay exception they satisfy, unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had an earlier chance to cross-examine; a frantic call to the police about an emergency in progress is not testimonial, but an account given to officers investigating events already past generally is. That line, however, protects the defendant's right to confront accusers rather than sorting reliable accounts from unreliable ones, and it will not always coincide with Whitlock's.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because renga was a social event whose written record is a mere residue, Shiki erred in judging the form by its texts.
The rule against returning to an earlier situation made renga a form in which unity could be achieved only through the rulings of the master who presided over a session.
Renga is best understood as the source of the haiku rather than as a form of poetry in its own right, as Shiki recognized.
Shiki was wrong to deny that renga is literature, since the disjointedness he objected to is an intended effect of the rules for joining stanzas.
The pleasure of renga lies in its overall arc, which emerges once a reader attends closely to the junctures between successive stanzas.
questions.explanation: The first two sentences of the third paragraph give the author's thesis: Shiki's verdict treats as a defect what the rule against returning was 'built to produce.' D paraphrases this. A is the admirers' reasoning, which the author rejects in the last paragraph, and E borrows 'junctures' but reverses the author's point about the 'overall arc.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about renga and Shiki's verdict on it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (Shiki's verdict) and paragraph 3, first two sentences (the author's reply).

breakdown.analysis: Is the passage just describing renga? No. It sets up Shiki's charge (no subject, no development, not literature) and answers it: the missing unity is deliberate, because the rule against returning exists to stop it. We need an answer that says Shiki was wrong and that the disunity is by design.

choices.note: Tempting, because it also says Shiki erred. But this is the admirers' reasoning from the last paragraph, which the author says 'concede[s] too much to Shiki.' Wrong party.
Borrows 'the rule against returning' and 'master,' but the author says the rule prevents unity; it doesn't make masters the source of it.
That's roughly Shiki's position, and the author argues against it.
CORRECT. It names Shiki's verdict, says the author rejects it, and gives the author's reason: the lack of unity is what the linking rule was built to produce.
Borrows 'junctures' but reverses the claim. The author says to attend to the junctures 'rather than to an overall arc.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following was a convention of renga composition?
choices: A stanza had to respond to its immediate predecessor while steering clear of the scene that predecessor had itself responded to.
Each new stanza had to reinterpret the scene of the stanza two places before it rather than that of the stanza immediately preceding it.
A sequence was expected to close by returning to an image from its opening stanza, so that the whole would seem complete.
References to the moon and to blossoms were allowed only in the opening stanza of a sequence, never in later stanzas.
No poet taking part in a session was permitted to contribute two stanzas in succession, whatever the master ruled.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says each stanza had to be linked to the one before it but 'was forbidden to return to the situation of the stanza before that,' which A restates. B reuses 'reinterpret' but attaches it to the wrong stanza, and D distorts the first paragraph, which says the conventions fixed where moon and blossom references should fall.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the rule of renga that the passage actually states.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence (the conventions) and paragraph 2, second sentence (linking and the rule against returning).

breakdown.analysis: Go back to the text instead of relying on memory. The big rule: link to the stanza just before, never return to the one before that. Watch for an answer that keeps the passage's words but attaches them to the wrong stanza.

choices.note: CORRECT. Respond to the immediate predecessor = 'linked to the one immediately preceding it'; steer clear of what that predecessor responded to = 'forbidden to return to the situation of the stanza before that.'
Tempting, because it uses the passage's word 'reinterpret.' But the reinterpreting links a stanza to the one immediately before it; the stanza two back is exactly what it may not return to.
Opposite. The form 'moves constantly' and forbids returning.
Distortion. The conventions set where such references 'should fall' in the sequence; nothing limits them to the opening.
Not stated. Poets 'took turns,' but no rule about consecutive stanzas is given.

questions.stem: In saying that the admirers' position "seems to concede too much to Shiki" (second sentence of the last paragraph), the author most probably means that the position
choices: acknowledges, as Shiki did, that a renga sequence lacks the unity of a lyric poem
grants part of Shiki's case by agreeing that the surviving texts cannot reward readers who were absent
grants part of Shiki's case by agreeing that the masters' records were never studied by poets who had not been present
gives Shiki's opinions more weight than the judgments of the masters who presided over renga sessions
surrenders to Shiki the claim that the conventions of renga were too elaborate for most poets to master
questions.explanation: Shiki held that linked verse is not literature; the admirers hold that its written record is a 'mere residue' only participants could appreciate. Both deny that the texts reward ordinary readers, which is the point the author answers with the later poets who studied the records, so B is correct. A is the near-miss: the author also accepts that a sequence lacks a lyric's unity, so agreeing on that is no excessive concession.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what concession the author thinks the admirers make to Shiki.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph (the admirers and the author's rebuttal); paragraph 2, last sentence (Shiki's verdict).

breakdown.analysis: What do the admirers hand to Shiki? Look at how the author rebuts them: later poets who were not present studied the texts closely. So the concession must be about whether the texts are worth reading for non-participants. Shiki said no (not literature); the admirers, from the other side, also say the record alone isn't enough. We need: 'they grant that the texts don't reward absent readers.'

choices.note: Tempting, because the admirers probably would agree with this. But the author agrees with it too, so it can't be what the author means by conceding 'too much.' The excess concession is about the texts' value to readers who weren't there.

CORRECT. Shiki denied that the texts are literature; the admirers say only participants could appreciate the record. Either way, a reader of the texts alone gets nothing, which is the ground the author refuses to give up.

Close, but it turns the admirers' claim about who could appreciate the records into a historical claim about who studied them. The admirers make no such claim, and the author's rebuttal shows the records were studied.
The masters' judgments aren't part of the admirers' argument.
Shiki is never said to have made this claim.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the records of renga sessions led by masters
choices: served later poets as examples of how stanzas could be joined
were studied by later poets chiefly to learn the social customs that governed the sessions
were revised by the masters after each session so that the finished sequences would show greater overall coherence
were regarded by Shiki as the only examples of linked verse that deserved to be read as literature
were made chiefly for the participants, who used them to recall the occasions on which they had composed
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says these records were 'copied, annotated, and studied by later poets as models of the art of linking,' which A paraphrases. B keeps 'studied by later poets' but supplies the wrong purpose.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the masters' records.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Only one sentence discusses these records: later poets copied, annotated and studied them as models of linking. The trap will keep the 'later poets studied them' part and change what they studied them for.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Studied by later poets as models of the art of linking' = used as examples of how to join stanzas.
Tempting: they were studied by later poets. But as models of linking, not of social customs. Right fact, wrong purpose.
No revision is mentioned, and adding coherence would cut against the form.
Shiki said linked verse was not literature 'at all,' with no exceptions.
The passage stresses use by people who were not present.

questions.stem: The author describes a series of stanzas about autumn rain, a lover's tears, and a grieving monk (third sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the reinterpretation of an earlier scene that, according to the author, gives a renga sequence its unity
illustrate the particular technique by which Sōgi and his disciples linked the stanzas of Three Poets at Minase
suggest that renga poets generally favored melancholy subjects over the seasonal imagery their conventions called for
show how the rule governing successive stanzas keeps a sequence from settling on any one topic
demonstrate that a stanza in renga has no meaning at all apart from the stanza that follows it in a sequence
questions.explanation: The example follows 'A sequence therefore moves constantly' and precedes 'such a sequence seems to have no subject,' so it shows the linking rule producing a sequence without a continuing topic, as D says. A is the near-miss: reinterpretation is illustrated, but the author says the rule prevents unity rather than creating it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author gives the rain-tears-monk example.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, sentences 2-4.

breakdown.analysis: What does the example sit between? Before it: the linking rule, with 'therefore.' After it: read straight through, the sequence seems to have no subject. So the example shows the rule causing drift. Beware an answer that says this produces unity.

choices.note: Tempting: the example does show reinterpretation. But the author says the rule prevents unity; it doesn't create it.
The example is hypothetical ('might be followed by'), not taken from Sōgi's sequence.
The moods are incidental; the point is the shifting scene.
CORRECT. 'Therefore moves constantly' leads into the example, and 'seems to have no subject' follows it. The example shows the linking rule producing drift.
Too strong. The author speaks of a stanza 'that seemed complete in itself.'

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the admirers of renga mentioned in the last paragraph is most accurately described as
choices: a shared regard for the form, joined to disagreement about who can properly appreciate it
general agreement with their position, tempered by a concern that they overstate the social character of renga sessions
respect for their emphasis on the social occasion, combined with doubt that the written records preserve enough of that occasion to be worth studying
qualified endorsement of their claim that the written record of a renga session is incomplete
neutrality toward a view that the author considers irrelevant to the dispute about Shiki's judgment
questions.explanation: The admirers 'go further' than the author, so they share the author's esteem for renga, but the author rejects their claim that only participants could appreciate the record. A captures both halves; B wrongly calls this general agreement.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author regards the admirers in the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two signals: 'go further' (same starting point: they admire the form) and 'concede too much' (the author rejects their claim). Mixed attitude: shared admiration, disagreement on the specific claim.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Go further' means they start from the author's admiration; 'concede too much' and the rebuttal show disagreement on who can appreciate the texts.
Tempting, since they share the author's admiration. But the author rejects their position itself, not just an emphasis within it.
Reversed on the key point. The author argues the records are worth studying; the doubt here belongs to the admirers, not the author.
The author doesn't endorse their claim in any form.
The author ties their view directly to Shiki ('concede too much to Shiki') and takes a side.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A modern reader can fully appreciate a renga sequence only after learning every convention that a presiding master enforced.
Reading a sequence from beginning to end as one reads a lyric poem is the surest way to perceive the inventiveness of its authors.
A sequence that developed a single subject throughout would have been especially prized by medieval masters.
Someone who never attended a renga session can still find in a written sequence the satisfactions the form was designed to provide.
Shiki's promotion of the haiku lowered the esteem in which Sōgi was held by poets of his own day.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph places renga's intended pleasure in the junctures between stanzas, available to a reader who attends to them, and the last paragraph says later poets who were not present studied the records closely, so D follows from the two together. A overstates: the author never makes knowledge of every convention a precondition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author's views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (what the form offers and how to read it) and paragraph 4 (the author's rebuttal of the admirers).

breakdown.analysis: Combine the two last paragraphs. Paragraph 3: the satisfactions come from the pairings, if you read for the junctures. Paragraph 4: the author rejects the idea that only participants can appreciate the record. So a non-participant can get what the form offers. Watch for answers that overstate what a reader needs.

choices.note: Tempting, since the author does stress the conventions. But 'only after learning every convention' is far stronger than anything the author says; attending to the junctures is what's required.
Reversed. That kind of reading is what makes a sequence seem to lack a subject.
The rule against returning was 'meant precisely to prevent' that kind of unity.

CORRECT. Paragraph 3: the form is designed to offer the pleasure of successive pairings, available to a reader who attends to the junctures. Paragraph 4: later poets who were not present read the records closely. Together: absent readers can get the intended pleasure.
Shiki lived four centuries after Sōgi.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: defend an archaeologist's account of a site against recent findings suggesting that the site was a settlement rather than a sanctuary
argue that recent excavations have refuted the claim that monumental building preceded domestication in the region
describe the methods by which archaeologists established that a site in southeastern Turkey was occupied throughout the year rather than seasonally
compare two competing theories about why the people who built a site eventually stopped constructing monuments there
argue that an influential hypothesis about a site survives two kinds of evidence against it, though a related interpretation does not
questions.explanation: The author concedes that Schmidt's sanctuary interpretation 'has not fared well' but argues that his farming proposal survives both the evidence of residence (third paragraph) and the wild plant remains (fourth paragraph), which is E. A misplaces the defense: the author gives up the sanctuary view and defends only the farming claim.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify why the author wrote the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first sentence; paragraph 3, first sentence; paragraph 4, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Is the author for or against Schmidt? Both, on different claims. Sanctuary: lost. Farming: defended twice ('it does not'; 'Nor is the proposal undermined'). We need an answer that separates the two claims and has the author defending the farming one.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author does defend Schmidt. But the author concedes the sanctuary interpretation; only his farming claim is defended.
Nothing refutes that sequence; the enclosures still predate domesticated crops.
No methods are discussed.
Invented frame; no such theories appear.
CORRECT. The hypothesis (farming) survives the evidence of residence (paragraph 3) and the wild plant remains (paragraph 4); the related interpretation (sanctuary) 'has not fared well.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, Schmidt held that the people who built the enclosures at Göbekli Tepe
choices: built ordinary dwellings beside the enclosures to house those working on the pillars
belonged to scattered groups that gathered at the site from time to time but did not live there
had already begun cultivating cereals in the surrounding hills before they started quarrying the pillars
carved the animals on the pillars in order to record the wild species on which they depended for food
abandoned the site once domesticated crops had become available elsewhere in the region
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says Schmidt saw the enclosures as 'sanctuaries visited periodically by hunter-gatherer groups from a wide area rather than the buildings of a settled community,' which B restates. A describes the later findings that undercut his view.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Schmidt believed about the builders.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Straight retrieval: periodic visits, groups from a wide area, no settled community. The trap swaps in the post-2014 picture.

choices.note: That's what later excavations suggested, the reverse of Schmidt's view.
CORRECT. 'Visited periodically by hunter-gatherer groups from a wide area rather than ... a settled community.'
Reversed sequence; for Schmidt cultivation came later.
The carvings are never interpreted in the passage.
Abandonment is never mentioned.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the grinding stones found at Göbekli Tepe
choices: count against Schmidt's account of how farming began, though not against his claim that the site was a sanctuary
demonstrate that the inhabitants had begun to cultivate the cereals they were processing
tell against one part of Schmidt's account while lending some support to another
indicate that the enclosures were built considerably later than Schmidt had supposed
show that the builders of the enclosures never needed to bring food to the site from elsewhere
questions.explanation: The stones appear twice: in the second paragraph as part of the evidence against a 'purely ceremonial center,' and in the third as indicating that processing wild cereals was central, which 'if anything' supports the farming proposal. C combines these. A reverses which part of Schmidt's account the stones bear against.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what role the grinding stones play in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, second sentence and paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Where do the stones show up? Twice, doing two different jobs. Paragraph 2: evidence of residence, so bad for the sanctuary claim. Paragraph 3: evidence of heavy cereal processing, so if anything good for the farming claim. We need an answer with both directions in the right order.

choices.note: Reversed. The stones undercut the sanctuary claim and, if anything, support the farming claim.
The plant remains are of wild varieties (paragraph 4).

CORRECT. Paragraph 2: they help show the site was not purely ceremonial (against the sanctuary claim). Paragraph 3: they indicate that processing wild cereals was central, which 'if anything' helps the farming claim.
Dating isn't affected by the stones.
Overreach; the passage says nothing about self-sufficiency.

questions.stem: The author's remark that "a resident community building monuments still had to be fed" (third paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: concede that the evidence of houses at the site is compatible with Schmidt's view that the enclosures were sanctuaries
suggest that the residents could not have fed themselves without cultivating crops
indicate why Schmidt's case about farming does not require that the site lacked permanent inhabitants
explain why archaeologists working since 2014 have concluded that the site was occupied year-round
introduce a consideration that tells against Schmidt's proposal about the way cultivation began in the region
questions.explanation: The third paragraph argues that Schmidt's farming claim depended on the scale of labor, not on the absence of residents; the remark shows that residents would face the same need for food, as C says. A applies the remark to the wrong part of Schmidt's account.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the 'still had to be fed' remark does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the builders lived there? The author's answer: they still had to eat, and the farming argument only needed a big workforce that had to eat. So the remark explains why the farming claim doesn't depend on the site being empty.

choices.note: Tempting, because the remark does soften the impact of the houses. But only on the farming claim; the author accepts the sanctuary view 'has not fared well.'
Too strong. They processed wild cereals.
CORRECT. The farming claim rests on labor needing food; residents need food as much as visitors, so the case survives the evidence of residence.
That conclusion rests on cisterns, tools and houses (paragraph 2).
Reversed; the remark supports that proposal.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, Schmidt would have been most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Hunter-gatherers in the region did not harvest wild cereals at all until they began to build monumental enclosures such as those at Göbekli Tepe.
The animals depicted on the pillars were among the first species in the region to be domesticated.
A large cooperative undertaking can create pressures that change the way people obtain their food.
Settled village life in the region preceded both monument building and the cultivation of plants.
The enclosures at Göbekli Tepe were erected only after farmers had settled the surrounding region.
questions.explanation: Schmidt proposed that 'the need to feed such gatherings may have encouraged the intensive harvesting of wild cereals that eventually led to their cultivation,' an instance of the general claim in C. A overstates his view: he spoke of intensified harvesting, not of harvesting beginning only with the monuments.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer a general view Schmidt would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Schmidt's chain: big building project → many workers to feed → intensive harvesting → cultivation. Abstract that: a big cooperative project can change how people get food. Watch for an answer that turns 'intensive harvesting' into 'harvesting began.'

choices.note: Tempting, since he linked building to harvesting. But he spoke of building encouraging intensive harvesting, not of harvesting starting from nothing. Too strong.
No link between the carvings and domestication is made.
CORRECT. His proposal: building required large gatherings → feeding them encouraged intensive harvesting → eventually cultivation. That's a general instance of this claim.
Schmidt denied the site was a settled community.
Reversed sequence.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The decisive changes that produced domesticated wheat most likely took place on the hilltop during the period of monument building.
Generations of heavy harvesting without domestication do not show that harvesting failed to bring about domestication eventually.
Evidence that the site was inhabited year-round makes it less likely that the need to feed its builders encouraged intensive harvesting.
The inhabitants of Göbekli Tepe deliberately refrained from domesticating the cereals they harvested.
Once people recognized the advantages of domestication, it spread rapidly through the region.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph argues that long intensive harvesting without domestication is 'what one would expect' if domestication was a slow, largely unintended consequence of harvesting, so the wild remains do not refute the farming proposal, as B says. A contradicts the author's statement that the decisive changes could have come later and elsewhere.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author's argument in the last paragraph supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Why don't the wild plant remains sink Schmidt? Because if domestication is slow and unintended, you'd expect a long stretch of heavy harvesting with no domestic plants yet. So the absence of domestic plants doesn't show harvesting failed to lead there. Beware the trap that pins the change to the hilltop.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author defends a link between building and domestication. But the author says the decisive changes 'could have occurred after the period of monument building and away from the hilltop.'
CORRECT. Paragraph 4: that long period is 'what one would expect' if domestication was a slow, unintended consequence of harvesting.
Paragraph 3 says the opposite.
The author treats domestication as largely unintended, not as something deliberately avoided.
Contrary to the view the author favors, that domestication was slow and not adopted for its advantages.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen Schmidt's proposal about the role of monument building in the origins of cultivation?
choices: At settlements in the region, cereal-processing tools became far more numerous once monument building began, but not at settlements that built no monuments.
Wild cereals grew abundantly in the hills around Göbekli Tepe throughout the period in which the enclosures were built.
Settlements in the region that built no monuments of any kind harvested wild cereals just as intensively as the people of Göbekli Tepe did during the same period.
The pillars could have been quarried and raised by a few dozen workers over several years.
Carvings in the style of those at Göbekli Tepe have been found at sites far from it.
questions.explanation: Schmidt's proposal is that the labor demands of monument building encouraged intensive harvesting of wild cereals, which eventually led to cultivation. A shows harvesting intensifying where and when monuments were built, and not elsewhere, which directly supports that causal link. B shows only that cereals were available, and C and D weaken the proposal.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the claim that monument building drove more intensive cereal harvesting.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence; paragraph 3, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What does Schmidt need? A causal link: building → pressure for food → intensive harvesting. The best support compares places with and without monuments and finds harvesting jumping only where building happened. An answer that only shows cereals were around is necessary background, not support for the link.

choices.note: CORRECT. This ties the intensity of cereal harvesting to monument building specifically, with a comparison group, which is exactly the link Schmidt's proposal needs.
Tempting, since the proposal needs harvestable cereals nearby. But abundance shows only that harvesting was possible, not that building drove it.
Weakens: if harvesting was just as intensive without monuments, building wasn't what drove it.
Weakens: a small workforce removes the feeding pressure the proposal relies on.
Irrelevant to how cultivation began.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Resource budget models explain both the timing and the size of masting better than a weather cue does, and field measurements have now confirmed them for most masting species.
Masting persists because concentrated reproduction lets plants overwhelm seed-eating animals and pollinate one another more effectively.
Masting plants are synchronized by pollen coupling rather than by weather, though the evidence for coupling remains uneven.
Because seed crops vary more widely than weather does, conditions in preceding years cannot influence when masting plants flower.
Models in which reproduction depletes reserves explain aspects of masting that a weather cue cannot, though their general applicability is unsettled.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the weather cue, which 'explains timing without explaining magnitude,' to resource budget models that 'address this gap,' then notes that the evidence is 'accumulating but uneven' and that for most species the measurements 'have not been made.' E captures this. A is right until its last clause, which claims a confirmation the author denies; C keeps the hedge but sets coupling against weather, which the author says can operate together.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage's main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence (the question); paragraphs 2-4.

breakdown.analysis: What question is the passage answering? Not why masting pays off (settled in paragraph 1) but how plants reproduce in sync. Weather explains when, not how much; resource budget models fill the gap; the evidence is incomplete. Two answers get most of this right and slip on one element: one claims confirmation, the other makes coupling replace weather. Check every clause.

choices.note: Tempting: the first half is the passage's argument. But the last element is wrong. The author says the evidence is 'uneven' and that for most masting plants the needed measurements 'have not been made.'
Paragraph 1 background. The passage is about how plants synchronize, which the author says these benefits 'do not explain.'
Has the right hedge but the wrong contrast. The author says a population could be coupled by pollen 'and also cued by temperature'; coupling doesn't replace weather.
Overreach. Weather can't explain the size of the swings, but it can still cue their timing.

CORRECT. The weather cue explains timing but not magnitude (paragraph 2); resource budget models address that gap and add pollen coupling (paragraph 3); the evidence is 'uneven' and mostly not yet gathered (paragraph 4).

questions.stem: According to the resource budget models described in the passage, which one of the following would be expected of a wind-pollinated plant that flowers heavily in a year when almost no other plant in its population flowers?
choices: It would set abundant fruit because it flowered heavily, and would then need several years to rebuild its reserves before flowering again.
It would probably be able to flower again sooner than a neighbor that had flowered in a year when most of the population did.
It would set little fruit, and so it would be unable to flower again until a warm summer supplied the cue that synchronizes the population.
Its seeds would be more likely to escape predators than seeds produced during one of the population's mast years.
It would add to its stored reserves more rapidly in the following years than plants of its population that had fruited heavily.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says a plant that 'flowers when few neighbors do receives little pollen, sets little fruit, and so keeps enough of its reserves to flower again soon,' while one that flowers with many others 'is depleted.' Applied to the new case, B follows. A assumes heavy flowering means heavy fruiting, ignoring the pollen step, and C gets the fruit right but adds a weather requirement the models do not contain.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the resource budget mechanism to a plant that flowers out of step.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, sentences 2-3 and the last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Run the mechanism step by step: 1. flowering alone → little pollen; 2. little pollen → little fruit; 3. little fruit → reserves mostly kept; 4. so it can flower again soon, unlike a plant that fruited with the crowd. The traps each break one step: heavy flowering read as heavy fruit, or little fruit followed by an invented wait for weather.

choices.note: Tempting: heavy flowering sounds like heavy fruiting. But in the models fruit depends on pollen from neighbors, and this plant has almost none. One element is wrong, and it changes the outcome.
CORRECT. Flowering alone → little pollen → little fruit → reserves largely kept → flower again soon. A neighbor that flowered with the crowd set abundant fruit and needs years to rebuild.
Right about the little fruit, wrong about the consequence. In the models it keeps its reserves and can flower again soon; nothing makes it wait for a weather cue.
Reversed predator logic, and the question asks about the reserve models, not predation.
The models assume a roughly constant yearly addition for every plant.

questions.stem: In stating that a shared cue "explains timing without explaining magnitude" (second paragraph), the author most probably means that such a cue
choices: could account for how much seed plants produce but not for the particular year in which they produce it
could account for when plants reproduce together but not for how much their output changes from year to year
explains why plants flower in the same season but not why they flower in the same year
accounts for the behavior of individual plants but not for the size of the populations in which those plants grow
explains the benefits of masting but not the mechanism by which plants achieve it
questions.explanation: The following sentence explains the phrase: seed production 'swings from year to year far more widely than temperature or rainfall does.' So the cue accounts for when plants reproduce together but not for the size of the swings, as B says. D takes 'magnitude' in a dictionary sense, and A reverses the two terms.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain 'timing without explaining magnitude.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the next sentence. Seed crops swing much more than weather does; a plant just matching the weather would vary only as much as the weather. So 'magnitude' is the size of the year-to-year swings, and the cue can't explain it.

choices.note: Reversed: timing is what the cue does explain.
CORRECT. The next sentence explains: seed production swings far more widely than the weather does. 'Magnitude' = size of the swings.
Splits 'timing' in a way the passage doesn't; the cue explains same-year flowering.
Dictionary sense of 'magnitude' (size), applied to populations. The passage means the size of seed-crop swings.
Borrows paragraph 1's benefit-versus-mechanism distinction, but the cue is itself a mechanism.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that resource budget models address the gap identified in the second paragraph by
choices: showing that plants amplify small differences in summer temperature into large differences in seed output
establishing that masting plants flower only in years when few of their neighbors are flowering, so that they avoid competing for pollen
attributing large swings in output to the plant's own cycle of depleting and rebuilding reserves
demonstrating that seed-eating animals cannot consume more than a fraction of a sudden glut
explaining why the benefits of concentrated reproduction are greatest among wind-pollinated species
questions.explanation: The gap in the second paragraph is that a weather cue cannot explain the size of the swings; the third paragraph says the models produce 'irregular and highly variable' output 'even when conditions never change,' because reserves are drawn down and rebuilt. C links the two paragraphs. A has the right effect but the wrong source, attributing the variability to amplified weather.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Connect the gap in paragraph 2 to how the models in paragraph 3 fill it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last two sentences; paragraph 3, first four sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What's the gap? Weather explains timing, not how big the swings are. How do the models produce big swings? Reserves build up, flowering and fruiting drain them, rebuilding takes years, so output varies wildly even with constant weather. The swings come from inside the plant.

choices.note: Tempting, since it pairs the warm-summer cue with large swings. But the models generate variability internally, from reserves, not by amplifying temperature. Right effect, wrong source.
Reversed. Plants out of step get pulled into the population's rhythm.
CORRECT. Paragraph 2's gap is magnitude; paragraph 3 says the models produce 'irregular and highly variable' output 'even when conditions never change,' through reserves drawn down and rebuilt.
That's the predator benefit from paragraph 1, not the models.
The models explain synchrony, not where the benefits are greatest.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the process the passage calls pollen coupling?
choices: Vendors at a market each return whenever their stock has been replenished, and because all are supplied by one wholesaler on the same day, they come to attend together.
A farmer leaves each of her fields fallow for a full year after it has been harvested, so that its soil can recover, regardless of what her neighbors do with theirs.
Birds of a certain species begin nesting at a site only after a few early arrivals have settled there, since newcomers are attracted by the presence of others.
A wholesaler buys large stocks of grain whenever prices are low and sells them off when a shortage elsewhere in the region drives prices up.
Vendors whose sales depend on how many others attend a market lose little stock on quiet days and sell out on crowded ones, and so come to attend together.
questions.explanation: In pollen coupling, a plant's payoff depends on how many others flower with it; out-of-step plants spend little and stay ready, while in-step plants are depleted, so stragglers are drawn into the group's rhythm. E has the same structure. A is the near-miss: it shares the setting, the depletion and the synchrony, but the synchrony comes from a common outside schedule, which corresponds to a weather cue rather than to coupling.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation that works the way pollen coupling works.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last three sentences.

breakdown.analysis: What makes coupling coupling? The payoff of acting depends on how many others act at the same time, and that payoff, through what it costs, sets when you can act next. Synchrony alone isn't enough: a shared calendar or supplier also makes people act together. Ask what brings them into step.

choices.note: Tempting: same setting, depletion and restocking, and synchrony. But the vendors fall into step because of a shared external schedule, which is like a weather cue, not because each one's payoff depends on how many others attend.
Depletion and recovery, like the resource budget, but nothing depends on neighbors, so there's no coupling.
Attraction to others, with no payoff that drains resources.
Timing to prices; no dependence on others acting at the same moment.

CORRECT. Payoff depends on how many others act at once (pollen from neighbors); acting out of step costs little (little fruit, reserves kept); acting with the crowd depletes (heavy fruit); the result is synchrony.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the claim that pollen coupling synchronizes the plants of a particular wind-pollinated masting species?
choices: Plants of that species flower heavily chiefly in the years that follow unusually warm and dry summers across their range.
In that species, the amount of nitrogen stored in plants declines steeply in the year after a heavy seed crop.
Seed-eating animals consume nearly all of that species' seeds in years when few plants flower.
In that species, plants flowering when few neighbors do set as much fruit per flower as plants flowering with many neighbors.
Plants of that species that are experimentally given extra nutrients flower more often than untreated plants of the same species growing nearby.
questions.explanation: Pollen coupling works because a plant flowering out of step receives little pollen and 'sets little fruit,' so it keeps its reserves and flowers again soon. If out-of-step plants set fruit at the same rate as in-step plants, that mechanism is gone, as D says. A is compatible with coupling, since the author says a population could be 'coupled by pollen and also cued by temperature.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would undermine pollen coupling in a given species.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last two sentences; paragraph 4, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Which link does coupling depend on? Flowering with few neighbors → little pollen → little fruit. Cut that link and stragglers deplete just like everyone else, so nothing draws them into step. Don't pick weather: the passage says weather and coupling can operate together.

choices.note: Tempting, because it points to weather. But the author says a population could be coupled by pollen 'and also cued by temperature.' A weather cue doesn't exclude coupling.
Supports the resource budget mechanism that coupling depends on.
About predators. Bears on the benefit of masting, not on how plants synchronize.
CORRECT. Coupling requires that out-of-step plants set little fruit (and so stay undepleted). If fruit set doesn't depend on how many neighbors flower, nothing pulls stragglers into step.
Consistent with reserves limiting flowering, which the models assume.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Whitlock's comparative defense improves on the traditional rationale, but its logic extends further than she proposes, and constitutional law already draws a partly similar line in criminal cases.
Because the psychology behind the exception is unsound, courts should adopt a general preference for early accounts, a change constitutional law already partly requires.
The exception should be abolished, since neither Wigmore's rationale nor Whitlock's comparative defense justifies admitting statements made hours after an event.
Whitlock has shown that early statements are more reliable than trial testimony, and courts should therefore ask whether a speaker had discussed an event before describing it.
Since Crawford and Davis, the excited-utterance exception has ceased to matter in criminal trials, so debate over its rationale is now largely academic.
questions.explanation: The last two paragraphs give the author's verdict: Whitlock's shift 'gives the exception better footing,' but 'her argument reaches further than her proposal,' and in criminal cases constitutional law 'already draws a line resembling hers,' though not always the same one. A states this. B turns the author's description of where Whitlock's logic leads into a recommendation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall position.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraphs 4 and 5.

breakdown.analysis: The author's own voice only enters in paragraphs 4 and 5: better footing, BUT 1. her logic goes further than her proposal; 2. in criminal cases the confrontation rules already draw a resembling line. We need the praise and both qualifications, without upgrading any of them into a recommendation.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Better footing' (praise), 'reaches further than her proposal' (first reservation), and the confrontation line that 'resembl[es] hers' but won't always coincide (second point).
Tempting, since the author says Whitlock's logic favors early accounts generally. But the author reports that implication as a 'far larger change than she defends,' without recommending it.
That's the critics' conclusion. The author calls Whitlock's defense better footing.
Whitlock's view without the author's reservations.
Too strong. Davis leaves emergency calls usable; the author says only that the constitutional line resembles Whitlock's.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the critics discussed in the second paragraph maintain that
choices: the stress of a startling event makes deliberate falsehood more likely than it would otherwise be
statements made hours after an event should be admitted only if the speaker remains visibly upset
the alternative to an excited utterance is usually the speaker's later testimony, which other influences have shaped
a speaker may describe an event honestly and still describe it inaccurately because of the stress the event produced
the exception should be limited to statements made to private persons, since statements made to the police are more likely to be shaped by questioning
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says research suggests 'intense stress can distort perception itself, so that a frightened witness may be sincere and still mistaken,' which D paraphrases. A overstates the critics' other point: they say agitation does not prevent lying, not that it encourages it. C is Whitlock's argument.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim the critics make.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The critics make two psychological points: 1. a few moments of agitation don't stop lying; 2. stress can distort perception, so a witness can be sincere and wrong. The trap upgrades point 1 into 'stress makes lying more likely.'

choices.note: Tempting: the critics doubt that agitation prevents lying. But 'little reason to think it prevents' is not 'makes it more likely.' Wrong degree.
That's what courts have done, and the critics count it against the exception.
That's Whitlock's argument, not the critics'.
CORRECT. 'Intense stress can distort perception itself, so that a frightened witness may be sincere and still mistaken.'
Never proposed. The critics want abolition.

questions.stem: The author mentions "a frantic call to the police about an emergency in progress" (last paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: mark the kind of early statement that falls on the permitted side of the constitutional line
illustrate the kind of statement that Crawford bars the prosecution from using against a defendant unless the caller can be cross-examined
show that courts have stretched the exception to cover statements made long after the event they describe
support Whitlock's view that excitement is rough evidence that a statement was made early
suggest that calls to the police are generally more reliable than accounts given to officers in person
questions.explanation: The call is the author's example of a statement that is 'not testimonial,' contrasted with accounts given to officers 'investigating events already past,' which generally are; it marks the side of the constitutional line on which the prosecution may use a statement, as A says. B reverses which side the call falls on, and D gives it a role in Whitlock's argument that the author never assigns it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author mentions the frantic call.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 5 (Crawford, Davis and the frantic call).

breakdown.analysis: Which side of the Crawford/Davis line is the call on? Not testimonial, so usable. Now hold it against Whitlock: a call made during the emergency precedes retelling and questioning, the earliest kind of account. So it illustrates the overlap between the two lines. The trap puts it on the barred side.

choices.note: CORRECT. The call is the author's example of a statement that is 'not testimonial,' set against accounts to officers investigating past events, which generally are. It marks the permitted side of the line.
Reversed. The call is the example of what is not testimonial; the account to investigating officers is the barred kind.
Stretching is paragraph 2's point; an emergency in progress is the opposite of 'long after.'
Tempting, since such a call is both excited and early. But the author uses it to illustrate the constitutional line, not to support her view of excitement.
The author says the line is not about sorting reliable from unreliable accounts.

questions.stem: Based on her argument in the third paragraph, Whitlock would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The exception should be extended to calm statements made just after an event, since these too precede later influences on memory.
Statements made under stress are generally more accurate than calm statements made at about the same time.
The critics who urged that the exception be abolished were mistaken about how intense stress affects a witness's perception.
Testimony given months after an event is so unreliable that courts should ordinarily exclude it in favor of earlier statements.
Whether a statement should be admitted depends partly on how trustworthy the evidence offered in its place would be.
questions.explanation: Whitlock says 'the question a rule of evidence must answer is comparative': an excited utterance should be weighed against the alternative, usually later testimony, which E states generally. A is the author's extension of her logic, which the author says goes beyond what 'she defends.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer a view Whitlock holds.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3; paragraph 4, second sentence (what she does not defend).

breakdown.analysis: What's Whitlock's key move? Not 'excited statements are reliable' (she concedes they aren't, in themselves) but the comparison: judge them against what you'd get instead. The trap is the author's extension of her reasoning, which the author says she doesn't adopt.

choices.note: Tempting, but wrong party. The author is the one who says her logic reaches calm statements and calls that 'a far larger change than she defends.'
She concedes excited statements aren't reliable in themselves and never makes this comparison.
She says 'the critics are right' on that.
Too strong. She says it is shaped by influences, not that it should be excluded.
CORRECT. 'The question a rule of evidence must answer is comparative': an excited utterance is weighed against the later testimony that would replace it.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A general preference for early accounts would be a better rule than the narrower reform Whitlock herself defends.
The exception should be retained in its present form, since no better rationale for it has been offered.
Research on memory shows that excited utterances are generally less accurate than the testimony the same speakers give months later at trial.
The line drawn by the law of confrontation always coincides with Whitlock's.
Reasoning like Whitlock's would rank some statements that courts now admit below some statements that the exception does not reach.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says courts admit statements made 'even hours after an event' if the speaker still seemed upset; the first paragraph requires stress of excitement, so a calm statement falls outside the exception; and the fourth paragraph says that on Whitlock's logic a calm statement made immediately afterward has 'a stronger claim than an excited statement made hours later.' Together these support E. A turns the author's description of where her logic leads into an endorsement.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author is committed to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, second sentence; paragraph 2, third sentence; paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so combine three pieces. 1. The exception requires stress of excitement, so calm statements aren't covered. 2. Courts admit upset statements made hours later. 3. On Whitlock's logic, calm-and-immediate beats excited-but-hours-later. So some admitted statements rank below some excluded ones. Watch for answers that turn the author's report into a recommendation.

choices.note: Tempting: the author says her logic favors early accounts generally. But the author calls that 'a far larger change than she defends' and never says it would be better.
The author calls Whitlock's defense better footing than the traditional rationale, and never endorses the present form.
The critics' research says stress can distort perception; no comparison with later testimony is reported.
Contradicts the last sentence: 'it will not always coincide with Whitlock's.'

CORRECT. Paragraph 2: courts admit upset statements made hours later. Paragraph 1: the exception requires the stress of excitement, so a calm statement isn't covered. Paragraph 4: on Whitlock's logic a calm immediate statement beats an excited one made hours later.

questions.stem: Given Whitlock's reasons for valuing excited utterances, which one of the following statements would she regard as having the strongest claim to admission?
choices: A shopkeeper, apparently composed, describes a theft to her employer the next morning, having said nothing about it to anyone overnight.
A robbery victim, still shaking an hour afterward, describes the robber to police after talking the event over with two other witnesses.
A frightened pedestrian tells a passerby what she saw a few minutes after an assault, having spoken to no one in the meantime.
A bystander, extremely agitated, repeats to a neighbor an account of an accident that she heard another bystander give moments earlier.
A driver, upset after a collision, describes it after a police officer has questioned him closely.
questions.explanation: Whitlock values a statement because it precedes 'repeated retelling, conversations with other witnesses, questioning by investigators, and the reconstruction that memory performs over time.' C precedes all four. A is the near-miss: the shopkeeper has told no one, but a night's delay allows memory reconstruction, the fourth influence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Whitlock's reasons to pick the statement she would favor most.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, third through last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Her list of influences: 1. retelling; 2. conversations with other witnesses; 3. questioning by investigators; 4. memory reconstruction over time. The winner must avoid all four. Check every choice against the whole list, especially item 4.

choices.note: Tempting: no one was told. But a night has passed, allowing the memory reconstruction Whitlock counts as contamination, and nothing signals that the account is early.
Discussed with other witnesses first, which is on her list of influences.
CORRECT. Minutes after, no conversations, no questioning, and the fear is rough evidence the account is fresh. It avoids every influence on her list.
She's passing on another witness's account; that's the kind of influence Whitlock wants to avoid.
Questioning by investigators came first.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: The statements that the confrontation rules allow the prosecution to use are exactly those that Whitlock's reasoning would regard as least contaminated.
Under Whitlock's proposal, a frantic call to the police about an emergency in progress would be excluded because it was made to law enforcement officers.
The constitutional law of confrontation was designed chiefly to separate reliable accounts from unreliable ones.
Some statements that Whitlock would consider shaped by later influences could be kept from a criminal jury even if they were excited utterances.
The critics described in the second paragraph would regard the Davis decision as a step toward abolishing the exception.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says accounts given to officers 'investigating events already past' are generally testimonial and barred 'whatever hearsay exception they satisfy'; the third paragraph lists 'questioning by investigators' among the influences Whitlock says shape later accounts. Combining these supports D. A overstates the overlap the author describes, since the line 'will not always coincide with Whitlock's.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement best supported by combining the constitutional discussion with Whitlock's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, third sentence (influences); paragraph 5 (Crawford and Davis).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase; look for a link across paragraphs. Crawford/Davis: accounts to officers investigating past events are testimonial and barred whatever hearsay exception applies. Whitlock: questioning by investigators contaminates accounts. So some accounts she'd consider contaminated can be barred even if they're excited utterances. The trap says the two lines match exactly; the author says they won't always.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author says the lines resemble each other. But 'exactly' contradicts 'it will not always coincide with Whitlock's.'
Her test asks whether the speaker had discussed the event; such a call is about as early as statements get.
Contradicts the last sentence, which says the line protects the right to confront accusers rather than sorting by reliability.

CORRECT. Accounts to officers 'investigating events already past' are generally testimonial and barred 'whatever hearsay exception they satisfy' (paragraph 5); such accounts follow 'questioning by investigators,' one of Whitlock's contaminating influences (paragraph 3).
Nothing connects the critics to Davis.

passages.title: The harmony of The Sacred Harp
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When The Sacred Harp, a tunebook compiled in Georgia by Benjamin Franklin White and Elisha J. King, first appeared in 1844, it entered a crowded market. Dozens of collections printed in "shape notes"—a notation in which the form of each note head indicates the syllable to which it is sung—were then in use in the singing schools of the rural South. That The Sacred Harp, unlike most of its rivals, became the basis of a practice that continues today has drawn considerable scholarly attention, much of it devoted to explaining why its music sounds as it does.

To the nineteenth-century reformers who promoted European models of church music, Lowell Mason prominent among them, the answer was simple: the composers did not know any better. The voices in shape-note music frequently move in parallel fifths and octaves; chords often omit the third, leaving bare, open sonorities; and the principal melody is assigned not to the highest part but to the tenor. All of these violated the rules of European harmony, and all were taken as signs of rustic incompetence.

The ethnomusicologist Lena Hartsell has argued that these features are better understood as consequences of how the music is sung. Sacred Harp singers do not perform for listeners. They sit in a hollow square, one voice part to each side, facing a leader who stands in the center and beats time. Because every singer hears the music from inside it, Hartsell contends, no part can be treated as mere accompaniment; each must be worth singing for its own sake, which accounts both for the melodic independence of every line and for a tolerance of parallel motion that a texture built around a single dominant tune would not require. Open fifths, she adds, ring out when untrained singers sing at full voice, whereas thirds are the intervals such singers most readily sing out of tune.

Hartsell's account has been welcomed for treating the music as a community's practice rather than as a failed attempt at something else. Some historians, however, doubt that the practice can explain how the tunes came to be written. A good many of the book's pieces were not composed for it; they were taken from earlier tunebooks, among them works by New England composers such as William Billings, who worked in the late eighteenth century. On this view the harmonic idiom came first, and what the hollow square explains is not why the music was composed as it was but why, among the many styles available to Southern singers, this one endured, since music in which every part carries interest suits a gathering in which everyone sings. Hartsell's defenders reply that the New England singing schools in which the idiom took shape were themselves gatherings of learners singing together rather than performances for an audience.

passages.title: The collateral source rule
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

Under the collateral source rule, a long-standing doctrine of American tort law, the damages owed by a defendant found liable for an injury are not reduced by compensation the plaintiff has received from sources independent of the defendant. If an injured pedestrian's medical bills have been paid by her health insurer, or her lost wages replaced by disability benefits, the driver who struck her must nonetheless pay the full amount of those losses, and in many jurisdictions the jury is not even told of the other payments.

The rule's critics contend that it permits the plaintiff to be compensated twice for a single loss. Tort damages are meant to restore an injured person, so far as money can, to the position she would have occupied had she not been harmed; they are not meant to leave her better off. A rule that allows recovery of expenses someone else has already paid departs from that principle without any compensatory justification. Nor does the cost of the departure fall on wrongdoers alone. Liability insurers pass it on through the premiums they charge, and those premiums are paid by physicians, businesses, and motorists generally, most of whom have injured no one.

For these reasons a number of state legislatures, particularly during the waves of tort reform in the 1970s and 1980s, modified the rule, either by permitting juries to hear evidence of collateral payments or by directing courts to deduct such payments from the award. Statutes of this kind bring damages into line with actual loss, and they do so at little cost to plaintiffs, who remain fully compensated for what they have suffered.

Passage B

Defenders of the collateral source rule are often accused of favoring windfalls, but the accusation rests on an incomplete picture of how collateral payments work. In a great many cases the plaintiff does not keep the money twice. Health insurers and other payers commonly hold rights of subrogation or reimbursement: having paid the plaintiff's expenses, they are entitled to be repaid from any recovery she obtains from the person who injured her. Where such rights exist, abolishing the rule prevents no double recovery, since none would occur; it merely shifts the cost of the injury from the wrongdoer to the insurer and, ultimately, to the insurer's other customers.
