Even where no right of repayment exists, it is not obvious that the defendant should be the one to profit. A plaintiff who bought insurance paid premiums for it, often for years, and an employee's disability benefits are part of the compensation she earned. Between an injured person who provided against misfortune and the person who caused it, the law has reasonably preferred that any surplus go to the former. The rule also preserves deterrence: a defendant whose liability shrinks whenever the victim happens to be insured has correspondingly less reason to take care.

passages.title: Harrison and the Board of Longitude
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
For most of the eighteenth century, a ship far from land could find its latitude easily but its longitude only with great difficulty, and the errors cost ships and lives. In 1714 the British Parliament offered a reward of up to £20,000 for a method of finding longitude at sea, and appointed commissioners, later known as the Board of Longitude, to judge proposals. The sequel is usually told as a contest between two methods and two kinds of men. On one side stood John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker whose fourth marine timekeeper kept time with remarkable accuracy on a trial voyage to Jamaica in 1761–1762. On the other stood the astronomers, above all Nevil Maskelyne, Astronomer Royal from 1765, who championed the method of lunar distances, which derived the time at a reference meridian from the Moon's observed position among the stars. In the popular telling, a Board dominated by astronomers repeatedly changed the rules to deny an outsider the reward his invention had earned.

Revisionist historians, among them Clare Ashdown, have argued that this account mistakes the Board's caution for prejudice. The commissioners were charged with rewarding a method that would be of practical use at sea, and they could reasonably doubt, Ashdown points out, that a single timekeeper, however precise, constituted such a method. No one knew whether other makers could reproduce Harrison's watch, or at what price, and the Board accordingly required him to disclose its construction and to show that copies could be made. That demand was vindicated, Ashdown argues, when a copy by the watchmaker Larcum Kendall performed admirably on James Cook's second Pacific voyage. The lunar method, meanwhile, though laborious, required only a good instrument and printed tables, which Maskelyne's Nautical Almanac supplied from the late 1760s, and for decades it remained the cheaper and more widely practiced technique.

Ashdown's correction is welcome, but it leaves an important question unresolved. To show that the commissioners' demands were reasonable is not to show that they were made for the reasons the commissioners gave. The Board's treatment of Harrison was inconsistent: conditions were added after trials had been completed, and the last substantial sum Harrison received came not from the Board but from Parliament, in 1773, after he had appealed to the king. Whether such conduct reflected principled doubt, institutional self-interest, or the ordinary friction of a committee confronting a technology it did not fully understand cannot be settled by showing that its doubts were plausible ones.

The chronometer did eventually displace the lunar method, though not in the form Harrison had given it. Its dominance depended on later makers, notably John Arnold and Thomas Earnshaw, whose simpler designs could be made in quantity at far lower cost, and even after chronometers became standard equipment, navigators long continued to check them against lunar observations.

passages.title: The Mpemba effect
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Since 2016 it has become common to say that the Mpemba effect—the claim that hot water can freeze faster than cold—has been shown not to exist. The claim is old: Aristotle reported it, and Francis Bacon and René Descartes repeated versions of it. It entered modern physics only in 1969, however, when Erasto Mpemba, who as a secondary-school student in what is now Tanzania had noticed that a warm ice-cream mixture froze before a cooler one, published an account of the observation with the physicist Denis Osborne. The verdict that the effect is illusory rests on a study whose findings are sound but whose bearing on Mpemba's claim has been misjudged.

That study measured, with care, the time that hot and cold samples took to cool to 0°C. Its authors found no case in which the hotter sample got there first, and they showed that apparent differences of the reported kind could arise merely from where in a sample the temperature was measured. Coming after decades of inconsistent reports, it was widely received as settling the matter. The result is valuable, and it casts doubt on a number of published claims. But reaching 0°C is not freezing.

Liquid water seldom begins to freeze at 0°C. It ordinarily cools further, remaining liquid until an impurity or a flaw in its container provides a site at which ice crystals can start to grow, and the temperature at which this happens varies widely from trial to trial. Several experimenters have reported that water previously heated tends to begin freezing at a higher temperature than water that was never heated, perhaps because heating alters the impurities or dissolved gases that serve as such sites. Where that is so, a hot sample can lag behind a cold one all the way down to 0°C and still form ice first, and a study that stops its clock at 0°C cannot detect the difference, however carefully it is conducted. Evaporation can add a further advantage after that point: in an uncovered container the hot sample has lost more of its water to the air, and so has less left to solidify once freezing begins.

The question Mpemba raised, then, is not the one the 2016 study answered. Mpemba was concerned with when his mixture set, not with when it passed a particular temperature, and on that question the relevant evidence comes from experiments that record the appearance of ice, which have reported the effect under some conditions and not under others. What the effect now requires is not more precise timing of the approach to 0°C but systematic study of nucleation: of which impurities, containers, and histories of heating lead water to begin freezing at higher temperatures, and why.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: defend an account that traces the distinctive harmony of a musical tradition to the way that tradition is performed
argue that a performance practice explains why a musical style survived rather than why it was composed as it was
describe a musical idiom and present competing accounts of how it relates to the way it is sung
trace the influence of New England composers on Southern music
show that nineteenth-century reformers misjudged a musical tradition by holding it to the standards of European church music
questions.explanation: The passage describes shape-note harmony and then presents the reformers' view, Hartsell's account, the historians' objection, and the defenders' reply, without taking a side; C states this. B is the closest trap: it presents the historians' position as the author's thesis, but the passage attributes it to 'some historians' and ends with the defenders' reply. A likewise makes the author an advocate for Hartsell.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage as a whole is trying to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Scan the paragraph openings: paragraph 1 (the tunebook), paragraph 2 (the reformers), paragraph 3 (Hartsell), paragraph 4 (some historians, then the defenders' reply).

breakdown.analysis: Is the author arguing for anything? Look at who owns each view: reformers, Hartsell, 'some historians,' 'Hartsell's defenders.' The author never says who's right. When the author is a referee rather than a player, the purpose answer uses neutral verbs like 'describe' and 'set out.' We need an answer about describing the music and presenting competing explanations of it.

choices.note: Tempting, because Hartsell's account gets the most space. But the passage also reports the historians' objection and never endorses either side. 'Defend' is too strong for what the author does.
Tempting: this is a position the passage states. But it belongs to 'some historians,' and the passage ends by giving Hartsell's defenders a reply. Stating a view isn't arguing for it. Wrong party.

CORRECT. The passage describes the harmony, then reports three views (the reformers', Hartsell's, the historians') and a reply from Hartsell's defenders. It describes and weighs; it doesn't take a side.
The New England composers come up as evidence in one paragraph. Too narrow to be the purpose.
The passage implies the reformers' view was too simple, but they appear only in paragraph 2. The rest of the passage is about Hartsell and her critics.

questions.stem: According to the passage, reformers such as Lowell Mason attributed the distinctive features of shape-note harmony to
choices: the inability of untrained rural singers to perform music written according to European rules
the influence of earlier tunebooks
the custom of giving the principal melody to the tenor rather than to the highest part
a lack of knowledge on the part of those who wrote the music
the acoustics of the buildings where the music was sung
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that to reformers like Mason 'the composers did not know any better' and that the features were taken as 'signs of rustic incompetence'; D paraphrases this. A is the near-miss: it blames the singers rather than the composers. C reuses the tenor detail, which is one of the features, not the reformers' explanation of them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the reformers blamed for the parallel fifths, open chords, and tenor melody.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Straight detail question. Paragraph 2: 'the answer was simple: the composers did not know any better.' Prephrase: the composers' ignorance. Watch for an answer that blames the wrong people.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'rustic incompetence' sounds like it could be about the singers. But paragraph 2 blames the composers: 'the composers did not know any better.' Untrained singers belong to Hartsell's argument in paragraph 3. Wrong people.
The New England tunebooks are the historians' point in paragraph 4. The reformers never mention them.
Same words as paragraph 2, wrong relation. The tenor melody is one of the features the reformers objected to, not the cause they gave for the features.
CORRECT. 'The composers did not know any better' and 'rustic incompetence' = the people who wrote the music lacked knowledge.
Acoustics never come up as the reformers' explanation.

questions.stem: In the first sentence of the fourth paragraph, the phrase "a failed attempt at something else" most probably refers to
choices: an early and imperfect stage in the development of American church music
a style of music that its own composers eventually came to regard as unsatisfactory
music measured against the conventions of a tradition other than its own
music intended to be performed before audiences but sung instead by participants
an unsuccessful effort to explain the music's sound by reference to the way it is sung
questions.explanation: Hartsell's account is welcomed for treating the music as a practice in its own right 'rather than as a failed attempt at something else', which points back to the reformers, who judged the music by European rules and found it incompetent (second paragraph); C says this. E misreads the phrase as describing a failed scholarly explanation, and A invents a developmental frame the passage never uses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decode 'a failed attempt at something else.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first sentence; connect it to paragraph 2.

breakdown.analysis: A failed attempt at what? Go back to paragraph 2: the reformers saw shape-note music as bad European harmony, written by people who 'did not know any better.' That's treating it as a failed try at being European church music. Prephrase: the music judged as a botched version of a different tradition.

choices.note: Invented frame. The passage never treats shape-note music as a stage in a progression toward something better.
Nothing in the passage says the composers judged their own music.

CORRECT. This is the reformers' approach from paragraph 2: they measured shape-note music against European harmony and found it incompetent. The phrase names that way of judging it, which Hartsell's account avoids.
Borrows the passage's performance vocabulary in the wrong relation. The point isn't about intended versus actual audiences.

Tempting, because paragraph 4 is about rival explanations. But 'something else' is what the music was supposedly trying to be, not a scholarly theory. Hartsell's account is the one being praised here.

questions.stem: The reference to William Billings in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to
choices: support the claim that the music's style predates the tunebook in which it survives
identify a composer whose tunes are central to Hartsell's analysis of the hollow square
illustrate the variety of musical styles that were available to Southern singers during the nineteenth century
suggest that the reformers' objections were aimed chiefly at New England composers
show that the eighteenth-century singing schools were gatherings of participants rather than performances
questions.explanation: Billings exemplifies the earlier New England composers whose tunes were drawn into The Sacred Harp, which supports the historians' claim that 'the harmonic idiom came first'; A states this. C borrows the phrase 'many styles available to Southern singers', but Billings illustrates the origin of one style. E describes what Hartsell's defenders say about the singing schools, a different point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why are Billings and his tunes mentioned?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second through fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read what follows Billings: 'On this view the harmonic idiom came first.' So Billings is evidence that the style existed decades before The Sacred Harp and its practice. Prephrase: to show the style is older than the book.

choices.note: CORRECT. Billings worked in the late eighteenth century, and his tunes were drawn into the 1844 book. That's evidence for 'the harmonic idiom came first.'
Billings appears in the historians' objection to Hartsell, not in her analysis.
Tempting, because 'many styles available to Southern singers' appears in the next sentence. But Billings is the source of the one style that endured, not an example of variety.
The passage never says whom the reformers' objections targeted, beyond shape-note composers generally.
That's the defenders' reply in the last sentence, which Billings is not used to support. Right paragraph, wrong role.

questions.stem: The reply attributed to Hartsell's defenders in the last sentence of the passage suggests that they would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?
choices: The New England composers wrote their tunes specifically for singers who sat facing one another in a hollow square.
Hartsell's explanation accounts for the New England tunes just as fully as for tunes written for The Sacred Harp itself.
The style endured in the South chiefly because it had first been composed by respected New England musicians.
The tunes' early date does not by itself show that Hartsell's explanation cannot apply to their composition.
The reformers were correct that the composers lacked training in European harmony.
questions.explanation: The historians argue that the idiom predates the hollow-square practice, so the practice cannot explain its composition; the defenders reply that the New England singing schools where the idiom arose were also groups singing together rather than performing for listeners. So the early date of the tunes does not by itself rule out a participatory explanation of their composition, as D says. B is the near-miss: the reply reopens that possibility but does not show that Hartsell's account fits the New England tunes 'just as fully.' A overreaches: the reply says nothing about a hollow square in New England.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the defenders' reply implies.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: the historians' objection, then the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Why would the defenders bring up the New England singing schools? Because the historians said 'the idiom came first,' meaning before the participatory practice. The defenders' comeback: the idiom was born in a participatory setting too. So the historians' inference (earlier date, therefore the practice can't explain composition) has a gap: Hartsell's mechanism (no audience, so every part must be worth singing) could have been at work from the start. The reply opens a possibility; it doesn't prove Hartsell right. We need an answer that says no more than that.

choices.note: Tempting, since it pushes the defenders' point back to New England. But the reply says only that the singing schools were gatherings of learners rather than performances. Nothing says they used a hollow square. Too specific.

Tempting: it's the direction the defenders are pushing. But the reply only reopens the possibility; it says nothing about how fully Hartsell's specific points (the hollow square, the leader, loud untrained singing) fit the New England schools. 'Just as fully' is too strong.
Garbles the argument. Neither side says New England origin explains survival.

CORRECT. The historians reasoned: the tunes came first, so the practice can't explain their composition. The defenders answer that the tunes were born among participants singing together too. So the date of the tunes alone doesn't rule out Hartsell's kind of explanation for their composition.
The reply has nothing to do with the composers' training.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the position of the historians described in the fourth paragraph?
choices: The eighteenth-century New England singing schools seated their students by voice part facing one another, much as Sacred Harp singers do.
Some tunes in later editions of The Sacred Harp were composed by Southern singers who had sung in the hollow square for years.
Lowell Mason's collections of church music sold widely throughout the South in the decades after 1844.
Among Southern singing groups, only those that sang in the hollow square abandoned tunebooks built around a single dominant melody.
Many shape-note tunebooks other than The Sacred Harp also contained tunes drawn from New England collections.
questions.explanation: The historians hold that the idiom came first and that the hollow square explains why it endured, since it suits a group in which everyone sings. D shows the rival kind of music falling out of use precisely among hollow-square groups, which supports that selection story. A is the trap: a hollow-square-like arrangement in the New England schools would let the practice have shaped the idiom from the start, which helps Hartsell, not the historians.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a fact that supports the historians' view: the practice explains why the style lasted, not how it was composed.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, second through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The historians' claim has two parts: 1. the style existed before the practice; 2. the practice favored it over rivals. Supporting part 2 means showing the competing style losing out where the hollow square operates. Watch for answers that support the defenders instead.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the singing schools. But it helps the other side: if the idiom arose in a hollow-square-like setting, the practice could have shaped the composition, which is what the historians deny.
This suggests the practice may have shaped new compositions, which cuts against the historians, if anything.
Doesn't tell us why the shape-note style endured among hollow-square singers.

CORRECT. The historians say the hollow square selected an existing style: it favored music where every part is interesting. Here the rival style dies out exactly where the hollow square operates. That's selection in action.
Shows the New England tunes circulated widely, but says nothing about why the style endured where the hollow square was used. Topical but inert.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: describing the statutes that modified the collateral source rule during the tort reforms of the 1970s and 1980s
comparing the rule's effects on plaintiffs with its effects on liability insurers
explaining how the collateral source rule came to be adopted in American tort law
evaluating proposals that would require insurers to seek repayment of their expenses from plaintiffs
considering whether a rule that disregards a plaintiff's payments from other sources yields unwarranted recoveries
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that the collateral source rule lets plaintiffs be paid twice and supports statutes that modify it; passage B argues that the 'windfall' charge is mistaken or that any surplus properly goes to the plaintiff. Both assess whether the rule produces unjustified recoveries, as E says. A describes only the last paragraph of passage A, and passage B never discusses the reform statutes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the shared topic of both passages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph ('compensated twice'); passage B, first sentence ('accused of favoring windfalls').

breakdown.analysis: What's the fight about? A says the rule gives plaintiffs double recovery; B says that's mostly not true, and where it is, the plaintiff deserves the surplus more than the defendant. So both are judging whether the rule gives plaintiffs more than they should get. In a 'both passages' question, test every choice against both passages.

choices.note: Tempting because it's accurate to passage A's last paragraph. But passage B never mentions the reform statutes. A 'both' answer has to fit both.
Neither passage makes this comparison. A mentions liability insurers passing on costs; B doesn't discuss liability insurers at all.
Neither passage explains the rule's origins. A calls it 'long-standing'; that's all.
Passage B mentions existing rights of repayment; nobody evaluates proposals to require them.
CORRECT. A says the recoveries lack justification ('without any compensatory justification'); B says they're often not double at all and are justified when they are. Same question, opposite answers.

questions.stem: According to passage A, in many jurisdictions that apply the collateral source rule
choices: plaintiffs must disclose any insurance payments to the court before trial
the jury deciding damages is not informed that the plaintiff has received payments from other sources
insurers that have paid a plaintiff's expenses may recover those amounts from the defendant directly, without involving the plaintiff
damages for lost wages are reduced by disability benefits, but damages for medical expenses are not
defendants may introduce evidence of a plaintiff's insurance only when lost wages are at issue
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph of passage A says that 'in many jurisdictions the jury is not even told of the other payments'; B paraphrases this. C borrows the idea of repayment from passage B and changes who pays: passage B says insurers are repaid from the plaintiff's recovery, not by the defendant directly.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says happens 'in many jurisdictions.'

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Simple locate-and-match. Passage A: 'in many jurisdictions the jury is not even told of the other payments.' Prephrase: juries don't hear about collateral payments.

choices.note: Nothing about pretrial disclosure in either passage.
CORRECT. 'The jury is not even told of the other payments' = the jury isn't informed of collateral payments.
Tempting if you're mixing the passages. Repayment rights are in passage B, and there the insurer is repaid out of the plaintiff's recovery, not by the defendant directly. Wrong passage, wrong party.
Opposite of the rule. Under the rule, neither wages nor medical bills are reduced.
Made up. Passage A doesn't carve out lost wages for special treatment.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions rights of subrogation or reimbursement (first paragraph of passage B) primarily in order to
choices: argue that collateral insurers, rather than plaintiffs, are the true beneficiaries of the collateral source rule
explain why liability insurers pass the rule's costs on to policyholders
show that the rule frequently does not leave plaintiffs with two payments for the same loss
propose a means by which legislatures could prevent double recoveries without changing the collateral source rule itself
concede that plaintiffs receive windfalls whenever no insurer holds such a right
questions.explanation: Right after saying that 'in a great many cases the plaintiff does not keep the money twice,' passage B explains that insurers holding these rights are repaid from the plaintiff's recovery; the rights are the reason double recovery often doesn't happen, as C says. A is tempting because insurers do get repaid, but passage B never says insurers are the rule's real beneficiaries.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why does passage B bring up subrogation and reimbursement?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The claim comes first: 'In a great many cases the plaintiff does not keep the money twice.' Then the mechanism: the insurer gets repaid out of her recovery. So subrogation is the evidence that the double-recovery charge is overblown. Prephrase: to show plaintiffs often aren't paid twice.

choices.note: Tempting, because the insurer is repaid. But passage B never calls insurers the 'true beneficiaries'; it uses repayment only to show the plaintiff isn't paid twice. Overreach.
That's passage A's point about liability insurers and premiums. Wrong passage, wrong kind of insurer.
CORRECT. Subrogation means the insurer takes its money back from the award, so the plaintiff ends up paid once. That answers the double-recovery charge.
Passage B describes rights that already exist; it doesn't propose any legislation.
Passage B doesn't concede windfalls. Its second paragraph argues that even without repayment rights, any surplus rightly goes to the plaintiff.

questions.stem: The authors of the passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: tort damages are intended to compensate an injured person for losses caused by the defendant
health insurers often pay the medical expenses of people injured by others
a defendant's liability for an injury should depend on whether the defendant acted carelessly
juries should be told about collateral payments that are subject to an insurer's right of reimbursement
awards under the collateral source rule commonly exceed the losses that plaintiffs actually bear
questions.explanation: Passage A holds that the rule lets plaintiffs be 'compensated twice' and that reform statutes 'bring damages into line with actual loss'; passage B replies that 'in a great many cases the plaintiff does not keep the money twice.' They disagree about whether awards typically exceed actual loss, as E says. D is tempting, but neither author takes a position on informing juries specifically about reimbursable payments.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would accept and the other would reject.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second and third paragraphs; passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: A: the rule overcompensates (double recovery; statutes bring damages 'into line with actual loss'). B: often it doesn't, because insurers get repaid. To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Check each answer for a clear position from both.

choices.note: Both would accept this. A says it outright; B never questions it.
Both assume this. A's pedestrian example and B's subrogation discussion both rely on it.
Neither passage discusses the standard of fault. Both take liability as given.
Tempting, because A mentions juries and B mentions reimbursement. But no one combines them, and neither author takes a position on this specific case.
CORRECT. A says yes (compensated twice, damages out of line with actual loss); B says often no (the plaintiff does not keep the money twice).

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the first paragraph of passage B and the second paragraph of passage A?
choices: The first paragraph of passage B offers a specific case that illustrates a general claim about double recovery made in the second paragraph of passage A.
The first paragraph of passage B disputes a factual claim underlying passage A's second paragraph and voices a similar concern about who bears costs.
The first paragraph of passage B accepts the compensation principle stated in passage A but denies that the rule is consistent with it.
The first paragraph of passage B proposes a remedy for the rising premiums described in passage A's second paragraph, namely enforcing insurers' existing rights of repayment.
The first paragraph of passage B accepts the facts asserted in passage A's second paragraph but denies that those facts support passage A's normative conclusion about the rule.
questions.explanation: Passage A's second paragraph rests on the claim that plaintiffs are compensated twice and complains that costs fall on premium payers who injured no one; passage B's first paragraph denies that double recovery usually occurs and warns that abolishing the rule shifts costs onto insurers' other customers. B captures both moves. E is the main trap: passage B's first paragraph rejects A's factual premise rather than accepting it; it is passage B's second paragraph that argues on normative grounds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B's first paragraph responds to passage A's second paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, paragraph 2 (double recovery; costs on innocent premium payers). Passage B, paragraph 1 (no double recovery where repayment rights exist; costs shift to insurers' other customers).

breakdown.analysis: A's second paragraph: plaintiffs get paid twice, and innocent premium payers foot the bill. B's first paragraph: no, they usually don't get paid twice, and killing the rule just moves the bill to a different set of innocent customers. So B attacks A's factual premise and borrows A's own worry about innocent people paying. We need both pieces.

choices.note: B's first paragraph contradicts A rather than illustrating it. Subrogation is evidence against double recovery.
CORRECT. It denies the double-recovery premise ('does not keep the money twice') and turns A's concern about costs on people who injured no one against reform ('the insurer's other customers').
Half right. B never contests the compensation principle, but its point is that the rule often is consistent with it (no double recovery). It doesn't deny consistency.
Tempting if you read subrogation as a fix. But B describes rights that already exist and uses them to deny that double recovery happens; it doesn't propose enforcing them as a remedy for premiums.
Tempting, because passage B as a whole does make a normative argument. But that's its second paragraph. The first paragraph denies A's facts ('does not keep the money twice'). Wrong paragraph.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to respond to the claim in the last sentence of passage A that statutes modifying the rule cost plaintiffs little by pointing out that
choices: the statutes cost plaintiffs little only because collateral insurers are ordinarily repaid out of plaintiffs' recoveries
plaintiffs who paid for their coverage or earned their benefits would lose its value to those who injured them
the cost of such statutes falls chiefly on liability insurers and on those who buy their policies
many injured plaintiffs have no collateral sources of compensation at all and so are unaffected by such statutes
plaintiffs frequently fail to recover the full amount of their losses even in jurisdictions that continue to apply the collateral source rule
questions.explanation: Passage B's second paragraph argues that the plaintiff paid premiums or earned her benefits, and that deducting them lets the defendant profit from her foresight; that is the cost to plaintiffs that passage A overlooks, as B says. C is a near-miss: passage B does say reform shifts costs, but onto the collateral insurer's other customers, not onto liability insurers, which in fact benefit from smaller awards.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how passage B's author would answer passage A's claim that reform costs plaintiffs little.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of passage A; passage B, second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: A says: plaintiffs lose nothing, they're still fully compensated. Would B agree? B's second paragraph: the plaintiff paid for that insurance or earned those benefits, and deducting them hands their value to the wrongdoer. So the plaintiff does lose something: what she paid for. We need an answer about plaintiffs losing the value of their own provision to the defendant.

choices.note: Garbled. Under a deduction statute the collateral insurer typically can't be repaid; that's B's point about cost-shifting. And B's response here is about plaintiffs, not insurers.
CORRECT. Straight from B's second paragraph: premiums paid and benefits earned are the plaintiff's own provision, and deduction lets the defendant profit from it.
Tempting, because B does say reform shifts costs. But B's shifted costs land on the collateral insurer's other customers. Liability insurers pay less under reform, not more. Wrong party.
Might be true, but it doesn't answer A; it just narrows who's affected. B makes no such point.
New information. B never makes claims about undercompensation under the rule.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the reasoning in the second paragraph of passage B?
choices: A person injured in an accident who later receives gifts of money from sympathetic relatives should have those gifts deducted from any damages owed by the person who caused the accident.
A tenant whose own carelessness contributed to a fire started by a neighbor may recover only part of the damage from the neighbor.
An employer that continued to pay an injured employee's wages may sue the person who caused the injury to recover them.
A lender that insured itself against default is barred from suing the borrower for amounts its insurer has already paid it.
A landlord who wrongfully keeps a tenant's deposit must repay all of it, though a relocation benefit the tenant earned already covered her new deposit.
questions.explanation: Passage B's second paragraph holds that a wrongdoer should not reduce what he owes by pointing to protection the victim paid for or earned. In E the wrongdoing landlord must pay in full despite a benefit the tenant earned, matching every element. C matches passage B's first paragraph (a payer's right to be repaid), not the second, and D reaches the opposite result.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation that follows the same principle as passage B's second paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: B's second paragraph boiled down: the victim provided for misfortune (paid premiums, earned benefits); the wrongdoer caused the loss; the wrongdoer doesn't get to pocket the value of the victim's provision. So the match needs: 1. a wrongdoer; 2. a cushion the victim paid for or earned; 3. the wrongdoer still pays in full. Check all three.

choices.note: Opposite result: the collateral payment is deducted. And a gift isn't something the victim paid for or earned.
This is about the victim's own fault reducing recovery, a different issue entirely.
Tempting, because it's a real collateral-source situation. But it matches B's first paragraph (a payer recovering what it paid), not the second paragraph's point about the victim's own provision.
Reversed. Here the insurance protects the wrongdoer (the borrower) from paying, which is exactly what B's second paragraph opposes.
CORRECT. Wrongdoer (landlord), earned cushion (relocation benefit), wrongdoer pays in full anyway. All three elements line up.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Recent historians have shown that the Board had sound grounds for caution about Harrison's timekeeper, but not that caution governed its treatment of him.
The Board of Longitude's resistance to Harrison is better explained by reasonable doubts about reproducing his timekeeper than by the astronomers' prejudice against an outsider.
The revisionist defense of the Board fails, because the Board's treatment of Harrison was inconsistent with the reasons it gave.
The popular account of the search for longitude is mistaken, since the lunar method rather than the chronometer was the solution navigators actually adopted.
Harrison's claim to the reward was vindicated when later makers succeeded in producing reliable chronometers at low cost.
questions.explanation: The author calls Ashdown's correction 'welcome' but argues that showing the Board's demands were reasonable 'is not to show that they were made for the reasons the commissioners gave' (third paragraph); A states this. B is Ashdown's own position. C catches the author's criticism but overstates it: the author never says the revisionist account fails.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall verdict on the two accounts of the Board.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first two sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Three voices: the popular story (prejudiced Board), Ashdown (cautious Board), and the author. Where does the author land? 'Welcome, but it leaves an important question unresolved.' The revisionists showed the doubts were reasonable, not that those doubts were the real motive. We need: revisionists partly right, but the motive question is still open.

choices.note: CORRECT. Concession (the revisionists showed the Board's caution was reasonable) plus the reservation (that doesn't tell us why the Board acted as it did). Both halves of paragraphs 2 and 3.
This is Ashdown's view stated as fact. The author says whether the Board acted from principle or self-interest 'cannot be settled' by showing its doubts were plausible. Wrong party.

Tempting: it captures the author's criticism. But 'fails' is too strong. The author calls the correction 'welcome' and says only that it leaves the motive question unresolved; inconsistency shows the question is open, not that the Board's reasons were false.
Distorts a detail. The lunar method stayed in wide use 'for decades,' but the last paragraph says the chronometer eventually displaced it.
The passage never says the later chronometers vindicated Harrison; they were other makers' simpler designs, 'not in the form Harrison had given it.' And this is one detail, not the main point.

questions.stem: The cost and wide practice of the lunar method are most likely mentioned in the second paragraph in order to
choices: suggest that the astronomers' support for that method need not be explained by loyalty to their own discipline
establish that the lunar method was more accurate than any timekeeper available before the designs of Arnold and Earnshaw
argue that the Board had no reason to require that copies of Harrison's watch be made
indicate that navigators were unwilling to adopt any technique Maskelyne had not approved
confirm the popular account's description of the Board as dominated by astronomers
questions.explanation: Ashdown's thesis is that the popular account 'mistakes the Board's caution for prejudice' (second paragraph), and she notes that the lunar method was cheaper and more widely practiced for decades. That supports A: the astronomers had practical grounds for favoring it. B is the near-miss; the passage praises the method's cost and modest equipment, never its accuracy.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out why the lunar method's cost and wide use are mentioned in Ashdown's argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, first and last sentences; paragraph 1 on the popular account.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a revisionist bring up the lunar method at all? The popular story says astronomers on the Board pushed their own method against an outsider. If that method was actually cheap, practical, and widely used, then backing it looks like good judgment, not bias. Prephrase: the astronomers' preference had legitimate grounds.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ashdown's thesis is that the popular account 'mistakes the Board's caution for prejudice.' If the lunar method was cheap and widely used for decades, astronomers who championed it had good practical reasons, not just partisan ones.
Tempting, but Ashdown's case for the lunar method rests on cost and ease ('required only a good instrument and printed tables'), not on accuracy. The passage never compares accuracy.
Opposite. Ashdown defends the demand for copies.
Nothing about navigators deferring to Maskelyne.
Borrows the popular account's wording. Ashdown's point is about the merits of the astronomers' method, not about who dominated the Board.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the last substantial sum Harrison received came from Parliament after he appealed to the king (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that the Board's treatment of Harrison was motivated by personal hostility toward him as an outsider
suggest that Parliament, unlike the Board, regarded Harrison's timekeeper as a practicable method of finding longitude at sea
offer evidence that the Board's conduct needs more explaining than the reasonableness of its doubts provides
indicate that Harrison was ultimately rewarded more generously than the popular account acknowledges
illustrate the institutional self-interest that the author regards as the likeliest explanation of the Board's conduct
questions.explanation: The payment from Parliament appears as evidence that 'the Board's treatment of Harrison was inconsistent,' and the author's point is that such conduct is not accounted for by showing that the Board's doubts were plausible; C says this. A is the near-miss: the author treats hostility or self-interest as only one possible explanation and says the question cannot be settled this way.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why does the author bring up the payment from Parliament?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The payment sits under the claim 'The Board's treatment of Harrison was inconsistent.' Then comes: whether that reflected principle, self-interest, or committee friction 'cannot be settled by showing that its doubts were plausible ones.' So the payment is evidence that there's something in the Board's conduct Ashdown's argument doesn't explain, not proof of bad motives. Watch for answers that take the evidence further than the author does.

choices.note: Tempting: it's evidence against the Board. But the author lists hostility-type motives only as one possibility ('institutional self-interest') alongside 'principled doubt' and says the question 'cannot be settled' this way. Too strong.
The passage never says what Parliament thought about practicability.

CORRECT. The payment is part of the evidence that the Board's treatment was 'inconsistent.' The author's point is that inconsistent conduct isn't explained just by showing the Board's doubts were plausible.
The popular account says the Board denied him his reward; the payment from Parliament doesn't show he got more than that account admits.
Borrows the passage's phrase, but the author doesn't pick self-interest as most likely. It's one of three options left open.

questions.stem: Ashdown would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The Board was right to favor the method of lunar distances over any method that relied on timekeepers.
Harrison's fourth timekeeper performed less well on its voyage to Jamaica than the popular account claims.
Had Kendall's copy performed poorly, the Board's demand that copies be made would have been unreasonable.
The sum Parliament paid Harrison in 1773 was more than his achievement merited.
Precision in a single instrument is not sufficient to show that a method based on it is practicable.
questions.explanation: Ashdown argues that the commissioners 'could reasonably doubt ... that a single timekeeper, however precise, constituted such a method,' because no one knew whether others could reproduce it (second paragraph); E generalizes this. A overstates her defense of the lunar method, and C reverses her reasoning: the demand was reasonable because the outcome of copying was unknown, so a failed copy would have vindicated the doubt rather than made the demand unreasonable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a view Ashdown holds or is committed to.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2.

breakdown.analysis: What's Ashdown's argument? The Board was asked to reward a practical method; one brilliant watch that nobody else can make isn't a method yet. That's why the Board demanded disclosure and copies. Prephrase: a single precise device isn't proof of a practical method.

choices.note: Tempting, since Ashdown defends the lunar method. But she defends it as cheaper and widely used, not as better than any timekeeper method, and she treats Kendall's copy as a success. 'Over any' is too strong.
Ashdown doesn't challenge the watch's performance. Her point is about reproducibility, 'however precise' the watch was.
Reverses the logic. The demand was reasonable because no one knew whether copies would work. A failed copy would have confirmed the doubt, not made the demand unreasonable.
Ashdown never comments on the 1773 payment; that's the author's evidence in paragraph 3.
CORRECT. This is her 'a single timekeeper, however precise' point in general form: one excellent watch isn't yet a usable method.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the revisionist account of the Board's conduct can most accurately be described as
choices: agreement with much of its evidence, alongside reservations about the conclusion drawn from that evidence
cautious agreement with its explanation of why the Board acted as it did
respect for its aims but doubt about the accuracy of the facts on which it relies
approval of its conclusions, qualified by regret that it slights Harrison's achievement
mild impatience with its readiness to excuse the Board's conduct toward Harrison
questions.explanation: The author calls Ashdown's correction 'welcome' and accepts that the commissioners' demands were reasonable, but says the account 'leaves an important question unresolved' about the Board's motives; A captures this. B is the near-miss: it has the author agreeing with the revisionists' explanation of the Board's conduct, which is the one part the author withholds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the description that matches how the author feels about the revisionists.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, first two sentences and last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What does the author accept? The evidence: the doubts were reasonable, and reproducibility was a real concern. What doesn't the author accept? That this shows why the Board acted as it did. Prephrase: accepts the evidence, doubts the conclusion. All five choices are moderate, so the test is which part of the account each says the author accepts.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author accepts the facts (doubts were reasonable, reproducibility was a real worry, 'welcome') but not the inference that the Board actually acted from caution.
Tempting: the author does agree with part of it. But the part the author withholds agreement from is exactly the explanation of why the Board acted. That's the 'unresolved' question.
Backward. The author accepts the revisionists' facts and questions only what they prove.
The author doesn't approve the conclusion about motives, and never defends Harrison's reputation.
Too negative. 'Welcome' isn't impatience, and the author never calls the account an excuse.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most helps to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: Was a copy of Harrison's timekeeper made by another maker ever tested at sea?
Was the lunar method still widely practiced when Kendall's copy of Harrison's watch went to sea?
What conditions did the Board add after Harrison's timekeeper had completed its trials?
How much money did the Board itself pay Harrison before his appeal to the king?
In what respects were the designs of Arnold and Earnshaw simpler than those of Harrison?
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says a copy by the watchmaker Larcum Kendall 'performed admirably on James Cook's second Pacific voyage,' which answers A. B is the near-miss: the passage says the lunar method was widely practiced 'for decades' from the late 1760s, but it never dates Cook's voyage, so the question can't be answered from the passage alone.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one question the passage actually answers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (Kendall and Cook); check paragraphs 3 and 4 for the others.

breakdown.analysis: No prephrase possible; test each question against the text. Watch for a question that seems answerable by combining two facts but needs a third fact the passage doesn't supply.

choices.note: CORRECT. Yes: Kendall made a copy, and it 'performed admirably' on Cook's second Pacific voyage.
Tempting, because both facts are in the passage. But you'd need the date of Cook's second voyage, which the passage never gives. Outside knowledge doesn't count.
The passage says conditions were added but never says which ones. Raised but not answered.
The passage gives the £20,000 ceiling and mentions a payment from Parliament, but no figure from the Board.
The passage says their designs were simpler but not how.

questions.stem: Which one of the following discoveries would be most relevant to resolving the question that the author says Ashdown's account leaves unresolved?
choices: records showing how much it cost to produce each of Kendall's copies of Harrison's watch
evidence that the chronometers of Arnold and Earnshaw were less accurate than Harrison's
figures showing how many navigators relied on the lunar method in the decades after 1767
private correspondence in which commissioners explained to one another how they intended to vote on Harrison's petitions
proof that Harrison's timekeeper met the terms of the 1714 act on its voyage to Jamaica in 1761–1762
questions.explanation: The question the author leaves open is whether the Board's conduct 'reflected principled doubt, institutional self-interest, or the ordinary friction of a committee' (third paragraph), and the author insists that this 'cannot be settled by showing that its doubts were plausible ones.' Only D, evidence of the commissioners' actual reasoning, addresses motive. A is the trap: production costs bear on whether the doubts were reasonable, which is exactly the kind of evidence the author says cannot settle the question.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the unresolved question, then find the evidence that bears on it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, especially the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What exactly is unresolved? Not whether the Board's doubts were reasonable; Ashdown has shown that. It's why the Board did what it did. The author separates two things: 1. were the doubts plausible? 2. were they the real reason? Evidence about cost, accuracy, or usage answers question 1. We need evidence about question 2, something that shows what the commissioners were actually thinking.

choices.note: Tempting, because cost and reproducibility are central to the passage. But this shows only whether the Board's doubts were reasonable, which Ashdown has already established. The author says reasonableness can't settle motive.
Bears on the chronometers' merits, not on why the Board acted as it did.
Again about whether the Board's preferences were sensible, not about its motives.
CORRECT. The open question is what actually governed the Board's conduct: principle, self-interest, or confusion. Only direct evidence of the commissioners' own reasoning bears on that.
This would show the popular account's grievance had a basis, but a Board acting from principled doubt about reproducibility could still have withheld the reward. It doesn't reveal motive.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The 2016 study was flawed because temperatures were measured at positions in the samples that produced misleading results.
The 2016 study is irrelevant to the Mpemba effect, which experiments recording the appearance of ice have firmly established.
Experiments recording the appearance of ice have established that hot water freezes faster than cold under all conditions.
A sound study has been wrongly read as refuting the effect, since it timed arrival at 0°C rather than the start of freezing.
Whether hot water can freeze faster than cold cannot be settled until researchers agree on a single criterion of freezing.
questions.explanation: The author argues that the 2016 study's findings are sound but have been wrongly read as refuting the effect, because the study timed arrival at 0°C while Mpemba's claim concerns when water begins to freeze (first and last paragraphs); D states this. E is the near-miss: the passage does raise the question of criteria, but the author takes a definite side rather than suspending judgment. A turns a finding of the study into a criticism of it, and B states the thesis too strongly.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's thesis.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1, last sentence; paragraph 2, last sentence; paragraph 4, first sentence.

breakdown.analysis: This author argues for one position: people misread the 2016 study. It's sound, but it measured the wrong thing for Mpemba's question (reaching 0°C, not starting to freeze). We need an answer with both the 'misread' verdict and the reason. Watch for answers that make the author more neutral, or more critical of the study, than the passage is.

choices.note: Tempting, because measurement position comes up in paragraph 2. But that's what the study showed about other experiments; the author calls the study's findings 'sound.' Wrong target.

Tempting: it has the author's direction. But it's too strong. The author says the study 'casts doubt on a number of published claims,' so it isn't irrelevant, and the ice-recording experiments found the effect only 'under some conditions and not under others.'
Too strong. Those experiments 'have reported the effect under some conditions and not under others.'

CORRECT. The thesis is in paragraph 1 ('sound but whose bearing ... has been misjudged') and paragraph 4 ('not the one the 2016 study answered'). The reason is the gap between reaching 0°C and starting to freeze.
Close to a point the passage makes, but the author does pick a criterion (when the water sets) and recommends studying nucleation. This makes the author more agnostic than the passage is.

questions.stem: The passage mentions each of the following as a possible advantage of a hot sample EXCEPT:
choices: reaching 0°C ahead of the cold sample
having less water left to solidify once freezing begins
changes caused by heating in the sites at which ice crystals start to grow
beginning to freeze at a higher temperature than the cold sample
losing more of its water to the air as it cools in an uncovered container
questions.explanation: The passage presents a higher freezing-onset temperature, heating-induced changes in nucleation sites, and evaporation in an uncovered container (losing more water to the air, and so having less left to solidify) as possible advantages of a hot sample. It never presents reaching 0°C first as one; the 2016 study found no such case, and the author's point is that a hot sample can lag 'all the way down to 0°C' and still form ice first, so A is the exception. C is easy to miss because the passage hedges it with 'perhaps.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Four choices are mentioned in the passage as possible advantages of a hot sample; find the one that isn't.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3; paragraph 2 for what the study found about reaching 0°C.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: the answer is the one the passage doesn't mention as an advantage. Common sense says the hot water must get to 0°C first to win, but the passage never says it does; the study found it never does, and the author argues it can lag to 0°C and still form ice first. Check the others against paragraph 3: higher freezing onset, altered nucleation sites, evaporation in an open container, less water to solidify.

choices.note: CORRECT. The passage never presents this as an advantage of a hot sample. On the contrary, the 2016 study found no case of it, and the author's argument is that a hot sample can freeze first even while lagging 'all the way down to 0°C.'
Mentioned: in an uncovered container the hot sample 'has less left to solidify once freezing begins.'
Mentioned, as a hedged explanation: 'perhaps because heating alters the impurities or dissolved gases that serve as such sites.'
Mentioned: previously heated water 'tends to begin freezing at a higher temperature.'
Mentioned: in an uncovered container "the hot sample has lost more of its water to the air" (end of the third paragraph). That loss is the evaporation advantage, so it is not the exception.

questions.stem: Suppose that in an experiment a hot sample and a cold sample, each in a sealed container, reach 0°C at the same moment, and ice then appears in the hot sample first. Which one of the following, as described in the passage, could best account for this result?
choices: the hot sample's having less water left to solidify once freezing began
the hot sample's cooling toward 0°C more rapidly than the cold sample
the greater amount of heat that the hot sample had to lose before reaching 0°C
an effect of the earlier heating on what allows ice crystals to start forming
a difference in where in each sample the temperature was measured
questions.explanation: Because both samples reached 0°C together, the difference must arise afterward; the third paragraph says water keeps cooling until a site lets ice crystals start, and that heating may alter those sites so that heated water begins freezing at a higher temperature. D states this. A is the near-miss: having less water to solidify is a post-0°C advantage in the passage, but it depends on evaporation in an uncovered container, and these containers are sealed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the passage's mechanisms to a new experiment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3.

breakdown.analysis: Two facts in the setup do the work: 1. sealed containers, so evaporation is out; 2. both hit 0°C together, so anything that only affects cooling to 0°C is out. What acts after 0°C in a sealed container? Only the nucleation story: heating may change the sites where ice starts, so heated water starts freezing at a higher temperature. The answer describes it abstractly; don't expect the word 'supercooling.'

choices.note: Tempting: it's a real post-0°C advantage in the passage. But it comes from evaporation, which needs 'an uncovered container,' and these are sealed. It would also bear on finishing, not on when ice first appears.
The setup says both reached 0°C at the same moment, so a faster approach isn't what needs explaining.
Wrong direction. More heat to lose would slow the hot sample, not explain why it froze first.

CORRECT. After 0°C the samples keep cooling until something lets crystals start. The passage suggests heating may alter those sites, so the heated sample starts freezing at a higher temperature, which means sooner.
The measurement point explains apparent differences in reaching 0°C. Here the question is when ice appears, which a thermometer's position doesn't change.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests which one of the following about the 2016 study?
choices: Its findings, properly interpreted, show that hot water does freeze faster than cold under certain conditions.
Its findings are consistent with some reports that hot water froze first, if those reports concerned when ice formed.
Its method was flawed because it ignored supercooling's effect on the time each sample took to reach 0°C.
Its authors measured the temperature of their own samples at positions that produced misleading results.
Its conclusions hold for samples in sealed containers but not for samples in uncovered ones.
questions.explanation: The study timed how long samples took to reach 0°C, and the third paragraph explains that a hot sample 'can lag behind a cold one all the way down to 0°C and still form ice first'; together these imply that the study's findings leave room for first-ice reports, as B says. A is the near-miss: it overstates the study's limits into positive evidence for the effect, which the study, having stopped at 0°C, cannot supply. C misplaces supercooling, which occurs below 0°C.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Combine what the 2016 study measured with the mechanism in paragraph 3.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (what the study measured) and paragraph 3 (lagging to 0°C but freezing first).

breakdown.analysis: The study says the hot sample never reaches 0°C first. The mechanism says that doesn't matter for freezing. So the study's result doesn't conflict with some first-ice reports. That's the whole implication. It doesn't make the study wrong, and it doesn't make the study evidence for the effect. Watch for answers that push too far either way.

choices.note: Tempting, because the author defends the effect. But the study can't show the effect: it never looked past 0°C. The author's evidence for the effect comes from other experiments that recorded ice. This overstates what the study's limits imply.
CORRECT. The study timed arrival at 0°C. Paragraph 3 says a hot sample can lag to 0°C and still form ice first. So 'never first to 0°C' and 'sometimes first to show ice' can both be true.
Supercooling happens below 0°C, so it can't affect the time to reach 0°C. And the author calls the findings 'sound'; the problem is what they're taken to show.
Reversal. The study showed that position could create spurious results; nothing says its own measurements were misplaced.
The passage never ties the study to a type of container. The open-container point concerns evaporation after 0°C.

questions.stem: The author's remark that Mpemba "was concerned with when his mixture set" (last paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: show that supercooling rather than evaporation produced Mpemba's original observation
justify using the onset of freezing, not arrival at a temperature, as the test
suggest that the 2016 study should have used ice-cream mixtures rather than water
concede that Mpemba's observation was too imprecise to count as evidence for the effect
indicate that the 2016 study measured the time samples took to solidify completely
questions.explanation: In the last paragraph the author argues that 'the question Mpemba raised ... is not the one the 2016 study answered'; the remark about when his mixture set supplies the reason, establishing that the proper criterion is the onset of freezing rather than reaching 0°C, as B says. A is the near-miss: the remark points toward what happens after 0°C, but the author never identifies the mechanism behind Mpemba's own observation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Why does the author say Mpemba cared about when his mixture set?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the sentence before: the question Mpemba raised isn't the one the study answered. The remark explains why: Mpemba's question was about setting, not about passing a temperature. So it's the justification for using the onset of freezing as the test. Prephrase: to establish the right criterion.

choices.note: Tempting, because the remark ties Mpemba to the onset of freezing, where supercooling operates. But the author never says which mechanism worked in Mpemba's mixture. Overreach.
CORRECT. The remark supports the paragraph's point that the 2016 study answered a different question. Mpemba cared about setting, so the right test is when ice appears, not when 0°C is reached.
Takes 'mixture' too literally. The point is the criterion (setting vs. temperature), not the substance.
The author doesn't disparage Mpemba's observation; the remark is used to define the right question.
Wrong. The study measured arrival at 0°C.

questions.stem: Which one of the following research projects would best carry out the program the author recommends in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: timing, with thermometers at several depths, how long previously heated and unheated portions of water take to cool to 0°C in several kinds of vessel
measuring how long hot and cold samples take to solidify completely, without noting when ice first appears in them
heating portions of one water supply but not others, then recording, in various vessels and with various additives, how far each cools before ice appears
surveying published reports of the effect to determine how many used sealed rather than uncovered containers
repeating Mpemba's original observation with hot and cold ice-cream mixtures placed side by side in an ordinary freezer
questions.explanation: The author calls for 'systematic study of nucleation': of which impurities, containers, and histories of heating lead water to begin freezing at higher temperatures. C varies heating history, vessel, and additive and measures the temperature at which ice appears in each sample. A is the near-miss: it varies the right factors but measures time to 0°C, the 'more precise timing of the approach to 0°C' the author says is not what is needed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the project that does what the last sentence asks for.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The program has two parts: 1. vary impurities, containers, and heating history; 2. measure when, at what temperature, water begins to freeze. Both are needed. A project that varies the right things but measures the wrong endpoint (0°C, or complete solidification) fails.

choices.note: Tempting: it varies heating history and containers, and it's careful about thermometer position. But it stops at 0°C, which is exactly the 'more precise timing of the approach to 0°C' the author says is not needed.
Measures the end of freezing, not its beginning, and ignores what makes water start to freeze. Not a study of nucleation.

CORRECT. The author wants to know which impurities, containers, and heating histories lead water to start freezing at higher temperatures. This varies all three and measures the onset temperature of freezing directly.
A literature count doesn't study what makes water begin to freeze.
One replication under uncontrolled conditions; it doesn't vary impurities, containers, or heating history.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
choices: Where both events were recorded, a sample reaching 0°C later than its partner almost never formed ice first.
Many earlier reports of the effect, like the 2016 study, timed only how long samples took to reach 0°C.
Some experiments that recorded the appearance of ice found no difference between hot and cold samples.
Previously heated water begins freezing at a higher temperature only when it contains certain impurities.
Mpemba's ice-cream mixture had been left uncovered in the freezer while it cooled.
questions.explanation: The author's case depends on the claim that a hot sample can lag to 0°C and still form ice first, so that timing to 0°C misses the effect. A reports that a sample reaching 0°C later almost never freezes first, which would make the 2016 study's criterion adequate after all. B is the near-miss: it weakens some reports of the effect, but the author already grants that and rests the argument on experiments that recorded the appearance of ice.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the claim that the 2016 study answered the wrong question.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (lagging to 0°C but freezing first) and paragraph 4 (the study answered a different question).

breakdown.analysis: What's the hinge of the argument? That reaching 0°C first and freezing first can come apart. If they almost never come apart, the study's 0°C timing is a fine stand-in for freezing, and the argument collapses. Don't be distracted by answers that hurt particular reports or that make the mechanism conditional; the author already allows for both.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument needs a sample that lags to 0°C to sometimes form ice first. If that almost never happens, timing to 0°C does track freezing after all, and the 2016 study answers Mpemba's question.

Tempting, because it suggests some reports were weak. But the author already says the study 'casts doubt on a number of published claims.' The argument rests on the experiments that recorded ice, which this doesn't touch.
Consistent with the author: those experiments 'reported the effect under some conditions and not under others.'
Fits the author's call to study 'which impurities' matter. A conditional mechanism is still a mechanism.
If anything this adds the evaporation advantage the author mentions. It doesn't undercut the argument.

passages.title: Lina Bo Bardi's SESC Pompéia
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
The leisure center that Lina Bo Bardi designed in São Paulo for SESC, a Brazilian social-services organization funded by the commercial sector, is often cited as a model for the reuse of industrial buildings. The site, in the district of Pompéia, held a disused factory that had produced steel drums: a row of long brick sheds built around a concrete frame. Bo Bardi, an Italian-born architect who had settled in Brazil after the Second World War, kept the sheds rather than demolishing them and filled them with a library, workshops, a theater, and open halls. Beside them she added two blocks of raw concrete, a larger one containing sports courts and a narrower one containing changing rooms, linked by walkways suspended in the air. The center opened in stages during the 1980s and has been heavily used ever since.

Much of the commentary on the building has treated it as a triumph of restraint. Bo Bardi spoke of a "poor architecture," and she recalled deciding to preserve the sheds after seeing people already using the vacant site for weekend recreation. Critics have largely taken her at her word. In their account, the building succeeds because its designer chose to do as little as possible, leaving the users rather than the architect to determine what the place would become.

This reading captures something real, but it misdescribes how that result was achieved. The informality that visitors sense at Pompéia is not the residue of things left undone; it is carefully produced. Consider the main hall, where a shallow channel of water runs across the concrete floor not far from an open fireplace. Neither belongs to the old factory, and neither was required by the program she was given; both were added to encourage the kind of unhurried lingering that libraries and exhibition halls ordinarily discourage. The sports block makes the same point more emphatically. Its windows are irregular openings punched into the concrete and closed not with glass but with red lattice panels, and their apparent randomness is itself a composition: no two are alike, yet together they give the block a consistent, almost figurative face. What looks like an absence of design is the outcome of many careful decisions, several of them aimed at making a public building feel unowned.

Bo Bardi's own statements invited the misunderstanding, and arguably she intended them to; a building announced as the work of a commanding author would have undercut the very openness it was meant to foster. Yet critics who repeat her modesty as though it described her working method risk drawing the wrong lesson for practice, namely that reuse is chiefly a matter of preservation and permission. Pompéia suggests instead that opening an old structure to new life can demand as much invention as building from nothing.

passages.title: Ego depletion and its explanations
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
In a widely cited 1998 study, Roy Baumeister and his colleagues instructed some hungry participants to eat only radishes while others, offered the same choice of foods, were permitted to eat chocolate chip cookies. When all were subsequently given puzzles that, unknown to them, had no solution, those who had been required to forgo the cookies abandoned the task considerably sooner. The researchers proposed that self-control draws on a limited inner resource that any act of restraint partly uses up, and they called the resulting state ego depletion. Over the following decade, hundreds of studies reported similar effects with other tasks, and the idea passed into popular advice about conserving one's willpower.

The resource model invited an obvious question: what is the resource? One proposal, advanced in the late 2000s, held that it was blood glucose, and several studies reported that a sugared drink restored self-control in depleted participants. The proposal fared poorly. Critics pointed out that the brain's total consumption of glucose rises only slightly during demanding thought, far too little to be exhausted by a few minutes of declining cookies. More tellingly, later experiments found that merely rinsing the mouth with a sugar solution, without swallowing it, could produce the same benefit, which suggests that glucose works, when it works at all, as a signal rather than as fuel.

Findings of this kind encouraged a rival interpretation. On a motivational account, an initial act of self-control does not drain a reservoir; it shifts priorities, so that people become less willing, rather than less able, to exert effort on whatever comes next, and more attentive to the rewards they have forgone. In support of this view, a 2010 study by Veronika Job, Carol Dweck, and Gregory Walton found the depletion effect mainly among participants who believed that willpower is easily exhausted; those who regarded it as self-renewing showed little or none. A resource that can be replenished by a change of belief, proponents argue, is hardly a resource at all.

Yet the motivational account may have arrived to explain an effect smaller than either side supposed. In 2016 a coordinated replication conducted in more than twenty laboratories, all following a single procedure agreed upon in advance, found an effect close to zero. Defenders of the original finding objected that the procedure chosen, a tedious letter-crossing task, was too weak a manipulation to deplete anyone, and the question of which tasks constitute fair tests remains open. Still, the episode is instructive. The motivational account was attractive partly because it explained so much: why beliefs mattered, why sugar on the tongue sufficed, why depletion sometimes failed to appear. If the effect is in fact negligible, however, some of those explanations may have been offered for results that reflected chance variation among small studies rather than any underlying process.

passages.title: Adult neurogenesis in the human brain
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists held that the adult mammalian brain makes no new neurons. The doctrine owed much to Santiago Ramón y Cajal, whose studies of nervous tissue found no sign of neurons forming in mature brains, and it seemed to explain why brain injuries so rarely heal. So when Joseph Altman reported in the 1960s that a radioactive marker of cell division appeared in newly formed neurons in the brains of adult rats, notably in the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, his findings were largely set aside. The marked cells, skeptics argued, might be glial cells, the supporting cells that do divide in adulthood, and the microscopy of the day could not reliably tell the two apart.

What changed minds was not one decisive study but evidence accumulating from several directions. In the 1980s Fernando Nottebohm showed that adult canaries generate neurons in the brain regions that control song, with seasonal turnover linked to the learning of new songs. In the 1990s improved labeling techniques, combined with markers specific to neurons, confirmed adult neurogenesis in the hippocampus of rodents and then of monkeys. In 1998 a study of cancer patients who had been given a labeling compound for diagnostic purposes found labeled neurons in their hippocampi after death. Later, researchers exploited the surge in atmospheric carbon-14 produced by nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and early 1960s: because a cell's DNA incorporates the carbon available when the cell is formed, the isotope's level in a neuron indicates roughly when that neuron was born. The method suggested that the adult human hippocampus adds on the order of seven hundred neurons a day.

By the 2010s the old doctrine had been reversed so thoroughly that adult neurogenesis was routinely invoked to explain the benefits of exercise and the action of antidepressants. That consensus has since met a reaction from within the field. In 2018 one research group, examining postmortem human brain tissue for markers of immature neurons, reported that such cells became vanishingly rare after childhood; another, using similar methods, reported that they persisted into old age. The conflict has since been traced in part to technical differences, among them how long tissue sat before it was preserved, since some of the proteins used as markers break down quickly after death. A study that controlled such delays carefully found immature neurons in abundance in adult brains.

These disputes do not restore the old doctrine, but they should temper the confidence with which its replacement is applied. Nearly everything known about the function of new neurons comes from studies of rodents, in which such cells can be labeled, counted, and suppressed far more directly than in people. Whether the human supply contributes measurably to memory or mood therefore remains unsettled; the carbon-14 estimates indicate how many neurons are added, not what they do.
