passages.title: Judicial deference to agency interpretations
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

When a statute that an agency administers is ambiguous, who should resolve the ambiguity, the agency or a reviewing court? For four decades after Chevron U.S.A. v. Natural Resources Defense Council (1984), the answer in United States law was usually the agency. Under the Chevron framework, a court first asked whether Congress had directly addressed the precise question at issue; if it had not, the court accepted any reasonable interpretation the agency had adopted, even one the court would not itself have chosen.

The framework is often described as a judicial surrender, but it rests on a defensible account of what statutory ambiguity is. Congress frequently cannot foresee the particular questions a regulatory scheme will raise, and when it leaves a gap it entrusts to someone the task of filling it. Choosing among reasonable readings of such a gap is seldom a purely legal exercise. Whether, in the Clean Air Act case that gave the doctrine its name, an entire industrial plant could be treated as a single "stationary source" of pollution turned less on grammar than on how to balance cleaner air against economic growth. Judgments of that kind are better made by an agency, which possesses technical expertise and answers, through the President, to the electorate, than by judges, who possess neither.

Deference also serves consistency. Without it, a single statutory provision may receive different readings in different federal circuits, leaving regulated parties subject to one rule in one region and another elsewhere until the Supreme Court intervenes, if it ever does. An agency's single, nationwide interpretation spares them that uncertainty.

Passage B

Interpreting statutes is what courts do; it lies at the core of the judicial function as the Constitution conceives it. The Administrative Procedure Act of 1946 directs a reviewing court to "decide all relevant questions of law" and to "interpret constitutional and statutory provisions," language that leaves no evident room for a rule requiring judges to adopt an agency's reading merely because it is reasonable. In 2024, in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, the Supreme Court accepted this argument and abandoned mandatory deference.

The policy case for deference is weaker than it appears. Agencies' expertise is real, but it bears on facts and on the likely consequences of competing rules, not on the meaning of the words Congress enacted, and nothing prevents a court from giving careful consideration to an agency's informed view, as courts did long before 1984. Moreover, the political accountability said to justify deference carries a cost seldom acknowledged: an agency answerable to each new administration may announce one reading of a statute and later its opposite, so that the law governing a business changes though not a word of the statute has. Regulated parties have more to fear from that instability than from occasional disagreement among the lower courts, which the Supreme Court can in any case resolve.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: SESC Pompéia succeeds chiefly because its architect let its users shape the old factory's uses, though she did add a few features of her own.
Contrary to what critics have assumed, converting an old industrial structure to public use generally demands more invention from an architect than designing a new building does.
Bo Bardi's talk of a "poor architecture" was a deliberate deception, meant to hide from critics how extensively she had redesigned the factory she found on the site.
Bo Bardi's remarks about a "poor architecture" accurately described her building, but critics have mistaken them for an account of how she worked.
SESC Pompéia's admired informality owes less to its architect's restraint, as is often claimed, than to deliberate and demanding design.
questions.explanation: The author grants that the critics' reading 'captures something real' but argues that the building's informality 'is carefully produced' (third paragraph), so E is correct. B is the near miss: it echoes the last sentence but turns 'as much invention as building from nothing' into 'more' and generalizes from Pompéia to all conversions. A grants the added features but still credits the users rather than the design, which is the critics' view, and D shifts the focus to Bo Bardi's statements, which the author never calls accurate. C hardens the author's guarded 'arguably she intended them to' into a charge of deception aimed at critics.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall claim about SESC Pompéia, not the critics' claim.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 (the critics' reading), the first two sentences of paragraph 3, and the last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Whose view is the passage pushing? The critics say Pompéia works because Bo Bardi did as little as possible. The author says that reading 'misdescribes how that result was achieved': the informality is real, but it was designed. We need 'praised for restraint, but really the product of careful design.' Two near misses: one concedes some design but still credits the users, and one is built from the last sentence: the author says reuse can take 'as much' invention as new building, about this case. 'More,' and 'generally,' go too far.

choices.note: Tempting, because it concedes that Bo Bardi added features. But it still says the building succeeds 'chiefly' because users shaped it. That's the critics' reading with a small concession, and the author says the informality was designed.

Tempting, because it borrows the last sentence. But the author says 'as much invention as building from nothing,' not more, and draws the lesson from Pompéia, not as a general rule. Two small overreaches make it wrong.
Too strong. The author says only that Bo Bardi 'arguably' intended her statements to invite the misunderstanding, and the reason given is to foster openness, not to fool critics.

Tempting, because the author does say critics treat her modesty 'as though it described her working method.' But the author never says her remarks accurately described the building, and the passage's main claim is about the design, not about her statements.
CORRECT. It keeps the contrast (often credited to restraint) and the author's correction (actually the product of deliberate, demanding design), in new words.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the interpretation of SESC Pompéia offered by the critics mentioned in the second paragraph is based at least in part on
choices: a comparison of SESC Pompéia with other converted factories
statements Bo Bardi made about her approach and about why she kept the sheds
observations of how visitors actually use the library, workshops, and halls of the complex
the fact that the sports block and its companion tower were left as raw concrete
evidence that the program Bo Bardi received called for only minimal changes to the existing factory buildings on the site
questions.explanation: The second paragraph reports Bo Bardi's talk of a 'poor architecture' and her recollection about seeing people use the site, then says 'Critics have largely taken her at her word,' so B is correct. E is tempting, but the program is mentioned only in the third paragraph, to say what it did not require. A, C, and D are never cited as the critics' grounds.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the critics' reading rests on.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, especially 'Critics have largely taken her at her word.'

breakdown.analysis: What's the 'word' the critics took her at? The two sentences right before: she spoke of a 'poor architecture' and recalled keeping the sheds after seeing people using the site. So the critics lean on her own statements.

choices.note: No comparison with other converted factories appears anywhere.
CORRECT. 'Taken her at her word' means the critics relied on her statements: the 'poor architecture' remark and her account of why she kept the sheds.
The passage says the center 'has been heavily used,' but never that critics studied how visitors use it.
The raw concrete is a fact from paragraph 1, not the critics' evidence.
Tempting, since it would fit a 'do as little as possible' reading. But the program appears only in paragraph 3, and only to say what it did not require.

questions.stem: By "unowned" (last sentence of the third paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: not held as the legal property of any private individual, business, or other organization
lacking any single feature that dominates the rest of the design
not credited by critics to any one architect
free of any sense that some authority dictates its use
open to the public without any charge for admission, membership, or the use of its facilities
questions.explanation: The third paragraph links the building's informality to features meant to encourage 'unhurried lingering,' and the fourth says a building presented as the work of 'a commanding author' would have undercut its openness; 'unowned' therefore means users don't feel someone controls how the place is used, as D says. A is the dictionary sense, and C contradicts the passage, since the critics plainly credit the building to Bo Bardi.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Decide what 'unowned' means in context, not in the dictionary.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of paragraph 3 and the first sentence of paragraph 4 ('commanding author ... openness').

breakdown.analysis: Does the author mean nobody holds the deed? No: SESC runs it. The design aims at informality and lingering, and paragraph 4 says a 'commanding author' would have undercut the building's 'openness.' So 'unowned' means it doesn't feel like anyone is in charge of how you use it. The dictionary sense is the usual trap.

choices.note: The dictionary meaning, the classic meaning-in-context trap. The passage is about how the building feels, not who holds title.
'Unowned' is about users' sense of freedom, not visual balance.
Contradicted. The critics plainly credit the building to Bo Bardi.
CORRECT. Feeling 'unowned' means no controlling hand seems to dictate use, the 'openness' a 'commanding author' would have undercut.
Fees are never discussed, and free entry isn't what makes a building feel unowned in the author's sense.

questions.stem: The author discusses the channel of water and the open fireplace primarily in order to
choices: illustrate how Bo Bardi preserved features of the old factory that people using the vacant site had found congenial
explain why critics have tended to describe SESC Pompéia as a triumph of restraint
provide evidence that elements producing the building's relaxed atmosphere were introduced on purpose
show that the program Bo Bardi was given required spaces for leisure as well as for study
contrast the unassuming interior of the main hall with the more emphatic design of the sports block
questions.explanation: The third paragraph claims the informality 'is carefully produced' and then cites the water channel and fireplace, which neither belong to the old factory nor were required by the program, as features added to encourage lingering, so C is correct. A is wrong because the features were not in the factory, and D because the program did not require them. E misreads 'the same point more emphatically': the sports block reinforces the point rather than contrasting with the hall.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the water channel and fireplace.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3: the claim before the example ('it is carefully produced') and the sentence after it ('Neither belongs to the old factory...').

breakdown.analysis: What claim comes right before 'Consider the main hall'? That the informality is 'carefully produced.' Then the author notes that neither feature came from the factory or the program; Bo Bardi added them to make people linger. So the example is evidence of deliberate design. A function question asks why, not what.

choices.note: Opposite of the text: 'Neither belongs to the old factory.' These weren't preserved features.
The critics' reading is in paragraph 2. This example is evidence against it, not an explanation of it.
CORRECT. The channel and fireplace show the relaxed atmosphere was designed: they weren't in the factory or the brief, and they were added to encourage lingering.
Opposite: 'neither was required by the program she was given.'
Tempting, since the sports block is 'more emphatic.' But it makes 'the same point,' so the author is stacking examples, not contrasting them.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: An architect's own description of a building can be an unreliable guide to the way it was designed.
Bo Bardi deliberately framed her remarks about a "poor architecture" so as to mislead critics about her working method.
Architects who convert industrial buildings to public use should generally retain as much of the original structure as they can.
The informality of SESC Pompéia would have been more convincing had its architect designed fewer of its features.
Visitors have mostly used SESC Pompéia in ways its architect did not foresee.
questions.explanation: The author says Bo Bardi's statements 'invited the misunderstanding' and warns against repeating her modesty 'as though it described her working method' (last paragraph), so the author holds that an architect's own account can mislead about how a design was made, as A says. B is the near miss: the author does say 'arguably she intended them to' invite the misunderstanding, but hedges it and gives the purpose as fostering openness, not misleading critics. C states a rule the author rejects ('not chiefly a matter of preservation').

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a statement the author's reasoning supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, especially 'Bo Bardi's own statements invited the misunderstanding' and 'as though it described her working method.'

breakdown.analysis: What does the author think of Bo Bardi's own talk about her work? It's misleading as a description of how she worked. Generalize: what an architect says about a design isn't a reliable guide to how it was made. The near miss takes the author's 'arguably she intended them to' and turns it into a confident claim about misleading critics. Check the degree and the purpose.

choices.note: CORRECT. Her statements 'invited the misunderstanding,' and critics err in treating them as a description of her method. That's an architect's own account misleading about the design process.

Tempting: the author does say she 'arguably' intended her statements to invite the misreading. But that's hedged, and the stated purpose is to keep the building open, not to mislead critics. Wrong degree and wrong purpose.
The author warns that reuse isn't 'chiefly a matter of preservation.' No such rule is endorsed.
Opposite. The author credits the designed features for the informality.
Closer to the critics' picture. The passage gives no evidence about uses Bo Bardi failed to foresee.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Later research has established that ego depletion reflects a shift in motivation rather than the exhaustion of a limited resource such as blood glucose.
A coordinated replication has shown that ego depletion does not exist, and the objections that defenders of the original finding raised against it are unfounded.
The glucose proposal failed because the brain uses too little glucose for brief acts of restraint to exhaust it.
The motivational account owes its appeal to its breadth, but that breadth conceals its inability to explain the original 1998 finding.
The motivational account improves on the resource model, but a large replication has cast doubt on whether either account has a substantial effect to explain.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from the resource model through its troubles to the motivational account, then reports a replication finding 'an effect close to zero' and suggests the effect may be 'negligible' (last paragraph); E keeps both the motivational account's advantage and the author's doubt. A is the near miss: it captures the third paragraph but presents the motivational account as established and drops the closing doubt. B overstates: the author says the question of fair tests 'remains open.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall point about ego depletion research.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole passage, especially the first sentence of paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: Where does the passage land? Not on 'the motivational account wins.' Paragraph 4 opens: that account 'may have arrived to explain an effect smaller than either side supposed.' So two parts: the motivational account beats the resource model, but the effect itself is now in doubt. Watch for an answer that stops at paragraph 3, and one that turns 'doubt' into 'refuted.'

choices.note: Tempting, since it's the story through paragraph 3. But 'has established' overstates, and it leaves out the author's final doubt about whether there's an effect at all.
Too strong. 'Close to zero' and 'remains open' are not 'does not exist' and 'unfounded.'
True to paragraph 2, but that's one step, not the point of the passage.
The author never says the account fails to explain the 1998 finding. This invents a criticism.
CORRECT. It credits the motivational account's advantage (paragraph 3) and keeps the author's hedged doubt about the effect (paragraph 4).

questions.stem: According to the passage, participants in the 1998 experiment who had been told to eat only the radishes
choices: persisted for less time on the puzzles than did the participants who ate cookies
did better on the later puzzles once they had been given a drink containing sugar
were told beforehand that the puzzles could not be solved
were more likely than the other participants to believe that willpower is a resource easily exhausted
reported feeling hungrier than those allowed the cookies
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says that 'those who had been required to forgo the cookies abandoned the task considerably sooner' when given puzzles that had no solution; the radish eaters are the ones who resisted, so A is correct. C reverses a detail: the puzzles' insolubility was 'unknown to them.' B and D import findings from later studies (the glucose experiments and the 2010 study of beliefs).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the radish group in the 1998 study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: Who resisted the cookies? The radish group. What happened? They 'abandoned the task considerably sooner' on the unsolvable puzzles. Watch for details borrowed from other studies in the passage.

choices.note: CORRECT. Those 'required to forgo the cookies abandoned the task considerably sooner,' i.e., they persisted for less time.
Borrowed from the glucose studies of the late 2000s (paragraph 2).
Opposite. The puzzles were unsolvable 'unknown to them.'
Borrowed from the 2010 study (paragraph 3).
Hunger ratings are never mentioned.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the significance the author attributes to the mouth-rinse experiments?
choices: They show that sugar does not in fact restore self-control in participants who have been depleted.
They confirm the critics' observation that the brain's consumption of glucose rises only slightly during demanding thought.
They show that the benefit of sugar depends on what participants believe about willpower.
They indicate that glucose, though not itself the resource, is one of several substances whose depletion impairs self-control.
They suggest that whatever benefit sugar confers does not require that the body take it up and use it.
questions.explanation: The author says the rinse experiments, in which sugar was not swallowed, 'more tellingly' undercut the glucose proposal and 'suggest' that glucose works as a signal (second paragraph): its benefit does not depend on the body absorbing and using it, as E says. B is the near miss: it links the rinse results to the critics' point, but the passage presents them as a separate and stronger line of evidence ('More tellingly'), and they say nothing about how much glucose the brain consumes. A contradicts the reported benefit, C borrows the 2010 belief study, and D invents a list of depletable substances.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the author thinks the mouth-rinse experiments show.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, from 'Critics pointed out' to the end of the paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: What did the glucose proposal claim? That glucose is the resource self-control uses up. The rinse experiments got the benefit without anyone swallowing the sugar. So whatever sugar does, it doesn't do it by being absorbed and consumed. That's why the author calls it 'more telling' than the critics' point. Prephrase: sugar helps without being used by the body. Watch the near miss that folds the rinse result into the critics' observation; they're two different pieces of evidence.

choices.note: Contradicted. The rinse produced 'the same benefit.' Sugar helped; the question is how.

Tempting, because both are evidence against the glucose proposal and sit side by side. But 'More tellingly' marks the rinse results as a separate, stronger line of evidence, and they measure nothing about brain glucose use. Wrong relation.
Borrowed from the 2010 belief study in paragraph 3.
Invented. The passage never mentions other substances, and 'signal rather than fuel' denies that glucose works by being depleted.
CORRECT. Rinsing without swallowing means the body never took the sugar in, yet the benefit appeared. So the benefit doesn't depend on the body using the sugar.

questions.stem: The author mentions the letter-crossing task (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the type of task on which most ego-depletion studies before 2016 had relied
point to a flaw that, in the author's view, invalidates the result of the coordinated replication
identify what an objection to the coordinated replication's finding is directed at
explain how the coordinated replication managed to detect an effect that smaller studies had overlooked
suggest that some of the participating laboratories departed from the agreed procedure
questions.explanation: The task appears in the sentence saying that defenders of the original finding 'objected that the procedure chosen, a tedious letter-crossing task, was too weak a manipulation,' so it names what their objection targets, as C says. B is the near miss: it gets the objection right but assigns it to the author, who says only that the question of fair tests 'remains open' and goes on to call the episode instructive. D reverses the result.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author mentions the letter-crossing task.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the sentence beginning 'Defenders of the original finding objected.'

breakdown.analysis: Who brings up the task? The defenders of the original finding. Their complaint: the replication used a weak manipulation, so its near-zero result proves little. Does the author sign on? No; the author calls the matter open and still treats the replication as a reason for doubt. So the task identifies the target of someone else's objection.

choices.note: The passage never says what earlier studies used.

Tempting, because the objection is real. But it belongs to the defenders, not the author, who calls the question 'open' and still treats the replication as casting doubt. Wrong party, and 'invalidates' is too strong.
CORRECT. The task is what the defenders' objection is aimed at: they say it was too weak to deplete anyone.
Reverses the result. The replication found an effect 'close to zero.'
Nothing suggests anyone broke the procedure; the objection is to the procedure itself.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, proponents of the motivational account would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: A sugared drink restores self-control because it replenishes the fuel that an act of restraint has used up.
Adequate incentive could restore normal persistence in someone who has just exercised self-restraint.
The 1998 effect was produced by the participants' hunger rather than by the restraint they exercised.
After an act of restraint, people attend less closely to the rewards they have given up.
Whether a person has any self-control left after an act of restraint depends on what that person believes about willpower.
questions.explanation: On the motivational account, people who have exercised self-control become 'less willing, rather than less able,' to exert effort (third paragraph); if capacity is intact and only priorities shift, enough incentive should restore persistence, as B says. E is the near miss: it uses the account's evidence about beliefs, but frames depletion as a question of how much self-control a person 'has left,' which is the capacity view the account rejects. D reverses the account's claim about forgone rewards.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim the motivational account's proponents would accept.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, especially 'less willing, rather than less able.'

breakdown.analysis: The heart of the account: restraint doesn't drain anything; it changes priorities. 'Less willing, rather than less able.' If the ability is still there, a good enough reason should get a 'depleted' person going again. Watch the near miss that cites the belief study but slips back into talk of how much self-control is 'left.'

choices.note: The resource model's fuel picture. The motivational side reads the sugar evidence as a signal. Wrong party.
CORRECT. If restraint makes people less willing but not less able, a strong enough incentive should bring persistence back.
Nobody in the passage offers hunger as an alternative cause.
Reversed. The account says people become 'more attentive' to forgone rewards.

Tempting, because beliefs matter in the 2010 study. But 'has any self-control left' treats self-control as a stock that runs out, the very view the account rejects. Proponents say depletion is about willingness, not what's left.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the motivational account is most accurately described as
choices: firm endorsement of it as the explanation that has settled the dispute over ego depletion
qualified approval, on the grounds that it alone can explain why the 2016 replication found almost no effect
skepticism grounded chiefly in its apparent failure to account for the mouth-rinse results
recognition of its advantages over its rival, tempered by doubt that the results it explains are all genuine
neutrality, since the author reports its proponents' arguments without evaluating them
questions.explanation: The author presents the evidence favoring the motivational account over the resource model, but in the last paragraph suggests that some of what it explains may reflect 'chance variation among small studies rather than any underlying process,' so D's mix of credit and reservation is right. B is the near miss: 'qualified approval' fits, but the account is never said to explain the replication's null result; the replication is what raises the doubt. C is wrong because the account explains 'why sugar on the tongue sufficed.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down how the author feels about the motivational account.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (the account and its support) and paragraph 4 (the author's reservation).

breakdown.analysis: Is the author a fan? Partly. The evidence that hurt the resource model helped this account, and the author presents it without objection. But paragraph 4 warns that the account may explain results that were just noise. So: credit plus a reservation. In the near miss, the tone is right but the reason is wrong.

choices.note: Too strong. The author ends by doubting there's much of an effect to explain.

Tempting, since 'qualified approval' sounds right. But the reason is invented: the passage never says the account explains the replication's null result. That result is the source of the author's doubt.
Wrong reason. The account explains 'why sugar on the tongue sufficed.'
CORRECT. Advantage over the resource model, plus doubt that the results it explains all reflect a real process.
Paragraph 4 evaluates the account directly. Not neutral.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the role that the mouth-rinse experiments suggest glucose plays (second paragraph)?
choices: A faint cyclist revives some twenty minutes after eating a banana, once its sugar has reached her bloodstream.
A runner who is told, falsely, that fatigue is mostly psychological runs farther than usual, having come to regard her endurance as less limited than she had thought.
A car's engine stalls when its tank runs dry and restarts only after the tank is refilled.
A tired hiker quickens her pace the moment she smells stew cooking at the camp ahead, before eating any of it.
A wilted houseplant revives after watering because the water it absorbs restores the pressure in its stems.
questions.explanation: The rinse results suggest glucose works 'as a signal rather than as fuel': something that could have been fuel restores effort merely by being detected. In D, food that could refuel the hiker restores her effort by being smelled, before any is eaten. B is the near miss: effort rises without fuel, but because of a changed belief about her capacity, which is the 2010 belief finding, not a sensed cue. A shares the sugar but works only after absorption, the fuel model; C and E are replenishment.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation whose structure matches glucose acting as a signal, not as fuel.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of paragraph 2 ('as a signal rather than as fuel').

breakdown.analysis: What's the role? Sugar is the kind of thing that could be fuel, yet rinsing without swallowing restores self-control. It works by being detected, not consumed. So we need: a potential fuel that restores effort just by being sensed. Two answers involve no fuel being consumed (B and D), so check the extra element: in B, nothing is sensed; a belief changes. That's a different mechanism, the one from the 2010 study.

choices.note: Tempting, with sugar and a revival. But the revival waits until the sugar 'has reached her bloodstream.' That's fuel, the very model the rinse result undercuts.

The strongest trap. No fuel is involved, so it looks signal-like. But the change is in her belief about her own limits, which parallels the willpower-belief study, not a cue being detected. One element off.
Pure fuel model: the engine runs again only when refilled.
CORRECT. The stew could refuel her, but it restores her effort merely by being smelled, just as sugar restores self-control by being tasted, not swallowed.
Replenishment again: the absorbed water physically restores the plant.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the objection raised by defenders of the original finding?
choices: Several laboratories in the coordinated replication had never before conducted research on ego depletion.
Studies before 2016 that used tasks other than letter-crossing reported depletion effects of widely varying sizes.
Participants who did the letter-crossing task reported more fatigue afterward than did those who did its easy control version.
Participants in the replication who believed that willpower is easily exhausted showed no larger effect than others.
Participants rated the letter-crossing task as calling for scarcely more self-restraint than the easy version used as a control.
questions.explanation: The defenders' objection is that the letter-crossing task 'was too weak a manipulation to deplete anyone.' If participants found it barely more demanding of self-restraint than the control version, the replication never really tested depletion, as E says. C is the near miss: it addresses the same question but points the other way, since more fatigue suggests the task did tax participants. A attacks the replication on a different ground (the labs' inexperience), not the one the defenders raised.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would most support the defenders' complaint.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the sentence beginning 'Defenders of the original finding objected.'

breakdown.analysis: What exactly is the objection? Not 'the replication was badly run' but 'the letter-crossing task was too weak to deplete anyone.' A strengthener must show the task didn't really demand self-control. Two traps: one on the right topic that cuts the wrong way, and one that criticizes the replication for a different reason.

choices.note: Tempting, since it also casts doubt on the replication. But inexperienced labs is a different objection. The defenders' complaint is about the task's strength.
Varying effect sizes elsewhere don't show that letter-crossing in particular was too weak.
On the right topic but in the wrong direction. More fatigue suggests the task did tax people, which weakens the objection.
About the belief finding, not the manipulation's strength.
CORRECT. If the depleting task demanded hardly more restraint than the control, there was little to use up, so a null result shows little. That's the defenders' point.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: recount how a long-held belief about the adult brain came to be abandoned and counsel restraint in applying the view that superseded it
recount how a long-held belief about the adult brain came to be abandoned and argue that the case for the view replacing it rests mainly on studies of rodents
explain why early evidence of adult neurogenesis was rejected and show that the methods responsible for that rejection have since been corrected
trace how a long-held belief about the adult brain was overturned and argue that what new neurons do in the human brain cannot be investigated
survey the evidence that overturned a long-held belief about the adult brain and explain how a later dispute over adult human neurogenesis was resolved
questions.explanation: The passage traces the old doctrine and its reversal, examines the 2018 dispute, and ends by saying the disputes 'should temper the confidence with which its replacement is applied,' so A is correct. B is a near miss built from the last paragraph: rodent studies are the source of what is known about the function of new neurons, but the case that they exist in adult humans rests on human evidence (the 1998 patients, carbon-14). D is another: the author says the human question 'remains unsettled,' not that it cannot be investigated. E fails because the dispute was explained only 'in part,' and it omits the caution.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Name what the whole passage is trying to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of paragraph 1, paragraph 2, and paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: What's the arc? Old doctrine → evidence reverses it → a 2018 dispute → a caution against overapplying the new view. Most answers get the first half right, so the second half decides it. Check each ending against paragraph 4: it says function in humans is known mostly from rodents and 'remains unsettled.' Not 'can't be studied,' and not 'the whole new view rests on rodents.'

choices.note: CORRECT. Paragraphs 1–3 trace the reversal; paragraph 4 cautions that the new view is applied with too much confidence.

Tempting, because paragraph 4 does stress rodent studies. But those concern what new neurons do. The evidence that adult humans make new neurons at all came from human tissue: the 1998 patients and the carbon-14 work. Wrong relation.
The 1990s methods appear as new evidence, not as a correction explaining Altman's rejection, and this drops the caution.
Tempting, because the author doubts what we know about function in humans. But 'remains unsettled' isn't 'cannot be investigated.' Too strong.
The conflict was traced to technical differences only 'in part,' so it isn't presented as resolved, and the closing caution is missing.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that Altman's findings would have been harder for other researchers to set aside if
choices: Altman had shown that the radioactive marker he used is taken up only by cells that are dividing
Altman had conducted his experiments on monkeys rather than on rats
researchers in the 1960s had possessed a dependable way to distinguish new neurons from the brain's other dividing cells
the doctrine that the adult brain makes no new neurons had not owed so much to the work of Ramón y Cajal
Altman's findings had concerned regions of the brain other than the hippocampus
questions.explanation: The skeptics argued that the marked cells 'might be glial cells, the supporting cells that do divide in adulthood,' and that the microscopy of the day 'could not reliably tell the two apart' (first paragraph); a dependable way to make that distinction would have removed their objection, as C says. A is the near miss: it uses the passage's language about the marker, but the marker already tracked cell division, and glial cells divide too, so showing it marks only dividing cells would not answer the skeptics. D is not supported: the passage names Cajal as a source of the doctrine, not as the reason Altman was dismissed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Infer what would have undercut the reason Altman's findings were dismissed.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of paragraph 1.

breakdown.analysis: Why were Altman's findings set aside? Skeptics said the labeled cells might be glia, which also divide, and microscopes couldn't tell glia from neurons. So the dismissal rested on that inability. Remove it, and the objection goes away. Watch the near miss: proving the marker tags only dividing cells doesn't help, because glia divide too.

choices.note: Tempting, since it sounds like tightening the evidence. But the marker was already 'a marker of cell division,' and glia 'do divide in adulthood.' Labeling only dividing cells still leaves the glia problem.
The passage never suggests the species was the problem. Monkey work came decades later as confirmation, not as a cure for this objection.
CORRECT. The skeptics' case rested on the inability to tell new neurons from glia. A reliable way to do so would have removed it.
The passage says the doctrine 'owed much to' Cajal, but the stated reason for setting Altman aside is the glial-cell problem, not Cajal's prestige. Unsupported.
The passage gives no reason to think another region would have been more convincing.

questions.stem: By "a reaction from within the field" (second sentence of the third paragraph), the author most probably means
choices: renewed doubt about how extensively new neurons form in the adult human brain
a return to the doctrine that the adult brain makes no new neurons of any kind
a chemical change that proteins used as markers of immature neurons undergo after death
an attempt by followers of Ramón y Cajal to discredit the carbon-14 method
the brain's response to exercise and to antidepressant drugs
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the claim that the old doctrine had been 'reversed so thoroughly' that neurogenesis was 'routinely invoked,' and it is followed by the 2018 report that immature neurons become 'vanishingly rare after childhood'; the reaction is renewed doubt about the extent of adult human neurogenesis, as A says. B overstates: the last paragraph says the disputes 'do not restore the old doctrine.' C takes 'reaction' in its chemical sense.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'a reaction' refers to in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3: the sentence before it and the sentence after it.

breakdown.analysis: A reaction against what? The new view had become so dominant it was 'routinely invoked.' The next sentence describes a 2018 finding that immature neurons nearly vanish after childhood. So the reaction is pushback against the new consensus. Not chemistry, and not a full return to the old view.

choices.note: CORRECT. After the new view became routine, the 2018 report questioned how much neurogenesis adults really have.
Too strong. Paragraph 4: these disputes 'do not restore the old doctrine.'
The chemical sense. Markers breaking down is a later explanation of the conflict, not the reaction.
No followers of Cajal appear, and the 2018 studies used tissue markers, not carbon-14.
Exercise and antidepressants come up as things the new view was used to explain, not as the reaction.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the carbon-14 method described in the second paragraph depends on
choices: atmospheric carbon-14 having stayed at the elevated level the weapons tests produced long after the tests ended
a change, over the years in which the neurons studied were formed, in how much carbon-14 the atmosphere contained
the administration of carbon-14 to patients for diagnostic purposes some time before their deaths
the persistence of carbon-14 in a neuron only for as long as the neuron remains immature
tissue from adults who had been directly exposed to nuclear weapons tests
questions.explanation: A cell's DNA takes up the carbon available when the cell forms, so a neuron's carbon-14 level can indicate when it was born only if the atmospheric level differed from year to year over the relevant period, as B says. A is the near miss: it borrows the passage's 'surge,' but if the level had stayed constant after the tests, every neuron formed since would carry the same reading and could not be dated. C confuses the method with the 1998 study of cancer patients.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the carbon-14 dating method requires in order to work.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the sentence beginning 'Later, researchers exploited the surge.'

breakdown.analysis: How does the method date a neuron? A cell locks in the carbon available at its birth, and the tests made atmospheric carbon-14 spike. That works only if the level changed over time; if it were flat, all neurons born in that stretch would read the same. Apply the mechanism to the near miss: a level that stayed high after the tests would make later-born neurons indistinguishable.

choices.note: Tempting, because the surge is what researchers 'exploited.' But a level that stayed flat after the tests would give every later-born neuron the same reading, and the method could not tell when they formed. The method needs change, not a plateau.
CORRECT. The isotope level can date a cell's birth only if atmospheric carbon-14 varied across the years when the cells formed.
Confuses this method with the 1998 study of cancer patients given a labeling compound.
Backward. The method reads carbon-14 in adult neurons long after they formed, so the isotope must persist.
The isotope entered the whole atmosphere; no direct exposure is needed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A long-standing view is set out together with an early objection to it that was set aside; a single line of research that eventually overturned the view is traced; a later controversy and its partial explanation are discussed; a remaining uncertainty is identified.

A belief is presented with the reasons an early challenge to it was dismissed; the evidence that later displaced it is reviewed; a subsequent disagreement is analyzed; a question still unresolved is noted.
A doctrine is described; evidence against it is presented and dismissed; a rival theory is introduced; the author argues that neither is adequately supported.
A consensus is described; the reasons for its formation are criticized; an older view that it displaced is defended.
A doctrine and an early challenge to it are described; the evidence that overturned the doctrine is surveyed; a dispute about the new view is examined; a method for settling that dispute is proposed.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph presents the doctrine and why Altman's challenge was set aside, the second reviews the evidence that displaced it, the third analyzes the 2018 disagreement, and the fourth notes that the function of new human neurons 'remains unsettled,' matching B. A is the near miss: it is accurate in three of its four steps, but it calls the evidence that overturned the doctrine 'a single line of research,' whereas the second paragraph describes 'evidence accumulating from several directions' (songbirds, rodents and monkeys, cancer patients, carbon-14). E matches the first three steps but fails at the last, since the author proposes no method. C and D fail earlier.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the passage's paragraph-by-paragraph structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of each paragraph, and the last paragraph as a whole.

breakdown.analysis: Sketch it: P1 old doctrine + Altman, dismissed. P2 evidence overturns it. P3 the 2018 dispute and a partial explanation. P4 a caution: function in humans remains unsettled. The strongest trap gets the overall arc right and slips in a middle step, so check every step against the text, including how paragraph 2 characterizes the evidence ('several directions'). Organization answers die on one wrong element.

choices.note: The strongest trap. Steps one, three, and four are fine, but step two says 'a single line of research.' Paragraph 2 says the opposite: 'not one decisive study but evidence accumulating from several directions' (canaries, rodents and monkeys, cancer patients, carbon-14).

CORRECT. Each step lines up: doctrine and the dismissed challenge (P1), the displacing evidence (P2), the 2018 disagreement (P3), the unsettled question of function (P4). It's reworded, but every step holds.
No rival theory is introduced, and the author doesn't reject both.
The older view isn't defended; the passage says it isn't restored.
Matches three steps, then fails: the author proposes no method. The last paragraph says the function question 'remains unsettled.'

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Findings about what new neurons do in rodents are unlikely to hold for the human brain.
The 2018 study that found immature neurons in old age probably used tissue that was preserved too slowly.
The carbon-14 estimates probably overstate how many neurons the adult human hippocampus adds.
Knowing how many neurons the adult human hippocampus adds would not settle whether those neurons influence mood.
The benefits of exercise and antidepressants are probably unrelated to new neurons.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says whether the human supply 'contributes measurably to memory or mood ... remains unsettled' and that the carbon-14 estimates 'indicate how many neurons are added, not what they do,' so a count would not settle the effect on mood, as D says. A is the near miss: the author says function is known mainly from rodents and is unsettled in humans, but never that rodent findings are unlikely to apply; 'unsettled' is not 'unlikely.' B reverses the preservation explanation, since delay destroys markers and would lower counts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, both sentences; paragraph 3 for the preservation details.

breakdown.analysis: What's the author's last move? We know function mostly from rodents; in humans it's unsettled; carbon-14 tells how many, not what they do. So a count wouldn't answer whether new neurons affect mood. Watch the near miss that turns 'we don't know whether it carries over' into 'it probably doesn't.'

choices.note: Tempting, since the author does stress that function is known mostly from rodents. But the claim is that the human question 'remains unsettled,' not that rodent findings probably fail. Wrong degree.
Reverses the mechanism. Markers break down after death, so slow preservation would make immature neurons look rarer, not more common.
The author never questions the carbon-14 counts; the point is that they show numbers, not function.
CORRECT. 'How many neurons are added, not what they do' plus 'memory or mood ... remains unsettled.'
Too strong. The author cautions against confident application, not that the link is probably absent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the explanation that has been offered for the conflicting results reported in 2018?
choices: Some of the proteins used as markers of immature neurons are also found in certain glial cells of the adult brain.
On average, the group that reported immature neurons persisting into old age waited longer before preserving its tissue than the other group did.
When samples from a single human brain are preserved after different delays, fewer cells display the immature-neuron markers the longer the delay.
In rodents, the proteins used to mark immature neurons remain detectable in brain tissue for many hours after death.
The later study that controlled preservation delays examined tissue from more brains than either 2018 study did.
questions.explanation: The explanation holds that the groups differed in how long tissue sat before preservation and that marker proteins 'break down quickly after death.' C confirms that mechanism: within a single brain, longer delays mean fewer marked cells, so a delay difference could produce the opposite results. B is the main trap: it names a delay difference between the groups, but in the wrong direction; under the mechanism, the group with longer delays should have found fewer immature neurons, not more, so B would undercut the explanation. A offers a different source of error, and D, about rodents, if anything suggests the markers are durable.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best supports the claim that preservation delays caused the 2018 conflict.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, the sentence beginning 'The conflict has since been traced in part.'

breakdown.analysis: What's the mechanism? Markers break down after death, so tissue that waits longer shows fewer immature neurons. The group that found almost none should, on this story, be the one with longer delays. Now apply it. An answer that gives the delay difference to the wrong group looks like support but actually cuts against the explanation. The best support confirms the causal link itself.

choices.note: A different source of error, echoing the glial problem from paragraph 1. It wouldn't explain why the two groups disagreed.
The strongest trap: it names exactly the kind of difference the explanation needs, but backward. Longer delays should mean fewer marked cells, yet this group found more. That weakens the explanation.
CORRECT. Same brain, only the delay differs, and marked cells drop as delay grows. That confirms the mechanism, making a delay difference between labs a plausible cause of their opposite results.
If anything this suggests the markers are durable, and it's about rodents, not human tissue.
Sample size has nothing to do with whether delays explain the conflict.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: whether the political accountability of agencies is a sound reason for courts to accept agencies' readings of statutes
the reasons the Supreme Court gave in 2024 for abandoning a framework it had followed for four decades
the history of a framework for judicial review from its adoption in 1984 to its abandonment in 2024
whether reviewing courts should adopt an agency's reasonable reading of an unclear statute that the agency administers
how the phrase "stationary source" in the Clean Air Act ought to be construed
questions.explanation: Passage A defends the practice of accepting an agency's reasonable reading of an ambiguous statute, and passage B argues against it, so D states their shared concern. A is the near miss: both passages discuss accountability (passage A as a justification, passage B as a cost), but it is one consideration among several, and passage B's opening argument from the Administrative Procedure Act has nothing to do with it. C is a content-versus-purpose trap: both passages mention dates (1984, four decades, 2024), but neither is a history; each uses the framework's history only as background for an argument. B fits only passage B, which does not even report the Court's reasons.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the topic both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of passage A, the first paragraph of passage B, and the overall direction of each.

breakdown.analysis: What question do both authors answer? Should courts defer to an agency's reasonable reading of an ambiguous statute? A says yes; B says no. Two traps are built from things that really appear in both passages: accountability, and the framework's dates. A 'primarily concerned with' answer must cover the whole debate, not one argument inside it.

choices.note: Tempting, because accountability appears in both passages. But it's one reason in the debate, and passage B's first argument (the statute's text) isn't about accountability at all. Too narrow.
Only passage B mentions the 2024 decision, and it doesn't report the Court's reasons. 'True of one passage only' trap.

Tempting, because passage A dates the framework to 1984 and passage B reports its 2024 abandonment. But those dates are background; both passages argue about whether deference is justified. Content, not purpose.
CORRECT. Passage A defends deference to reasonable agency readings; passage B attacks it.
'Stationary source' is an example in passage A only.

questions.stem: The language that passage B quotes from the Administrative Procedure Act is most directly at odds with which one of the following features of the Chevron framework as passage A describes it?
choices: its directing a court first to determine whether Congress had directly addressed the precise question at issue
its requiring courts, in some cases, to let stand interpretations of a statute that they themselves consider mistaken
its reliance on agencies' accountability to the electorate through the President
its tendency to produce a single nationwide interpretation of a statutory provision
its treatment of an entire industrial plant as a single source of pollution
questions.explanation: The quoted provision directs a reviewing court to 'decide all relevant questions of law,' and passage B says it leaves no room for adopting an agency's reading 'merely because it is reasonable'; passage A says that under Chevron a court accepted a reasonable agency reading 'even one the court would not itself have chosen.' Combining the two, the conflict is with B. A is the near miss: it is a real feature of the framework, but at that step the court itself decides what Congress said, which the APA language endorses. C and D are passage A's rationales for deference, which passage B answers with policy arguments, not with the statutory text, and E is the example the doctrine arose from, not a feature of the framework.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Connect passage B's statutory quotation to the specific part of the Chevron framework it conflicts with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of passage A (the two steps) and the first paragraph of passage B (the APA quotation).

breakdown.analysis: What does the APA language demand? That the court itself 'decide all relevant questions of law.' Which part of Chevron, as passage A describes it, has the court not deciding? Step two, where it accepts a reasonable agency reading 'even one the court would not itself have chosen.' So the clash is with deferring to readings the court thinks wrong. Step one is a trap: it's a real feature, but there the court does decide the question.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's a genuine feature of the framework. But at this step the court decides for itself what Congress said, which is just what the APA language asks of courts. No conflict.
CORRECT. The APA tells courts to decide questions of law themselves; Chevron's second step had them accept a reasonable agency reading even when they would have read the statute differently.
This is a reason passage A gives for deference, not a feature of the framework, and passage B answers it with a policy argument about instability, not with the APA.
Also one of passage A's justifications. Passage B weighs it against instability; the APA quotation doesn't address it.
That was the agency's interpretation in the case that named the doctrine, not a feature of the framework.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions that an agency "may announce one reading of a statute and later its opposite" (last paragraph of passage B) primarily in order to
choices: identify a drawback of an agency characteristic that defenders of deference cite in its favor
support the claim that agency expertise bears on facts and consequences rather than on the meaning of statutes
show that agencies are less responsive to the electorate than defenders of deference suppose
show that agencies' changing interpretations produce instability of a kind that the Supreme Court can resolve
support the claim that the Administrative Procedure Act forbids agencies to change an interpretation of a statute once they have announced it
questions.explanation: Passage B introduces the point with 'the political accountability said to justify deference carries a cost seldom acknowledged,' and shifting readings are that cost, so A describes the move. D is the near miss built from passage B's own words in the wrong relation: the passage says the Supreme Court can resolve 'disagreement among the lower courts,' and it contrasts that with agency instability, which no such resolution cures. C reverses the logic, since the shifts happen because agencies do answer to each new administration, and B attaches the point to the previous sentence's argument about expertise.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why passage B brings up agencies reversing their readings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last paragraph of passage B, from 'Moreover, the political accountability' to the end.

breakdown.analysis: Read the setup: 'the political accountability said to justify deference carries a cost seldom acknowledged.' The cost is that the law changes with each administration though the statute doesn't. So the flip-flop is the downside of a trait deference's defenders praise. The trap borrows 'the Supreme Court can resolve' from the last sentence, but that clause is about lower-court disagreement, the thing B contrasts with agency instability.

choices.note: CORRECT. Accountability is cited to justify deference, and passage B shows its cost.
Expertise is the previous sentence's point; 'Moreover' starts a new one about accountability.
Reverses the logic. Agencies flip because they are responsive to each new administration.

Tempting, because it uses the last sentence's words. But the Supreme Court resolves 'disagreement among the lower courts,' and B sets that against agency instability, which is the worse problem precisely because no such fix exists. Wrong relation.
Passage B quotes the APA on what courts must do, not on what agencies may do.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A presents the reasoning behind a legal doctrine; passage B reports the doctrine's later abandonment and endorses the court's reasoning without addressing the practical considerations passage A raises.
Passage A defends a legal doctrine on practical grounds; passage B accepts those grounds but argues that a statute nonetheless forbids the doctrine.
Passage A offers a justification for a legal doctrine; passage B rejects the doctrine, partly by disputing the weight of the considerations that justification invokes.
Passage A argues that a legal doctrine should be abandoned; passage B reports that a court later abandoned it.
Both passages are primarily historical accounts of a legal doctrine, passage A of its origins and passage B of its abandonment.
questions.explanation: Passage A defends deference by appeal to expertise, accountability, and consistency, and passage B argues against it both on statutory grounds and by reweighing those considerations ('The policy case for deference is weaker than it appears'), so C is correct. A is a near miss that fits passage B's first paragraph but fails on its second, which addresses exactly those practical considerations. B is another: passage B does make a statutory argument, but it disputes passage A's practical grounds rather than accepting them. D reverses passage A's stance, and E mistakes the passages' historical content for their purpose: each uses a date or a decision as background to an argument.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second and third paragraphs of passage A and both paragraphs of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: A defends deference with practical reasons. B attacks it, first with the statute, then by saying 'the policy case for deference is weaker than it appears' and reweighing expertise, accountability, and uniformity. So B opposes A's doctrine partly by reassessing A's kind of reasons. Two traps describe only B's first paragraph: one says B never engages A's practical points, the other says B accepts them. B's second paragraph sinks both.

choices.note: Tempting, since B's first paragraph does report the 2024 decision and its statutory argument. But B's second paragraph addresses the practical considerations head on (expertise, accountability, consistency). 'Without addressing' is false.
Tempting, since B really does argue from the statute. But B doesn't accept A's practical grounds; it says the policy case 'is weaker than it appears.' Half right is wrong.
CORRECT. A justifies; B rejects, partly by disputing the weight of expertise, accountability, and consistency.
Reverses passage A, which defends the doctrine.
Content-versus-purpose trap. Passage A mentions the 1984 decision and passage B the 2024 one, but both are arguments about whether courts should defer, not histories.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: agencies possess expertise relevant to the statutes they administer
disagreement among the federal circuits over the meaning of a statute imposes any real burden on the parties it regulates
Congress is frequently unable to foresee the particular questions that will arise under the regulatory statutes it enacts
agencies are answerable to the electorate through the President in a way that federal judges are not
choosing among plausible readings of an unclear statute calls mainly for judgments that courts are ill equipped to make
questions.explanation: Passage A says choosing among readings of a statutory gap 'is seldom a purely legal exercise' and is better done by agencies than by judges; passage B says interpreting statutes 'is what courts do' and that agency expertise bears on facts and consequences, 'not on the meaning of the words,' so they disagree over E. B is the near miss: passage B says regulated parties have 'more to fear' from instability than from circuit disagreement, which ranks that burden lower without denying it. Both authors accept A and D, and passage B is silent on C.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would affirm and the other would deny.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 of passage A and both paragraphs of passage B.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. A: choosing among readings of a gap is mostly a policy call judges are poorly placed to make. B: interpretation is the courts' job; expertise doesn't bear on meaning. Clean yes/no. Check the near miss: does B deny circuit splits burden anyone? No, it just says instability is worse.

choices.note: Both agree: 'Agencies' expertise is real.'

Tempting, since the passages weigh this cost differently. But B only says parties have 'more to fear' from instability than from 'occasional disagreement.' That ranks the burden lower; it doesn't deny it. 'Any real burden' is a claim B never rejects.
Only passage A addresses this. Silence isn't disagreement.
Both accept it; B treats accountability to each new administration as real, just costly.
CORRECT. A: 'seldom a purely legal exercise,' better done by agencies than judges. B: interpreting statutes is what courts do; expertise doesn't bear on meaning.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the relationship between reviewing courts and agencies that the author of passage B regards as appropriate?
choices: A homeowner adopts any design recommendation by her architect that is not unreasonable, though she can dismiss the architect at any time.
An editor declines to read specialist reviewers' comments on a manuscript, holding that the decision to publish is hers alone.
A trial judge facing a technical question appoints an engineer to study it and adopts the engineer's conclusions unless they are clearly mistaken.
A judge deciding what a disputed clause in a building contract requires reaches her own conclusion after weighing engineers' testimony about its likely effects.
A city council puts a disputed zoning question to a referendum and adopts whichever option wins.
questions.explanation: Passage B holds that courts must decide questions of law themselves while 'giving careful consideration to an agency's informed view,' whose expertise bears on 'the likely consequences of competing rules'; in D the judge decides the clause's meaning herself after weighing experts' testimony about its effects. C is the closest trap: it has a judge and an expert, but the judge adopts the expert's conclusions unless clearly mistaken, which is deference of the kind passage A defends. A is passage A's model as well, and B drops the careful consideration passage B endorses.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation whose structure matches the court-agency relationship passage B favors.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph of passage B ('nothing prevents a court from giving careful consideration to an agency's informed view').

breakdown.analysis: What does passage B want? Two elements: (1) the court decides the legal question itself, and (2) it weighs the expert's informed view without being bound by it. The right analogy needs both. The judge-and-engineer trap looks right on the surface but builds in deference: 'unless clearly mistaken' is a cousin of 'unless unreasonable.'

choices.note: Adopting any recommendation that's 'not unreasonable' is passage A's deference model.
Gets element (1) but drops (2): passage B wants careful consideration, not refusal to read.
The strongest trap: same cast (judge, engineer). But adopting the expert's conclusions 'unless clearly mistaken' is deference, the thing passage B rejects.
CORRECT. The judge decides for herself (1) after weighing expert testimony about consequences (2).
Decision by popular vote: neither element.

questions.stem: The author of passage A would be most likely to respond to the claim in passage B that agency expertise bears "not on the meaning of the words Congress enacted" by asserting that
choices: an agency's accountability to the electorate through the President makes its reading of a statute more legitimate than a court's
deciding what an ambiguous provision means can turn on weighing practical effects of the kind expert knowledge illuminates
courts gave careful consideration to agencies' views of statutes long before the Chevron framework was adopted
a single nationwide reading of a statute is worth more to the parties it regulates than a reading that is more accurate linguistically
the meaning of a statute's words is fixed when it is enacted and cannot be altered by later administrations
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that choosing among readings of a statutory gap 'is seldom a purely legal exercise,' as in the 'stationary source' question, which 'turned less on grammar than on how to balance cleaner air against economic growth'; on that view expertise about consequences does bear on meaning, as B says. A and D are near misses built from passage A's other arguments (accountability and consistency): passage A would accept them in some form, but neither answers the specific claim that expertise is irrelevant to meaning. C is passage B's own point, and E would undercut passage A.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how passage A's author would answer the claim that expertise doesn't bear on meaning.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2 of passage A ('seldom a purely legal exercise' and the 'stationary source' example); the second paragraph of passage B for the claim.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B splits facts and consequences (where expertise helps) from meaning (where it doesn't). Would A accept the split? No: for A, settling what a gap means 'turned less on grammar than on how to balance cleaner air against economic growth.' Deciding meaning is often weighing consequences, which is exactly where expertise counts. Two traps restate A's other reasons for deference. They're things A believes, but they don't answer this claim. The question is 'respond to this claim,' not 'what else does A think.'

choices.note: Tempting, because passage A does cite accountability. But accountability is a separate reason, and it doesn't answer the claim that expertise is irrelevant to meaning. 'More legitimate than a court's' also goes beyond what A says.
CORRECT. A treats filling a gap as a judgment about practical effects, so expertise about consequences does bear on what the statute comes to mean.
That's passage B's own point, which supports B.
Tempting, because A values a single nationwide rule. But that's the consistency argument, not a response to the expertise claim, and A never ranks it against linguistic accuracy.
This would hurt A: if meaning were fixed at enactment, agency judgment would matter less.
